sections.heading: The components, the roles and the limits that apply to each
paragraphs: The current course asks students to work as researcher, performer and creator across four areas of inquiry, and to submit evidence in defined components. Exploring music in context combines written work with supporting musical material. Experimenting with music documents a student's own experimentation with excerpts of the results. Presenting music is a selection of material accompanied by written programme notes. Higher Level adds a project rooted in a real-life context, presented as a continuous audio-visual piece with a report.

Each component has limits on words, durations or quantities, and they are specified rather than advisory. The exact figures should be confirmed with your school's music teacher or IB coordinator against the current subject guide, because the course was revised relatively recently and a good deal of material circulating online describes the previous one. That is not a disclaimer for its own sake: planning a portfolio around an obsolete requirement is a real and recurring loss, and online sources for this subject are unusually unreliable.

The structural trap is breadth. A student who loves one repertoire will evidence one area of inquiry superbly and the others barely at all. A pianist who works entirely on Western art music, or a producer who works entirely in a digital audio workstation, will produce a submission with a visible hole in it. Tracking coverage across the year is dull, takes five minutes a fortnight, and is the difference between a balanced portfolio and a lopsided one.

The second trap is the role nobody practises. Most Dubai Diploma musicians are confident performers, competent researchers once taught, and genuinely inexperienced creators. Creating material and then explaining the decisions behind it is uncomfortable, so it gets postponed, and postponement in this component is fatal because the evidence has to be produced in real time to be documentable at all.

sections.heading: Links asserted against links evidenced: where the written marks actually go
paragraphs: The single most common weakness in Diploma Music written work is the asserted link. A student writes that a piece 'reflects the political tensions of its time' or that a track 'uses technology to create atmosphere', and believes a connection to an area of inquiry has been made. Nothing has been evidenced. An evidenced link names what is audible, says where in the material it occurs, and explains the mechanism by which it does what the student claims.

The repair is mechanical and teachable. For every claim, three things must appear: a locatable moment, a described musical feature, and a consequence. 'The texture thins from bar 54, leaving the vocal unaccompanied for eight bars, which isolates the lyric at the point the text turns to direct address' is evidence. 'The arrangement creates emotional impact' is not. Students generally produce the second kind, and one session spent converting six sentences from the second kind to the first changes their whole register.

Sources are the second front. Research in this subject means citable material: scholarly writing, liner notes with an author, documented interviews, archival material. It does not mean an anonymous blog or a video with no attribution. Dubai students often research in English only, which narrows the available context for regional repertoire considerably, when Arabic-language sources on maqam practice and Khaleeji traditions are available and far less picked over.

The third front is the programme notes, which carry a tight word limit and are consistently misused. Students write what the pieces are. The notes should justify why this material, in this order, for this context, and what a listener is being invited to notice. Within a small word budget every sentence that merely identifies a work is a sentence that could have done something.

sections.heading: Recording, scoring and submitting audio from a Dubai apartment
paragraphs: Because so much evidence in this subject arrives as audio and notation files, the technical side is part of the academic side, and it is the part most Dubai students have never been taught. A performance recorded badly sounds worse than it was played. A score exported as a phone photograph of a screen is harder to read than it needs to be. Neither is a musical failing and both cost marks indirectly, because an assessor can only work with what arrives.

Dubai interiors create specific problems. Newer apartment stock in Arjan, Dubailand and the Marina towers has hard surfaces, large glazed areas and little soft furnishing, which produces bright, slapback reflections that smear detail. Air conditioning adds a constant low-frequency bed that a phone microphone handles poorly. The practical fixes cost nothing: record away from parallel hard walls, put soft material behind the microphone position, turn the air conditioning off for the take, and keep the microphone closer than instinct suggests.

Consistency matters as much as quality. A submission in which three recordings are mono phone captures and one is a stereo interface recording looks accidental. Choosing one workflow and repeating it across every file is more useful than chasing the best possible single take. Levels should be checked so nothing clips and nothing is so quiet that the assessor has to compensate, and file naming should make clear which evidence supports which claim.

Notation and digital audio workstation work should be exported as intended rather than screenshotted. A legible score as a document, a stem or bounce at a sensible bit rate, and a short written note saying what the listener should hear. Apartment living also pushes many Dubai students towards headphone and digital workflows, which is perfectly legitimate evidence for the music-technology area of inquiry and worth framing as a deliberate choice rather than an apology.

sections.heading: The Higher Level project: finding a real-life context in Dubai
paragraphs: Higher Level students take on an additional project rooted in a real-life musical context, presented as a continuous audio-visual piece with a report alongside it. The requirement that catches students out is the word real: the project needs a genuine context with genuine constraints, not a hypothetical scenario invented to fit an idea the student already had. A project described as 'composing music for a film' with no film, no director and no brief is a project with nothing to respond to.

Dubai is unusually rich in workable contexts, and students systematically overlook them. The emirate runs a continuous calendar of events, community performances, school productions, and festival and exhibition programming. There are venues from Dubai Opera down to community arts spaces, student film-making in Studio City and Media City, independent recording studios, charity and community organisations that need music for events, and a large expatriate community sustaining musical traditions from a dozen countries. Any of those supplies a brief, a client, a deadline and a constraint.

The strongest projects we see in this emirate tend to come from genuine cultural intersection: arranging a traditional repertoire for an available ensemble, producing music for a student film with a real director and a real cut, documenting and working with a community tradition with the community's consent, or building something for a specific venue with specific limitations. All of those generate the decisions the report needs to explain.

Two cautions. Consent and credit are not optional when other people are involved, particularly when a project documents a living tradition or uses other musicians' playing. And the project has to be scoped to finish: ambitious projects that collapse in February produce no presentation at all, which is a worse outcome than a modest project completed well. The scoping conversation belongs in DP1, not after the first attempt has already failed.

sections.heading: Dubai's musical infrastructure, and the regional repertoire nobody uses
paragraphs: Diploma Music rewards breadth across the areas of inquiry, and students in this emirate have access to source material that students elsewhere would find difficult to reach. Khaleeji musical traditions, the maqam system of Arab art music, the oud and qanun repertoire, and the devotional and ceremonial musics present across the UAE's communities all supply exactly the kind of culturally contextualised material the course asks for. South Asian classical and film-music traditions are present in depth across Dubai too, with practitioners and teachers who are reachable.

What makes this an advantage rather than a nice idea is examiner fatigue. A study of a widely taught Western canon piece has been read many times. A rigorous analysis of maqam structure in a named recording, with Arabic-language sources and an interview with a practitioner, is both more interesting and easier to make original. The barrier is usually that students research in English only and so never find the material, which is a solvable problem in a city where the language is spoken everywhere.

On the practical side, Dubai has venues, school ensembles, community choirs, peripatetic teaching networks, independent studios, and a graded-exam infrastructure through boards operating locally. For a Diploma student the useful thing about all of this is access: to performers for a creator-role project, to a venue with constraints for a Higher Level project, to practitioners who can be interviewed as primary sources rather than cited from a website.

The caution is about accuracy. Writing about a tradition that is not your own carries a responsibility to get it right and to name sources, and a page of confident generalisation about Arab music is worse than a careful paragraph with a citation. Where a student is working with a community's repertoire, consent and acknowledgement are part of doing the work properly, not an administrative extra.

sections.heading: Arrangement, sampling, collaborators and generative audio
paragraphs: Music raises honesty questions that written subjects do not, because almost all musical practice builds on other people's material. The Diploma does not prohibit that. It requires the student's own decisions to be visible and other people's contributions to be credited. Arranging an existing piece is legitimate musical work and the arrangement decisions are exactly what the creator role assesses; presenting someone else's arrangement as your own is not.

Samples and loops sit in the same frame. Using a library loop is normal production practice, and the assessable decisions are what was chosen, how it was processed and why. What fails is a submission in which the loops do all the work and the student's documented decisions amount to importing them. Where other musicians play on a recording, they are named, and where a producer or engineer contributed, that is stated. None of this reduces a mark; concealing it risks the whole submission.

A tutor's boundary is the same as everywhere else and worth repeating plainly. A tutor teaches, questions, marks against published criteria and explains why a paragraph or a passage does not score. A tutor does not compose, arrange, perform on, mix or write any part of a submission. Every note and every word must be the student's own, and any provider offering finished portfolio material is offering a breach whose consequences land on the student.

Generative audio tools are the live question in this subject now. If used at any stage, the use needs declaring and describing, and it cannot stand in for the documented experimentation the course assesses. A student who generates a passage has nothing to document about how it was arrived at, which is a practical reason for caution as well as a rule-based one: the component rewards visible decision-making, and generated material has no visible decisions behind it.

sections.heading: Cost in AED, fortnightly rhythm, availability and delivery
paragraphs: Published figures from other Dubai providers, collected in October 2026, set the context. Budget online help is advertised from roughly AED 45 to 65 an hour. A qualified online subject tutor sits at AED 150 to 300. IB specialists are quoted at AED 200 to 450 and above, and one Dubai provider advertises AED 650 for examiner-level work. In-home visiting in Dubai is published at AED 180 to 500 with travel priced into the hour. IB Gram publishes no rate card here: the trial lesson is free with no card required, and a quote follows the component and the hours.

Fortnightly works better than weekly for this subject, because evidence has to accumulate between reviews. A written work and research block typically runs six to eight sessions. A creator and experimentation cycle runs fortnightly across a year and costs more in total while applying far less pressure per session. A submission and technical audit is one or two sessions placed a fortnight before a school deadline. Buying a generic weekly hour without naming the component is the most expensive way to make the least progress here.

Availability needs stating honestly. Tutors who have marked this course's written components are not numerous anywhere, and demand concentrates in the weeks before school internal deadlines. If nobody suitable is free in the window you need, you will be told that, with the nearest alternative and the rate that would apply, rather than matched to a performance teacher described as a Diploma specialist. No ranking page in this market discloses a coverage limit, which does not mean none exists.

Delivery is fixed. Lessons run online, one to one, over live video, in Gulf Standard Time, with timing moved later during Ramadan by prior agreement. IB Gram does not run in-person lessons in Dubai, and home visits are a service we offer only in India. Anyone providing private tuition inside the UAE needs the MoHRE private tuition work permit introduced under Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, granted free of charge for two years through MoHRE's e-services under 'Issuance of a New Work Permit - Private Tutor Licensing'.

faqs.question: My child has Grade 8 piano. Will Diploma Music be straightforward?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily, and this is the commonest surprise in the subject. Graded exams assess performance of prepared repertoire in a single sitting. Diploma Music assesses evidence: written analysis, documented experimentation, presented material with justification, and at Higher Level a project in a real-life context. Technique, reading fluency and aural skill transfer substantially and are real advantages. What does not transfer is documenting a decision, researching with citable sources, or producing imperfect material and explaining why it changed. Strong players often struggle most, because playing well has always been enough and in this course it is not.

faqs.question: What are the four areas of inquiry in Diploma Music?
faqs.answer: They are the frames that run through the whole course: music for sociocultural and political expression, music for listening and performance, music for dramatic impact, movement and entertainment, and music technology in the electronic and digital age. The mistake students make is treating them as labels to attach to a piece after the fact. They are analytical frames, and a link to one has to be evidenced with a locatable moment in the material, a described musical feature and a consequence. Coverage across all four also has to be tracked, because a student working in one favourite repertoire leaves a visible hole.

faqs.question: What are the three musical roles and does my child have to do all of them?
faqs.answer: Researcher, performer and creator, and yes, evidence is required in all three. Most Dubai Diploma musicians arrive as confident performers, become competent researchers once taught, and are genuinely inexperienced creators. The creator role is the one that gets postponed, which is the worst possible choice, because experimentation has to be documented as it happens to be documentable at all. A student who starts producing and recording short experiments in DP1, with two sentences written the same day about each decision, has a portfolio. One who starts in DP2 has photographs of finished work.

faqs.question: How long should the written work and programme notes be?
faqs.answer: Each component carries a specified limit on words or duration, and the exact figures should be confirmed with your school's music teacher against the current subject guide. This matters more in Music than in most subjects, because the course was revised relatively recently and a lot of material circulating online still describes the previous version. Two practical points regardless of the numbers: draft to the limit rather than cutting to it in the final week, and treat the programme notes word budget as scarce, because every sentence that merely identifies a work is a sentence that achieved nothing.

faqs.question: What does it mean to evidence a link rather than assert one?
faqs.answer: An asserted link sounds like analysis and contains none: 'the piece reflects the political tensions of its era', 'the production creates atmosphere'. An evidenced link names a locatable moment, describes the musical feature, and explains the consequence: 'the texture thins from bar 54, leaving the vocal unaccompanied for eight bars, which isolates the lyric at the point the text turns to direct address'. Students almost always produce the first kind. Converting six sentences from the first kind to the second in a single session is usually the highest-value hour anyone buys in this subject.

faqs.question: Our Dubai apartment makes recordings sound terrible. What can we do without spending money?
faqs.answer: Four changes fix most of it. Move away from parallel hard walls, which is what produces the bright slapback common in newer apartment stock in Arjan, Dubailand and the Marina towers. Put something soft behind the microphone position, even a duvet on a chair. Turn the air conditioning off for the take, because its low-frequency bed is exactly where a phone microphone performs worst. And get the microphone closer than instinct suggests. Consistency then matters more than quality: one workflow repeated across every file beats one excellent recording among three poor ones.

faqs.question: Can my child submit work made entirely on a laptop with headphones?
faqs.answer: Yes, and in a city where acoustic practice is often restricted by community noise expectations it is frequently the sensible route. Digital workflows are legitimate evidence, and they sit naturally with the music technology area of inquiry. What matters is that the decisions are the student's and are documented: what was chosen, how it was processed, why it changed. Library loops and samples are normal production practice, and the assessable work is the selection and treatment rather than the raw material. Frame the digital workflow as a deliberate choice, with reasons, rather than apologising for it.

faqs.question: What counts as a real-life context for the Higher Level project?
faqs.answer: Something with a genuine brief, a genuine constraint and usually a genuine other person. A student film with an actual director and an actual cut. Music for a community event with a date. An arrangement for an ensemble that exists and has a specific instrumentation. A piece built for a particular venue with particular limitations. What fails is a hypothetical: 'music for an imagined film' responds to nothing. Dubai supplies plenty of workable contexts through school productions, student film-making in the media districts, community organisations and venues, and the scoping conversation belongs in DP1.

faqs.question: Should we hire our child's instrumental teacher to help with the Diploma instead?
faqs.answer: Usually not, and an honest instrumental teacher will say the same. Peripatetic teaching in Dubai is often excellent and is aimed at performance: repertoire, technique, graded exam preparation. The Diploma problem is almost always documentation, research and written justification, which is a different skill set. Keep the instrumental teacher for playing and add someone who has marked this course's written components. Also check the professional position: in Abu Dhabi, ADEK's ethics rules bar school staff from paid tutoring of students at their own school, and the MoHRE permit carries a code of conduct.

faqs.question: How much does Diploma Music tutoring cost in Dubai?
faqs.answer: Other Dubai providers published these figures, collected in October 2026: roughly AED 45 to 65 an hour for budget online help, AED 150 to 300 for a qualified online subject tutor, AED 200 to 450 and above for IB specialists, and AED 650 at one provider's examiner level. In-home visiting is advertised at AED 180 to 500 with travel in the hour. What matters more is which component you are funding: a written work block of six to eight sessions prices very differently from a fortnightly experimentation cycle across a year. IB Gram publishes no rate card on this page.

faqs.question: Can a tutor compose or arrange something for my child's portfolio?
faqs.answer: No, and any provider offering to is offering a breach whose consequences fall on your child rather than on them. A tutor teaches, questions, marks against the published criteria and explains why a passage or a paragraph does not score. Nothing is composed, arranged, performed, mixed or written for the student. Where other musicians genuinely play on a recording, or a producer contributed, they are named, and naming them costs no marks. Concealing a contribution risks the whole submission, which is a very poor trade for a slightly better-sounding file.

faqs.question: Is regional music a sensible choice for the research side of this course?
faqs.answer: It is one of the strongest choices available to a student living here, and it is badly under-used. Maqam structure in Arab art music, Khaleeji traditions, oud and qanun repertoire, and the South Asian classical and film-music traditions present across Dubai all supply exactly the culturally contextualised material the course asks for, with practitioners reachable for interview as primary sources. A rigorous analysis of a named recording in one of these traditions is easier to make original than another study of a widely taught canon piece. Accuracy, citation and consent are part of doing it properly.

faqs.question: How often should sessions run, and when in the two years?
faqs.answer: Fortnightly rather than weekly, because evidence has to accumulate between reviews and there needs to be something new to read. The written work and research block belongs in DP1 once the first material exists. The experimentation cycle should run continuously from early DP1, since it depends on documenting decisions in real time. The Higher Level project needs scoping in DP1 before any work starts. Programme notes and the submission audit belong in the final months. Sessions run in Gulf Standard Time, with later timing during Ramadan agreed before the month begins.

faqs.question: My child is in DP2 with almost nothing documented. Is it recoverable?
faqs.answer: Partly, and honesty about which parts matters. Written work and research are the most recoverable, because they depend on material and sources that still exist. Programme notes can be rewritten. What cannot be reconstructed is experimentation that was never documented at the time, and no tutor should pretend otherwise. The practical sequence is to secure the written components first, then document whatever genuine process evidence exists in notebooks, voice memos and project files, and then scope anything outstanding to something that can actually be finished rather than something ambitious that will not.

faqs.question: Does a Diploma Music grade help with a conservatoire or university application?
faqs.answer: It helps as an academic qualification, and conservatoires generally also run their own audition and portfolio requirements assessed separately from the Diploma grade. University music courses vary: some weight the subject heavily, others accept any combination with an audition or portfolio. Courses with specific science or maths prerequisites will look at those subjects instead. Read the entry requirements for the named institution and the named course for the year of entry before DP1 subject selection, rather than relying on an impression, and check audition dates early because they often sit inside the DP2 coursework crunch.

dubai/ib-dp-music-tutor.tutorsIntro: The tutors below work with Diploma Music students in Dubai on the written and recorded components: the portfolio, the process documentation, the selected programme and the Higher Level project. They are matched to the student's instrument, software and school deadlines, not to a general music-teaching brief.

intro.heading: Diploma Music is graded on a folder, not on a concert
paragraphs: A Dubai parent whose child plays well is often surprised by the first real Music mark. The instrument is rarely the problem. Diploma Music asks the student to be a researcher, a creator and a performer, and then marks the documentation of all three. A student can be the strongest cellist in a Jumeirah school orchestra and still submit a thin portfolio, because the portfolio is a piece of writing with musical evidence attached, and nobody has taught them to build one.

That is useful news for a family trying to work out whether support is doing anything. Subjects assessed by a terminal paper give you very little to look at until the mock. Music gives you artefacts. There is a written portfolio with a word limit. There are experiments that are supposed to be captured as they happen. There are recordings with dates on them. At Higher Level there is a project with a real audience. Each of those is a thing you can ask to see, and each of them either exists or does not.

So the question a Dubai family should be asking a Music tutor is not whether the sessions are enjoyable. It is what came out of the last four sessions, where it sits against the criteria the school is using, and what the next four will produce. An IB DP Music tutor in Dubai who cannot answer that in specifics is working on impressions, and impressions are what got the family worried in the first place.

IB Gram works this way because the alternative is unverifiable. We match the student with a Music specialist, the first lesson is free, and the session output is logged: what was reviewed, what the student was asked to redo, what evidence now exists that did not exist last week. Lessons are delivered online over live video so that the specialist can be chosen for the component in trouble rather than for proximity to your neighbourhood. Dubai has deep instrumental teaching and very few people who read Diploma Music criteria for a living.

This page sets out what counts as evidence in Diploma Music, how to read a marked draft, how a school mark becomes a final grade, what the Dubai market charges, and what twelve weeks of real movement looks like. It assumes you are not a musician. It also assumes you have been told everything is fine, and are not convinced. One more thing worth saying early: Diploma Music rewards selection. Students who submit everything they can play, or everything they wrote, score lower than students who submit a defensible subset and explain the choice. Most of the mark movement a Dubai family will see over a term comes from that single shift in habit, and it is a habit a tutor can teach in a handful of sessions rather than a talent anyone has to be born with.
bullets: Standard Level carries three assessed components; Higher Level adds a fourth project worth roughly a third of the grade
The written portfolio and the process documentation carry word limits - over-length work is a predictable loss
Recordings need dates and an index, or they cannot be used as evidence of process
A school's predicted grade is an estimate; the component marks behind it are the thing to request
Online delivery over live video lets a family pick a Diploma Music specialist rather than the nearest available musician

dubai/ib-dp-music-tutor.programmesIntro: Dubai families arrive at Diploma Music from three directions: a Middle Years arts course, an IGCSE or GCSE music qualification, or no formal music study at all beyond instrumental grades. The route changes what the first term of support has to cover.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme Arts
programmes.description: Middle Years Music is assessed on four criteria covering knowing and understanding, developing skills, thinking creatively and responding. Students keep a process journal, which is the closest thing in the IB to the documentation habit Diploma Music later demands. A student who kept that journal properly arrives in Year 12 already able to record a decision and explain why they made it.
programmes.countryNote: Several Dubai schools run the full IB continuum, so a student may move from Middle Years Arts into Diploma Music inside the same building with the same teacher. That continuity helps, but it also means nobody flags the step up in writing demand. The portfolio is longer, the context work is researched rather than described, and the deadlines are externally fixed.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme Music
programmes.description: The Diploma course asks students to work across four areas of inquiry and to take on three roles: researcher, creator and performer. Standard Level submits an exploring-music-in-context portfolio, an experimenting-with-music process portfolio and a presenting-music submission. Higher Level adds the contemporary music maker project, a piece of real-world music making delivered to an audience and documented as a continuous multimedia presentation.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai cohorts are small. A school running Diploma Music may have six students in a year group and one teacher covering the subject alongside Middle Years classes. That is not a criticism of the schools; it is arithmetic. It does mean a student with an unusual instrument, an unfamiliar tradition or a software-based practice can end up without a second opinion inside the building.

programmes.name: Extended Essay in Music
programmes.description: A 4,000-word independent research essay, supervised by a school teacher and assessed externally. A Music Extended Essay has to be answerable with musical evidence, which usually means score study, recorded comparison or fieldwork rather than a general history question. The commonest failure is a title so broad that no amount of listening settles it.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai gives Music Extended Essay candidates genuinely unusual access: resident orchestras, touring programmes, a recording and events industry, and communities whose musical traditions are living practice rather than library material. A narrow local question with primary recordings usually beats a wide question answered from secondary sources.

dubai/ib-dp-music-tutor.subjectsIntro: Diploma Music students in Dubai rarely take Music in isolation. The subjects below are the ones that most often sit either side of it on a timetable, with a note on what each one adds to or takes from the Music workload.

subjects.name: Music
subjects.description: Assessed on the exploring, experimenting and presenting components, with the contemporary music maker project added at Higher Level. Marks are lost on documentation, over-length writing and unselected recordings far more often than on playing.

subjects.name: Visual Arts
subjects.description: The other group 6 subject most Dubai schools run. Shares the documentation habit: a process portfolio, a curated selection, a written commentary. Students who take both arts subjects carry two sets of internal deadlines in the same term.

subjects.name: Theatre
subjects.description: Also marked on submitted documentation rather than live performance. Theatre and Music students often share a school production schedule, which is why their coursework weeks collide in the same fortnight each year.

subjects.name: Film
subjects.description: Useful alongside Music for students interested in sound design and scoring. The comparative study and portfolio demand the same evidence discipline: dated artefacts, sourced claims, a documented process.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: The subject that most directly affects a Music grade, because the Music portfolio is written work. A student who cannot build a paragraph around evidence will lose Music marks for reasons that have nothing to do with music.

subjects.name: Psychology
subjects.description: A common pairing for Dubai arts students. The experimental write-up habit transfers well to the experimenting-with-music component, where the record of what was tried matters more than whether it worked.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: The usual mathematics route for arts-heavy Diploma students in Dubai. Scheduling matters: an Applications student with a Higher Level Music project often needs maths support in the same term the project is due.

subjects.name: Theory of Knowledge
subjects.description: Music supplies some of the most usable Theory of Knowledge material in the Diploma, particularly on evidence and interpretation in the arts. The two can be revised together rather than sequentially.

subjects.name: Arabic as an additional language
subjects.description: Mandatory in Dubai private schools regardless of the licensed curriculum, with class organisation and language-of-instruction rules set out in the KHDA mandatory-subjects guidelines. It occupies timetable space that Music students often assume is free.

subjects.name: Extended Essay
subjects.description: Four thousand words, externally assessed, due in the same window as several Music internal deadlines. Sequencing the two is a planning problem rather than a subject problem, and it is the single most common source of a rushed Music portfolio.

dubai/ib-dp-music-tutor.regionsIntro: Where a family lives in Dubai changes the practical shape of Music support more than the academic content: practice space, instrument access, commute time after school, and how late a session can start in Gulf Standard Time.

regions.name: Jumeirah
regions.note: Villa communities with space for a piano and a practice room, and short runs to the older British and IB schools along Al Wasl Road. Sessions here usually start early, around 16:00, because the school day finishes before the afternoon traffic builds.

regions.name: Al Barsha
regions.note: Dense school cluster and a mix of apartments and villas. Apartment practice constrains recording more than anything else: a submitted performance take recorded at 21:00 through a neighbouring wall is a technical problem, not a musical one.

regions.name: Dubai Marina
regions.note: High-rise living, strong instrumental teaching nearby, and almost no space for percussion or amplified work. Marina students often record in a school music room at lunchtime, which makes the recording calendar dependent on room bookings.

regions.name: Arabian Ranches
regions.note: Villa community with a long school run on Emirates Road and a sizeable Jumeirah English Speaking School cohort. Sessions tend to work better at 17:30 or later, once the car is actually home.

regions.name: Mirdif
regions.note: Established family district feeding several IB and British schools to the east. Practice space is usually available, specialist instrumental teaching less so, which is why Mirdif families more often need an online specialist for the written components.

regions.name: Dubai Silicon Oasis
regions.note: Newer apartment and villa mix close to Academic City and the IB continuum schools around it. Reliable connectivity and a short school run make a weekday 16:30 session straightforward here.

regions.name: Umm Suqeim
regions.note: Older low-rise area near the beach schools, with several students taking conservatoire-style instrumental lessons alongside the Diploma. The gap is almost always the portfolio writing rather than the playing.

regions.name: Dubai Hills Estate
regions.note: Fast-growing community with new school capacity and young Diploma cohorts. Small Music classes here mean a student's work may be the only example of its kind in the year group, so an outside second reading is worth more than usual.

schoolClusters.city: Central and coastal Dubai
schoolClusters.note: The older IB cohorts sit along the Jumeirah and Al Barsha corridor. Music provision varies widely between these schools: some run a full ensemble programme with recording facilities, others deliver Diploma Music with one teacher and a shared practice room. Ask which it is before assuming the school can absorb a portfolio crisis in March.

schoolClusters.city: Eastern and new-growth Dubai
schoolClusters.note: Schools around Mirdif, Academic City, Dubai Festival City and the newer southern communities. Several run the IB continuum, so Music students may have come through Middle Years Arts in the same building. Cohorts are small and often include students whose instrument nobody else in the school plays.

dubai/ib-dp-music-tutor.modesIntro: Three shapes of support cover almost every Diploma Music request we take from Dubai. All three are delivered one to one over live video; the difference is the unit of work, not the delivery.

modes.title: Weekly one-to-one across the two years

The session follows whatever the student produced that week: an experiment log, a draft paragraph, a take of a performance. The output is dated and kept, so by the time a school deadline arrives the portfolio already exists in rough form.

sections.heading: What counts as evidence in Diploma Music, and what only resembles it
paragraphs: Evidence is something a third party could inspect and reach the same conclusion from. In Diploma Music that means a dated artefact tied to a component: a portfolio draft with a word count, a logged experiment with a note on what was being tested, a recording with a date and an index entry, a project plan with an audience and a venue. Everything else is testimony, and testimony is what families are usually given.

The distinction matters in Dubai because the feedback loop is long. Internal deadlines are set by the school, and schools set them differently; some want the exploring portfolio complete by the end of Year 12, others run it into the second year. A family relying on report-card language can go eight months without learning that the experimenting component has no documented process behind it. By the time that surfaces, the work cannot be reconstructed, because process evidence has to be captured while the process happens.

The table below is the one we use in a first session. The left column is what families are usually shown. The right column is what to ask for instead. Asking is not an act of distrust; most Dubai music teachers will produce component-level marks immediately if someone asks a specific question rather than a general one. The question that works is narrow: which component is currently weakest, and against which criterion. The question that produces a vague answer is the broad one about how the student is getting on, because a teacher with a full timetable will answer it in the same broad register it was asked in.

sections.heading: Reading a marked Music draft: the phrases and what each one is pointing at
paragraphs: Music teachers write in a shorthand that is clear to colleagues and opaque to parents. Three comments account for most of the written feedback a Dubai Diploma Music student receives, and each one has a specific fix. Knowing which fix is being requested is the difference between a redraft that moves marks and a redraft that reorganises sentences.

'Needs more analysis of context' almost never means add more history. It means the claim being made about the music is not evidenced from the music itself. A student who writes that a work reflects political tension in a given decade has made an assertion; a student who points to a specific passage, names what is happening in it and connects that to the context has made an argument. The repair is nearly always to go back to the score or the recording and find the bar numbers.

'Where is the process?' is a different problem and a more expensive one. It means the submitted work shows a result without the trail that produced it. In the experimenting component the trail is the assessed thing. If a student tried four approaches to a rhythmic idea and kept only the one that worked, the three discarded attempts were the marks. Rebuilding that honestly after the fact is not possible, which is why documentation has to be a weekly habit rather than a deadline activity.

'Over length' is the cheapest fix available and the one students resist most. A portfolio above its word limit does not gain credit for the extra material. Cutting to length forces selection, and selection is itself assessed. A tutor's most useful hour is often spent removing a third of a draft while the student defends each paragraph and discovers which ones they cannot justify.
bullets: Ask for the criterion letter or descriptor behind every comment, not just the comment
Treat bar numbers, timings and track positions as the currency of a Music argument
Capture process weekly; it cannot be reconstructed at the deadline
Cut to the limit before polishing, never after

sections.heading: The components, their weightings and the limits attached to each
paragraphs: Standard Level Music submits three components and Higher Level submits four. On the current Diploma Music course, Standard Level weights the exploring-music-in-context portfolio and the experimenting-with-music process portfolio at roughly 30% each, with the presenting-music submission at around 40%. Higher Level redistributes: the first two sit near 20% each, presenting music near 30%, and the contemporary music maker project carries the remaining 30%.

Each component has limits. The exploring portfolio is capped in words and accompanied by short musical excerpts of the student's own creating and performing. The experimenting process portfolio is shorter in words but demands recorded evidence of the experiments themselves. The presenting submission is a selected programme with supporting notes rather than everything the student can play. The Higher Level project is documented as a continuous multimedia presentation with a defined maximum length.

Those limits are set in the subject guide, and the guide is revised. The figures above are the course structure as published for the current cohort; the exact word counts, timings and internal deadlines for your child's year group should be confirmed with the school's IB coordinator, who holds the version the cohort is being assessed against. Any tutor who quotes limits without asking which guide the school is using is guessing. A Dubai family can ask for the component summary sheet at a parents' evening and get the authoritative answer in two minutes, and it is worth doing in Year 12 rather than discovering a limit in the week a draft is due.

sections.heading: Twelve weeks of evidence: what real movement looks like week by week
paragraphs: A family asking whether tutoring is working after two sessions is asking too early; after two terms, too late. Twelve weeks is the honest unit. It is long enough for a component to be rebuilt and short enough that a family can hold the plan in their head. Below is the pattern a Dubai Diploma Music student typically follows when the exploring portfolio is the problem, which it usually is.

The first fortnight produces no new music at all. It produces an inventory: what exists, what has a date on it, what the school has marked, where the word counts sit, which component is weakest against the criteria. Families sometimes find this frustrating. It is also the only part of the process that cannot be skipped, because the alternative is working on whichever component feels most urgent rather than the one costing the most marks.

From week three the pattern is produce, mark, redo. Each session takes in something the student made since the last one, reads it against the criterion in question, and sends them away with one specific repair. The artefacts accumulate with dates attached, which is what gives a parent something to look at. By week twelve there should be a portfolio section the student can defend line by line, a set of experiments with a documented process, and a clear statement of which component is now the weakest. That last item is the one families forget to ask for, and it is what decides whether the next twelve weeks are worth buying at all.

sections.heading: From school mark to final grade: who decides what, and when it can still change
paragraphs: Parents often assume the IB marks everything. For Diploma Music it does not. The coursework components are marked inside the school by the teacher who taught them, against IB criteria, and those marks are then subject to external moderation. Understanding that sequence tells a family when a conversation is still useful and when it is not.

The practical consequence is that the window for influence is early and internal. Once a submission has gone, the student's mark is fixed relative to the cohort; moderation can move a whole school's marks up or down for consistency, but it does not re-mark an individual against a different standard. A family that wants to affect a Music grade has to act while drafts are still drafts. That is an argument for starting support in Year 12 rather than in the spring of Year 13.

It also changes what a tutor is for. A tutor cannot negotiate with a moderator and should never claim access to marking standards or boundaries. What a tutor can do is read a draft against published criteria before the internal deadline, which is the only point at which the mark is genuinely movable. After results, the route is an enquiry upon results requested through the school, not through any tutoring provider. Any tutor implying otherwise is selling something that does not exist. The honest framing for a Dubai family is therefore a calendar one: support bought in September of Year 12 can change the artefacts, support bought in May of Year 13 can only change how the student feels about them.

sections.heading: What Diploma Music support costs in Dubai, and what moves the number
paragraphs: Three of the six most visible tutoring pages for Dubai publish no price at all, and the two that do quote in US dollars. That is not useful to a family budgeting in dirhams. The figures below are market rates published by providers operating in Dubai as of October 2026, with the provider named. They are the market, not an IB Gram price list; our own model starts with a free trial lesson and a conversation about how many hours the component in question actually needs.

Arts subjects sit at the upper end of the specialist band for a structural reason. The pool of people who can read Diploma Music criteria and also discuss notation, production software and performance selection is small in any city. In Dubai it is small enough that proximity-based matching usually fails: a family in Mirdif looking for someone who can work on an experimenting portfolio is not choosing between five candidates within a twenty-minute drive.

What moves the number is mostly structure rather than subject. Higher Level costs more than Standard Level because there is a fourth component to document. Exam-year support costs more than Year 12 support because the work is more urgent and the sessions are longer. In-home visits add travel, and in Dubai that means a surcharge on every session rather than a one-off. Group sessions are cheaper per student and almost useless for a component built around one student's own creative output.

sections.heading: The Dubai calendar: when Music evidence actually has to exist
paragraphs: Diploma Music deadlines are internal, which means they are set by your child's school and vary between schools in the same neighbourhood. The IB sets the session and the upload windows; the school decides when drafts are due so that it can mark, standardise and submit in time. Anyone publishing a specific IB exam or results date without checking it against the IB directly is guessing, and we do not. Confirm every date with the school's IB coordinator.

What is predictable is the shape of the Dubai year. The first term is long and relatively uninterrupted, which makes it the cheapest time to build documentation habits. The second term carries the school production season in many Dubai schools, and Music students are the people in it. Rehearsal weeks remove exactly the evening hours that portfolio work needs, and they arrive at the same time as Theatre and Visual Arts internal deadlines.

Ramadan shifts the working day. School hours shorten, afternoons get slower, and families often prefer sessions after Iftar. That is workable online: a 21:00 Gulf Standard Time session is straightforward when the tutor is not driving across the city to reach it. The practical planning rule is to front-load written work into the first term and reserve the lighter weeks for recording, which needs a quiet house more than it needs a fresh brain. Summer is the other underused window: a student who logs two or three experiments in July arrives in Year 13 with evidence nobody had to chase.
bullets: Get the school's internal deadline calendar in writing in September, not in February
Expect production season and arts coursework deadlines to collide; plan the collision
Keep recording for weeks when the house is quiet rather than weeks when the diary is empty
Post-Iftar sessions during Ramadan are normal and easy to timetable online

sections.heading: Honesty, software and whose music is being assessed
paragraphs: Diploma Music sits awkwardly with academic-honesty rules because so much modern practice involves other people's material: loops, samples, generative tools, backing tracks, arrangements of existing works. The rules are not mysterious, but they are specific, and a student who breaches them loses more than marks. Anything not created by the student has to be identified as such, with its source, wherever it appears in a submission.

The tutor boundary is equally specific. A Music tutor teaches, questions, models technique and gives feedback on work the student has made. A tutor does not compose for a student, does not record a take for them, does not edit a portfolio into its final state, and does not supply material that will be submitted as the student's own. We say this plainly because the market around these searches includes operators who sell completed coursework. That is malpractice under IB rules and it puts the student's whole diploma at risk, not just one grade.

Generative audio tools are the live question in Dubai classrooms. The safe position is that any tool used in the making of a submission should be declared and described, and that the assessed musical thinking has to be the student's. A tutor's job there is to help a student articulate what they decided and why, which is also the part the criteria reward. Schools are writing their own policies on this; the school's policy is the one that binds the student.
bullets: Every borrowed loop, sample or arrangement needs attribution inside the submission
A tutor gives feedback on the student's own work and produces none of it
Declare any generative tool used and describe what the student decided
The school's academic-honesty policy, not a tutor's view, is the binding document

process.title: Tell us the component, not just the subject
process.description: A message saying the exploring portfolio is due in three weeks and the school has flagged weak contextual evidence gets a better match than one saying Music help needed. The component, the level and the school's deadline are the three facts that determine who can usefully take the student.

process.title: Free trial lesson with the work in front of us
process.description: The first session is free and is spent on the student's existing material: a draft, a recording, a set of teacher comments. The tutor says where it sits against the criteria and what the first repair is. If that reading is not useful, nothing has been spent.

process.title: Agree a twelve-week shape
process.description: Sessions are booked around the school's internal deadlines with a stated output per fortnight. The plan names which component is being worked on and what artefact should exist by when, so the family can check progress against something concrete rather than a feeling.

process.title: Session notes you can read
process.description: After each session the family gets a short written note: what was reviewed, what the student was asked to redo, what now exists. Those notes are the audit trail. They are also what makes a conversation with the school's Music teacher specific rather than anxious.

process.title: Reassess at the deadline
process.description: When the school marks the component, we compare that mark with the plan and decide what happens next: continue on the same component, move to the next weakest, or stop. Stopping is a legitimate outcome and we will say so when the work is done.

whyPoints.title: Specialists chosen for the component
whyPoints.description: A student stuck on process documentation needs a different conversation from one stuck on performance selection. Matching online means choosing the person who has read those criteria recently rather than the musician who lives nearest to your community in Dubai.

whyPoints.title: Dated artefacts, not reassurance
whyPoints.description: Every session is designed to leave something behind with a date on it. That is what lets a family judge whether support is working, and it is also what the Music criteria reward, since both the experimenting and exploring components are assessed on documented process.

whyPoints.title: Honest about what a tutor cannot do
whyPoints.description: No tutor can promise a grade, negotiate with a moderator, or supply work for submission. We say what is movable, which is the quality of drafts before the internal deadline, and we decline requests that cross the academic-honesty line.

whyPoints.title: Timed to the Dubai week
whyPoints.description: Sessions run in Gulf Standard Time around Dubai school finishing times, production weeks and Ramadan hours. Online delivery is what makes a 21:00 session or a Saturday morning review practical rather than theoretical.

whyPoints.title: Prices discussed before hours are booked
whyPoints.description: The market rates on this page are published figures from named providers so you can see where any quote sits. Our own conversation starts with how many hours the component needs, which is sometimes four and rarely forty.

whyPoints.title: Independent of the schools we name
whyPoints.description: IB Gram has no affiliation with any Dubai school, group or examination board. That independence is why a tutor can tell a family that the school's own marking looks reasonable and the problem is the student's documentation habit.

faqs.question: How can we tell whether Diploma Music tutoring is actually working?
faqs.answer: Ask what exists now that did not exist a month ago. Diploma Music is marked on submitted artefacts, so working support produces dated things: a rebuilt portfolio section, a logged set of experiments, a selection rationale, a draft inside its word limit. If the only available answer is that sessions are going well, you have testimony rather than evidence. We send a short written note after each session naming what was reviewed and what the student was asked to redo, which gives a family something checkable at the four-week mark rather than at the internal deadline.

faqs.question: What should be in the Music folder by the end of Year 12?
faqs.answer: That depends on your school, because the internal deadlines are set locally and vary across Dubai. A reasonable expectation is a substantial draft of the exploring-music-in-context portfolio, a running log of experiments with dates attached, and a shortlist for the presenting-music submission. Higher Level students should also have a project scope that a teacher has read and considered deliverable. Ask the IB coordinator for the school's own draft calendar in September. Schools will usually hand it over immediately, and it is the single most useful document a Music parent can hold.

faqs.question: Who marks IB Music, the school or the IB?
faqs.answer: The coursework components are marked inside the school by the teacher who taught the course, against IB criteria, and then a sample of that marking is externally moderated by the IB. Moderation can move a whole school's marks for consistency; it does not re-mark one student against a different standard. The practical consequence for a family is that the time to influence a Music grade is while drafts are still drafts. After submission, the only route is an enquiry upon results requested by the school.

faqs.question: What does a teacher mean by saying the context work needs more analysis?
faqs.answer: It usually means a claim has been made about the music that is not evidenced from the music. Writing that a work reflects the politics of its decade is an assertion. Pointing to a passage, naming what happens in it musically and connecting that to the context is an argument, and the criteria reward the second. The repair is to go back to the score or the recording and locate the evidence by bar number or timing. Most students can do this once somebody shows them one worked example.

faqs.question: How do we keep evidence of a composition that changed over six months?
faqs.answer: Save versions rather than overwriting, date every file, and keep a one-line note with each version saying what was being tried. A folder of dated exports with notes is worth more in the experimenting component than a single polished final file, because the assessed material is the process. Students lose marks here constantly and avoidably: they keep the version that worked and delete the three attempts that did not, which were the evidence. Build the habit in the first term, because it cannot be reconstructed later.

faqs.question: Is a predicted grade in Music based on anything a parent can see?
faqs.answer: It is based on the teacher's professional judgement of work so far, which usually includes marked drafts and class performance. The useful question is not whether the prediction is right but which component is holding it down. Ask for the mark on each component and the gap to the next band. A Dubai teacher with six Music students will normally answer that in a sentence. Once you have component-level numbers, support can be aimed at the weakest one rather than spread evenly across a subject.

faqs.question: Can a tutor mark a Music draft the way a moderator would?
faqs.answer: A tutor can read a draft against the published assessment criteria and say where it currently sits and what is missing. That is genuinely useful. What no tutor can do is replicate a moderator's decision, claim access to marking standards or grade boundaries, or guarantee a mark. Anyone offering that is overstating what they have. We also do not rewrite drafts: feedback is given so the student can make the change themselves, which is both the academic-honesty requirement and the only version that improves their work.

faqs.question: How many hours does a Dubai Music student usually need before a component deadline?
faqs.answer: A pre-submission review is one or two sessions. Rebuilding a weak portfolio section typically takes four to eight sessions over three to five weeks, because the student has to produce material between sessions and that takes calendar time rather than tutor time. A Higher Level project that has lost its scope can need more, mostly spent narrowing it. We would rather tell you the work is four sessions than sell twenty, and the free trial lesson exists so the estimate is made against real material.

faqs.question: What does Diploma Music support cost per hour in the Dubai market?
faqs.answer: Published Dubai rates as of October 2026 run from roughly AED 45-150 an hour for budget online tutoring, AED 150-300 for a qualified subject tutor online, AED 180-500 for in-home visits including travel, and AED 200-450 or more for IB and IGCSE specialists, with one provider publishing AED 650 at the top of the market. Arts components usually sit in the specialist band because the pool of people who read these criteria is small. Those are market figures from named providers, not our price list.

faqs.question: Our recordings were made on a phone. Does that cost marks?
faqs.answer: Audible is the threshold, not studio quality. What costs marks is a recording the assessor cannot hear clearly enough to judge, or one that is unindexed so nobody can tell which take is being submitted. A phone in a quiet room with the microphone not pointed at a wall is usually adequate. In a Dubai apartment the real constraints are neighbours and air conditioning noise, which is why many students book a school music room at lunchtime rather than recording at home in the evening.

faqs.question: Can an online Music tutor hear enough over video to be useful?
faqs.answer: For the written and documentation components, which carry most of the marks, video is not a compromise at all: the work is text, scores and files that both people can see on screen. For performance feedback, live video compresses audio, so the normal approach is to review an uploaded recording rather than judge sound quality live. That is closer to how the component is assessed anyway, since assessors work from recordings. Instrumental technique stays with the instrumental teacher, which is the right place for it.

faqs.question: Does a student need fluent notation reading to score well in Diploma Music?
faqs.answer: The course is designed to accommodate students whose practice is not notation-based, including producers and players from traditions that are not notated. What a student does need is a way of pointing precisely at musical events, whether that is a bar number, a timing in a recording or a position in a session file. Vagueness is what costs marks, not the absence of staff notation. A tutor's early work with a production-based student is often building that vocabulary of precise reference.

faqs.question: What happens to the Music folder if we change school mid-Diploma?
faqs.answer: The work belongs to the student, so the files travel, but the internal deadlines and the teacher's marking do not. A new school may be running the components in a different order and may have different expectations about what should be complete. Move with a dated inventory of every artefact and any marked feedback, and ask the new coordinator which components the cohort has already submitted. Transfers mid-Diploma are common in Dubai and are survivable; undocumented work is what makes them painful.

faqs.question: Can a tutor help if the school has no specialist Music teacher this year?
faqs.answer: Yes, with a clear boundary. A tutor can teach the content, read drafts against the criteria and help a student structure documentation. A tutor cannot mark the component officially, cannot submit on the school's behalf and cannot replace the supervision the school owes the student. If a Dubai school has lost its Music specialist mid-year, the first conversation is with the IB coordinator about who is signing off the internal marks. Outside support works best alongside that conversation rather than instead of it.

faqs.question: How do Dubai production weeks and Ramadan change a Music submission plan?
faqs.answer: Both remove evening hours, and both are predictable. School production season takes the students who are in the school production, which in Music is most of them, and it tends to land in the same term as arts coursework deadlines. Ramadan shortens the school day and shifts family time later. The workable plan is to front-load written components into the first term and keep recording for weeks when the house is quiet. Online sessions after Iftar are straightforward to timetable, since nobody is driving.

faqs.question: Does a tutor working with a Dubai student from outside the UAE need a permit?
faqs.answer: The UAE private tuition work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023 and is issued through MoHRE free of charge for two years, covering individuals providing private lessons in the UAE. Eligible applicants include registered school teachers, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and students aged 15 to 18. Anyone tutoring inside the UAE without one is subject to penalties under the applicable laws. For a UAE-resident tutor, ask to see the permit. The official route is mohre.gov.ae.

dubai/ib-dp-music-tutor.closingHeading: Start with the folder, not with a package
dubai/ib-dp-music-tutor.closingBody: If you are weighing up an IB DP Music tutor in Dubai, the first useful step costs nothing: gather what your child has actually produced, with dates, and ask the school for the mark on each component. That takes an afternoon and it tells you whether the problem is the exploring portfolio, the missing experiment log, the presenting selection or the Higher Level project scope. Book the free trial lesson with those files open and a specialist will tell you which one is costing the most marks and roughly how many sessions it takes to repair. Lessons run online over live video in Gulf Standard Time; IB Gram does not send tutors to homes anywhere in the UAE, as home visits are a service we run only in India.

dubai/ib-dp-philosophy-home-tutor.tutorsIntro: These tutors teach Diploma Philosophy: the core theme, the optional themes your school has chosen, the prescribed text set for Paper 2, the Higher Level unseen paper, and the internal assessment. Each starts by marking one piece of your child's own writing against the published assessment criteria.

intro.heading: What Diploma Philosophy is marked on, and why reading more does not help
paragraphs: Philosophy attracts the students who most enjoy it and rewards them least reliably. A Dubai family hiring a Philosophy tutor has usually watched a capable child read Nietzsche for pleasure, hold a position in a seminar, and come home with a 5. That is not a knowledge problem and more reading will not fix it. The Diploma course credits a small set of specific operations: explaining a philosophical position accurately before testing it, identifying the issue in a stimulus rather than reacting to it, constructing an argument that survives an objection, and using a prescribed text as evidence rather than as a topic.

Each component tests those operations in a different form. Paper 1 opens with a question on the compulsory core theme, Being human, which is stimulus-based: a short text or image that must be read philosophically before anything is argued. The rest of Paper 1 is an essay on an optional theme, one at Standard Level and two at Higher Level. Paper 2 is a single hour on a single prescribed text. Higher Level adds a paper on an unseen passage about the nature of philosophy itself. The internal assessment is a 2,000-word analysis of something that is not philosophy at all.

That variety is why generic essay coaching does so little here. The skill that gets a student from a 5 to a 7 on the optional theme essay is not the skill the core theme question demands, and neither is the skill the unseen Higher Level paper tests. A useful first session therefore does one thing: marks a piece of your child's actual writing against the published criteria and names which operation is failing. Most students have exactly one or two consistent failure modes, and they are visible in a single essay.

This page is organised around those failure modes rather than around the syllabus. There is a breakdown of every component and what it is worth, a table of the seven optional themes with the marks each one tends to lose, the prescribed texts and what an essay must do with one, how the unseen Higher Level paper differs from everything else, the internal assessment and the stimulus choice that decides it, and a diagnostic list of the seven ways Dubai students most often lose marks in this subject.

Lessons are delivered online, one-to-one, over live video, scheduled around Dubai school hours in Gulf Standard Time. IB Gram does not send a tutor to any UAE address; home visits are a service offered only in India. Philosophy is a small Diploma subject taught in a minority of Dubai schools, so the pool of specialists is narrow. A family choosing from those available at 7pm on a weekday has a much better chance of finding one who has taught their child's actual prescribed text online than within driving distance. The first lesson is free.

dubai/ib-dp-philosophy-home-tutor.programmesIntro: Philosophy exists only at Diploma level in the IB, so the question for younger students is what prepares them for it. IB Gram teaches the Diploma course, the Middle Years thinking that makes it manageable, and the Career-related version where Philosophy is one of the Diploma courses taken.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme Philosophy
programmes.description: A compulsory core theme, one optional theme at Standard Level or two at Higher Level, one prescribed text examined by essay, an internal assessment analysing a non-philosophical stimulus, and at Higher Level an additional paper on an unseen text about philosophical method. Four distinct assessment skills, which is why diagnosis matters more here than coverage.
programmes.countryNote: Philosophy is offered by a minority of Dubai Diploma schools, so groups are small and a student often has nobody to compare their own writing against. Dubai's private sector is large — KHDA recorded 387,441 students across 227 schools in 2024-25, with the IB at 7 per cent of enrolment — but Philosophy sits at the thin end of that, and few schools have a second specialist in the building.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme Individuals and Societies
programmes.description: Nothing in the Middle Years Programme is called Philosophy, and the preparation that matters is a habit rather than a content list: stating somebody else's position fairly before disagreeing with it. Students who can do that at fifteen find DP1 Philosophy straightforward. Students who argue well and represent opponents carelessly find it unexpectedly hard.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai students arrive in DP1 from Middle Years, IGCSE and American middle-school backgrounds, and the gap in Philosophy is almost never factual. It is the instinct to answer a question before working out what the question is asking. A first session usually shows a student producing a confident, well-written response to a question slightly different from the one on the paper.

programmes.name: Career-related Programme with Diploma Philosophy
programmes.description: Career-related students take Diploma courses alongside a career-related study and a reflective project. Philosophy is a strong pairing with that structure, because the reflective project asks for ethical reasoning about a real dilemma and the Philosophy course teaches exactly how to construct one without either piece of work being double-submitted.
programmes.countryNote: Where Dubai schools offer the Career-related Programme, a Philosophy candidate may be the only one in the school. That removes the seminar entirely, and seminar argument is how this subject is normally learned. One-to-one teaching is the closest substitute, because the method is dialogue rather than lecture, and a tutor can take the opposing position on demand.

dubai/ib-dp-philosophy-home-tutor.subjectsIntro: A Dubai school chooses which optional themes it teaches and which prescribed text it sets, and those two choices define half your child's examination. The list below covers the core theme, the seven optional themes, the prescribed text component and the Higher Level unseen paper. Check your child's course outline before booking anyone.

subjects.name: Core theme: Being human
subjects.description: Compulsory at both levels. Personhood, identity, the self, freedom and the human condition, examined through a stimulus that must be read philosophically. Students who react to the stimulus rather than identifying the philosophical issue in it lose marks before writing a sentence of argument.

subjects.name: Optional theme: Ethics
subjects.description: Normative ethical theories, metaethics and applied problems. The most commonly chosen optional theme and the most commonly mishandled, because students substitute their own moral intuitions for the theory the question names. Accuracy about what a theory actually claims is where the marks sit.

subjects.name: Optional theme: Epistemology
subjects.description: Knowledge, justification, scepticism, the sources and limits of what can be known. Rewards precision and punishes fluency. An essay that uses knowledge and belief interchangeably has lost the top bands however elegantly it is written.

subjects.name: Optional theme: Philosophy of religion
subjects.description: Arguments for and against the existence of God, religious experience, language and the problem of evil. The theme where students most often argue a conclusion rather than evaluate an argument. The examiner credits the handling of the argument's structure, not the position reached.

subjects.name: Optional theme: Political philosophy
subjects.description: Political obligation, justice, liberty, equality and the state. Pairs well with Global Politics if a student takes both. The failure mode is conflating a descriptive claim about how states behave with a normative claim about how they ought to.

subjects.name: Optional theme: Philosophy of science
subjects.description: Scientific method, explanation, realism, demarcation and the problem of induction. Science-strong students choose it and then write about science rather than about the philosophy of it, which is the single clearest example of the subject's core trap.

subjects.name: Optional theme: Aesthetics
subjects.description: Art, beauty, judgement, representation and the value of aesthetic experience. Chosen less often and taught with fewer resources, which makes a tutor's own reading list matter more. Essays here drift into personal taste, which earns nothing.

subjects.name: Optional theme: Philosophy and contemporary society
subjects.description: Philosophical questions raised by technology, equality, the environment and social change. Feels the most accessible and is marked the most strictly, because topicality tempts students into commentary where the paper wants conceptual analysis.

subjects.name: Paper 2: the prescribed text
subjects.description: One essay in one hour on one text from the published list, chosen by the school. Worth 25% at Standard Level and 20% at Higher Level. The essay must argue from the text with accurate reference to it, not write about the author's general reputation.

subjects.name: Higher Level Paper 3: doing philosophy
subjects.description: An unseen passage about the nature, method and value of philosophy itself, answered in 75 minutes and worth 20% of the Higher Level grade. Nothing else in the course rehearses it, and no amount of content revision prepares a student who has never practised the paper.

subjects.name: Internal assessment: philosophical analysis of a non-philosophical stimulus
subjects.description: Up to 2,000 words analysing a stimulus that is not itself philosophy — a film, an advertisement, a news item, a photograph, a song. Worth 25% at Standard Level and 20% at Higher Level. Stimulus choice determines the ceiling of the piece before any writing happens.

sections.heading: The four components and what each one is worth
paragraphs: Standard Level and Higher Level Philosophy are not the same course with extra reading. The Standard Level grade is dominated by Paper 1 at 50 per cent, with the prescribed text and the internal assessment taking 25 per cent each. Higher Level redistributes: Paper 1 falls to 40 per cent, the prescribed text and the internal assessment to 20 per cent each, and a third paper arrives worth the remaining 20 per cent. Higher Level also adds a second optional theme, so Paper 1 itself grows from 105 minutes to 150.

The practical consequence is that a Standard Level student should spend most of their effort on one paper, and a Higher Level student cannot. For Standard Level, Paper 1 technique is the whole game: the core theme stimulus question and one optional theme essay together decide half the grade. Everything else is worth a quarter each and can be banked steadily. That is a simple plan and most Standard Level students do not follow it, because the internal assessment feels more urgent than exam technique.

For Higher Level the plan is genuinely harder, because the fourth component asks for something nothing else rehearses. Paper 3 presents an unseen passage about the nature and method of philosophy and asks the student to engage with it philosophically. A student can know the optional themes thoroughly and still be unprepared, which is why Higher Level sessions build in Paper 3 practice from early in DP2 rather than treating it as a final-term topic.
