dubai/ib-dp-theatre-home-tutor.tutorsIntro: The tutors listed below teach DP Theatre as a documented, criterion-marked subject: notebook structure, theatre-tradition research, collaborative project reports, and the HL solo piece. Each card shows levels covered, Gulf Standard Time availability and current coursework capacity.

intro.heading: Theatre marks are lost on paper, not on stage
paragraphs: An IB DP theatre home tutor in Dubai gets hired for a specific and slightly surprising reason. The student is usually confident on their feet. They have been in school productions since Year 7, they are not frightened of an audience, and their teacher likes them. What they cannot do is write twenty pages that an external examiner will read as directorial thinking rather than as enthusiasm. Every externally assessed component in DP Theatre is a document or a recording accompanied by a document, and the document is what carries the marks.

This catches Dubai cohorts out more than most because the emirate's school drama culture is strong. Many Dubai schools have proper studio spaces, visiting practitioners, and productions that run to a standard well above the subject's demands. A student who has played a lead in a main-house show arrives at the director's notebook assuming the hard part is behind them. It is not. The notebook asks them to take a published play they have not studied, imagine a production of it, and justify every choice against the play's own demands and its original context. That is research and argument, done on a page limit.

The failure modes are consistent and they are diagnosable, which is what makes this subject responsive to tutoring. A notebook fails because the student wrote a production diary instead of a set of justified decisions. A research presentation fails because the student chose a theatre tradition they already half-knew, and so had nothing to discover. A collaborative project report fails because the group talked for three months and documented nothing. A solo theatre piece fails because the chosen theorist's idea was too broad to be converted into a four-minute performance.

None of those needs rehearsal time to fix. They need someone to read the draft, name which criterion the writing is failing, and ask the question the student has not asked themselves. In Dubai, the practical difficulty is finding that person locally. DP Theatre cohorts here are small, often taught by one teacher who also runs the school production, and the window when everyone needs feedback is the same fortnight for the whole cohort. The probability that an experienced Theatre examiner lives a short drive from your community and is free at 5pm is not high.

IB Gram does not run home visits in Dubai; home visiting is a service we operate only in India, as every page in our UAE set states. Dubai Theatre students work with us over live video, one to one, with the draft notebook open on a shared screen. That is the right medium for this subject for the same reason it is the right medium for an essay: the thing being marked is text, and both people need to be looking at the same paragraph when the comment is made.
bullets: Director's notebook: maximum 20 pages, externally assessed, 35% at SL and 20% at HL
Research presentation: maximum 15 minutes plus a list of sources, externally assessed

Every externally assessed component is a document or a document plus a recording

dubai/ib-dp-theatre-home-tutor.programmesIntro: Dubai students reach DP Theatre by several routes, and the route determines which failure mode shows up first. These are the programme stages we support and what each demands.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme Theatre
programmes.description: Two years covering theatre in context, theatre processes and presenting theatre, assessed through a director's notebook on an unstudied play text, a research presentation on an unstudied theatre tradition, a group collaborative project devised from a non-theatre stimulus, and at Higher Level a solo theatre piece drawn from the work of a theatre theorist. No examination is sat in a hall.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai DP Theatre groups are typically small and frequently taught by the teacher who also directs the school production, so feedback capacity thins exactly when the school show is in tech week. Families here tend to buy support in the autumn of DP2 and again six weeks before internal deadlines.

programmes.name: MYP Arts, drama strand
programmes.description: Assessed on knowing and understanding, developing skills, thinking creatively and responding, each on an eight-point scale, with a process journal running underneath. The journal habit is the single best predictor of a usable DP director's notebook, because both reward recorded intention rather than recalled intention.
programmes.countryNote: Schools in Dubai running MYP straight into DP, including Dubai International Academy and Uptown International School, give students five years of process-journal practice. Students who transfer into a Dubai IB school at 16 from a different system usually have none, and that gap shows up in DP1.

programmes.name: IGCSE Drama
programmes.description: Cambridge IGCSE Drama pairs a written paper on a pre-release stimulus booklet with coursework performances. The written paper trains exactly the skill the DP notebook needs — explaining a staging decision in prose — but at a scale of paragraphs rather than chapters. Scaling that up is a specific, teachable step.
programmes.countryNote: British-curriculum schools account for 37% of Dubai private-school enrolment (KHDA, 2024-25), so IGCSE Drama is the commonest feeder into DP Theatre here. Students arriving from the Indian curriculum, 26% of the market, often have performance experience but no assessed written drama work at all.

programmes.name: Literature and Performance
programmes.description: An interdisciplinary course sitting across Studies in Language and Literature and the Arts, combining literary analysis with transformation of a text into performance. Where a Dubai school offers it, students sometimes take it instead of Theatre and then need help with its written transformation task rather than with Theatre's notebook.
programmes.countryNote: Provision in Dubai is rare — a handful of schools at most — so students taking it are frequently the only candidate in the building. Online one-to-one is often the only route to subject-specific feedback for them.

dubai/ib-dp-theatre-home-tutor.subjectsIntro: Theatre is usually one of two or three subjects a Dubai Diploma student needs support with in the same term. These are the courses we most often run alongside it.

subjects.name: Theatre
subjects.description: Director's notebook, research presentation and collaborative project at both levels, plus the solo theatre piece at HL. Marks are lost to page limits, undocumented process and theatre traditions the student already knew.

subjects.name: Visual Arts
subjects.description: Comparative study, process portfolio and curated exhibition with an exhibition text. The nearest subject in assessment logic: process documented as it happens beats process reconstructed afterwards.

subjects.name: Music
subjects.description: Exploring music in context, experimenting with music, presenting music, and at HL a contemporary music-maker project. Another Group 6 course where the recording is accompanied by written commentary that carries most of the marks.

subjects.name: Dance
subjects.description: Composition and analysis, world dance studies, performance and, at HL, a dance investigation. Offered by very few Dubai schools, and students taking it face the same documentation problem Theatre students do.

subjects.name: English A: Literature
subjects.description: Paper 1 guided literary analysis, Paper 2 comparative essay, individual oral and, at HL, an essay on a studied work. Theatre students frequently study drama texts here and can reuse the close-reading discipline in the notebook.

subjects.name: History
subjects.description: Source papers, a world-history topic and a historical investigation. The research habits History demands are the ones that rescue a research presentation on an unfamiliar theatre tradition.

subjects.name: Psychology
subjects.description: Biological, cognitive and sociocultural approaches plus an experimental study report. A common sixth subject for arts students in Dubai, and the one where command-term discipline matters most.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Statistics-led route with a graphical-calculator paper and a mathematical exploration due in the same term as most Theatre internal deadlines. Scheduling, as much as content, is the problem.

subjects.name: Theory of Knowledge
subjects.description: A 1,600-word prescribed-title essay plus an exhibition of three objects with commentaries. Theatre students write strong exhibitions because they already think about how meaning is made for an audience.

subjects.name: Extended Essay
subjects.description: A 4,000-word independent research essay. Theatre is a demanding EE subject because the question has to be answerable from performance evidence rather than from what reviewers wrote about a production.

schoolClusters.city: Dubai IB schools with established drama provision
schoolClusters.note: Students we support in Theatre most often attend schools in this group, where the subject runs as a timetabled course with a dedicated space rather than as an independent study. Group 6 choice is widest here, which is also why the whole cohort's deadlines land together.

schoolClusters.city: Dubai schools where Theatre runs as a minority option
schoolClusters.note: In this group Group 6 is often a choice between two subjects and Theatre runs only when enough students request it. Candidates can end up as one of two or three, with limited contact time, which is where external subject feedback does the heaviest work.

schoolClusters.city: British-track schools feeding DP Theatre at 16
schoolClusters.note: Several Dubai schools run IGCSE Drama to 16 before a sixth form that is partly or wholly IB. Students crossing over bring performance confidence and short-form written analysis, and need the step up to a twenty-page argued document.

dubai/ib-dp-theatre-home-tutor.modesIntro: Theatre support is bought around documents and deadlines rather than evenly across two years. These are the three patterns Dubai families use, all one-to-one over live video.

modes.title: Notebook build, from blank page to submission
modes.description: Six to ten sessions taking a director's notebook from the choice of play text through to a submitted document inside the page limit. The sequence is fixed: text chosen, context researched, production concept argued, then individual decisions justified and evidenced. Nothing is drafted for the student; each session ends with a specific writing task they complete before the next.
bullets: Play text pressure-tested for whether it can sustain twenty pages
Each session ends with a writing task, not a reading list
Page count tracked from the first session, not audited at the end

modes.title: Single-task blocks for the research presentation or project report
modes.description: Four to six sessions scoped to one component. For the research presentation that means choosing a theatre tradition genuinely unfamiliar to the student, building a source list as the research happens, and timing a fifteen-minute delivery that does not run over. For the collaborative project it means reconstructing a documented process from what the group actually did.
bullets: Scoped to one task and its criteria
Booked backwards from the school's internal deadline
Ends at submission rather than rolling into a subscription

modes.title: HL solo piece supervision
modes.description: The HL component with the widest spread of outcomes, because the choice of theatre theorist determines whether a four-to-eight-minute solo piece is possible at all. Sessions here are short and frequent: theorist narrowed to one convertible idea, performance concept tested against it, then the 2,500-word report built from the student's own rehearsal record.

One identified aspect of the theory, held throughout

sections.heading: What an IB DP theatre home tutor in Dubai can fix, and what only rehearsal can
paragraphs: An IB DP theatre home tutor in Dubai is useful for the written and research half of the course and close to useless for the rest. That is worth saying first, because it is the honest division of labour and because plenty of providers will happily sell you sessions that overlap entirely with what your child's school already does well. A tutor can read a director's notebook and name the criterion a paragraph is failing. A tutor cannot give a student the hours in a rehearsal room that a solo piece needs.

The division runs roughly like this. Fixable from outside the school: the choice of play text for the notebook, the choice of theatre tradition for the research presentation, the choice of theorist for the solo piece, the structure and page discipline of every written component, the quality of sources, the gap between a described decision and a justified one, and the student's ability to say what their own work was trying to do. Not fixable from outside: ensemble rehearsal, the physical craft of performance, access to a space, and the group dynamics of a collaborative project.

The commonest waste of money in this subject is paying a specialist rate for coaching that duplicates the school's strongest area. Dubai schools with studio theatres and drama staff generally handle performance well. What thins out is written feedback capacity in the fortnight the whole cohort submits, and that is the window where an external reader changes an outcome. Scoping the booking to that gap, rather than buying a standing weekly hour from September of DP1, is usually both cheaper and more effective.
bullets: A tutor reads documents and names criteria; a tutor does not direct a performance
Text, tradition and theorist choices are where the biggest mark differences are made
The useful window is the fortnight before an internal deadline, not the whole of DP1
Duplicating what a school already does well is the commonest overspend in this subject

sections.heading: The four assessed tasks, their weightings and their hard limits
paragraphs: DP Theatre is assessed entirely through produced work. At Standard Level there are three components; at Higher Level, four. The weightings are not evenly spread, and they change between the levels in a way that should determine where a family spends support hours. At SL the director's notebook and the collaborative project each carry 35% and the research presentation 30%. At HL the solo theatre piece takes 35%, the collaborative project 25%, and the notebook and presentation 20% each.

That shift matters practically. An HL student who pours twenty hours into the notebook and treats the solo piece as something to sort out in March has mis-allocated effort against a component worth nearly twice as much. An SL student who neglects the collaborative project report because the performance went well has done the same thing in the opposite direction. Reading the weighting table before planning the year is a ten-minute exercise that most cohorts never do.

Every component also carries a hard ceiling, and ceilings are where examiners stop reading. The director's notebook is capped at twenty pages. The research presentation runs to a maximum of fifteen minutes and is submitted with a list of sources. The collaborative project report is capped at ten pages and accompanied by a video of the devised piece. The HL solo report is capped at 2,500 words. Confirm every limit against the subject guide your school is teaching, because the IB revises guides between syllabus cycles and a limit taken from a tutoring page is not a limit you should rely on.

sections.heading: The director's notebook: where twenty pages go wrong
paragraphs: The notebook asks a student to take a published play text they have not studied, research its context and demands, and build an argued account of how they would stage it. The marks are for directorial thinking: a concept that answers something in the play, decisions that follow from the concept, and evidence that the student understands what the text and its original conventions actually require. The marks are not for enthusiasm, for the number of ideas, or for the quality of the sketches.

Four failures recur. The first is text choice: a student picks a play they love and have discussed in English, which breaches the spirit of the task and leaves them restating a reading rather than discovering one. The second is the production-diary drift, where pages narrate what the student thought on Tuesday instead of justifying a choice. The third is page bloat — images, title pages and quotations consuming a quarter of the twenty-page allowance, after which the argument has nowhere to live. The fourth is the undemonstrated claim: a staging decision asserted without reference to the moment in the text that provokes it.

A session on the notebook is slow and specific. The student reads a page aloud while the tutor follows the criterion wording, and every sentence gets sorted into one of three piles: justified decision, description, or padding. Then the student rewrites one paragraph from the second pile. Nothing is typed for them, and the page count is tracked from the first session rather than discovered in the last week. Most students who do this properly end up submitting a shorter notebook than they expected, with a higher proportion of it doing work.
bullets: Choose a play text genuinely unstudied — the task depends on discovery
Every staging decision needs the moment in the text that provokes it
Treat images and front matter as part of the twenty pages, because they are
A shorter notebook with a higher density of justified decisions beats a full one of description

sections.heading: The research presentation: the theatre-tradition trap
paragraphs: The research presentation asks a student to research a theatre tradition they have not previously studied, identify a convention from it, and demonstrate that convention practically inside a recorded fifteen minutes, submitted with a list of sources. It is the component where the single biggest decision is made before any work happens, and it is routinely made badly.

The trap is familiarity. A student who has already done a module on Greek tragedy picks Greek tragedy, because it feels safe. They then have nothing to find out, so the research half of the presentation becomes a summary of what they already knew, and the practical demonstration becomes a reproduction of something their teacher once showed them. The criteria reward research that visibly changed the student's understanding and a convention demonstrated accurately enough that its logic is clear. Neither is available from a tradition the student half-knows.

Dubai students have an advantage here that very few of them use. The emirate's population draws on traditions that are genuinely accessible in person and in Arabic and South Asian scholarship — Ta'ziyeh, Kathakali, Kutiyattam, Noh, Beijing opera, West African masquerade forms — and the student who picks one of those and reads properly on it has source material competitors in other markets cannot reach as easily. The practical work in a session is narrowing: one tradition, one convention, one demonstrable mechanism, and a source list built as the reading happens rather than reconstructed from memory the night before.
bullets: Pick a tradition you have not studied — the criteria reward discovery, not recall
Narrow to a single convention that can be demonstrated inside fifteen minutes
Build the source list while researching; a reconstructed list is both weaker and riskier
Dubai's own cultural reach makes genuinely unfamiliar traditions easier to research well

sections.heading: The collaborative project: marks for the documented process
paragraphs: The collaborative project asks a group to devise an original piece from a non-theatre starting point and submit a report of no more than ten pages alongside a video of the result. It is internally assessed and externally moderated, which means the school marks it and the IB checks the school's marking. Students consistently misread what is being marked: they believe it is the piece, and it is the process the report evidences.

The structural failure is documentation drift. A group meets weekly from October, argues productively, tries things, discards things, and writes none of it down. In February they have a decent fifteen-minute piece and nothing to say about how it came to exist. Reports written in that state read as reconstruction, because they are, and the criteria that reward the student's own contribution and reflection have nothing concrete to attach to. A group that keeps a dated log of decisions, even a rough one, writes a better report in a third of the time.

The second failure is contribution blur. Each student writes their own report and each is marked on their own engagement, so a student who deferred to a dominant group member for four months has a weak report even if the piece is strong. In a session we go through what the student personally proposed, what was adopted, what was rejected and why, and whether any of it is evidenced in the video. Where it is not, the honest move is to write about the rejected proposal rather than claim credit the footage does not support — overclaiming is an honesty problem, not just a weak paragraph.
bullets: The report evidences the process; the video shows the result. Marks follow the report
Keep a dated decision log from the first meeting — reconstruction always reads as reconstruction
Each student is marked on their own contribution, not the group's collective quality
Never claim a contribution the recording does not support

sections.heading: The HL solo theatre piece and the theorist problem
paragraphs: The solo theatre piece is Higher Level only and carries 35% of the HL grade, more than any other single component. The student researches a theatre theorist they have not previously studied, identifies an aspect of that theorist's theory, and creates and performs a solo piece of four to eight minutes based on it, submitted with a report of up to 2,500 words. It is the component with the widest spread of outcomes in the subject, and almost all of that spread is set by one decision.

The decision is which aspect of the theory to take. A student who chooses Brecht and then writes about epic theatre in general has chosen something too large to convert into four minutes of solo performance; the piece becomes an illustration of a lecture. A student who chooses one mechanism — the interruption of emotional identification at a specific moment, say — has something a short solo piece can actually enact and a report can actually argue. The same applies to Grotowski, Boal, Artaud, Stanislavski, Lecoq or Suzuki: the theorist is less important than the narrowness of the aspect.

A tutor's useful contribution here comes almost entirely before rehearsal. We interrogate the theorist choice, test whether the identified aspect is small enough to perform, and check that the student has read the theorist rather than read about them. After that, the student rehearses — in their school space, with their teacher, as they should — and we return at the report stage to make sure the writing argues from their own documented rehearsal rather than from the theory in the abstract. The performance is theirs. The report is theirs. What we supply is pressure on the thinking at the two points where pressure helps.

sections.heading: What Theatre support actually costs in Dubai, by task
paragraphs: Because Theatre support is bought by component rather than by term, the useful cost question is not the hourly rate alone but how many hours a task genuinely needs. Published Dubai market rates as of October 2026 put qualified subject specialists online at roughly AED 150 to 300 an hour, with the IB and A-Level specialist band running AED 200 to 450 and above — TutorChase publishes AED 270, Bestimate's 2026 Dubai rate table gives 200 to 450-plus, and Unitors lists IB from AED 200. In-home one-to-one in Dubai runs higher, AED 180 to 500 once travel is priced in, on Bestimate's figures and independent tutors' own advertising.

Those are other providers' published numbers, cited with their source so you can check them rather than take our word for it. IB Gram does not publish a price list on these pages; the trial lesson and a consultation are how we quote. What we can do usefully is tell you how many hours each Theatre component tends to need, because that is the number that determines the bill and it is the number no competitor page in this market publishes at all.

The pattern across Dubai students is reasonably stable. A director's notebook needs the most hours and benefits from being spread over two months rather than compressed. The research presentation needs fewer hours but the earliest start, because the tradition has to be chosen before any research can begin. The collaborative project report needs very few hours if the group kept a log and a great many if it did not. The HL solo piece needs two short, early sessions and then a gap of several weeks while the student rehearses.

sections.heading: Rehearsal, performance and the Dubai school calendar
paragraphs: Theatre is the DP subject most exposed to the shape of the Dubai school year, because two of its four components need a group of teenagers physically in the same room repeatedly. Dubai private schools are regulated by the Knowledge and Human Development Authority, which u.ae describes as responsible for enhancing and overseeing the quality of private education in the emirate, and which inspects annually on a six-band scale from Outstanding to Very Weak. What KHDA does not regulate is how a school sequences its own production calendar against DP coursework, and that sequencing is where Theatre students lose time.

The pinch points are predictable. A school production in the autumn of DP2 absorbs the drama staff and the studio space in exactly the weeks the collaborative project needs both. Ramadan shortens the school day and removes the after-school hours group devising depends on, so collaborative groups who have not devised their piece before Ramadan begins compress it badly afterwards. The winter break lands in the middle of notebook research for most cohorts, and the students who use it arrive in January several weeks ahead.

Tutoring itself is the flexible part. Sessions move to post-Iftar timing during Ramadan without difficulty, and most of our Dubai Theatre students do exactly that. Written components are perfectly workable in a shortened day; group devising is not. The planning advice we give every Dubai family in this subject is the same: treat the production term and Ramadan as unavailable for collaborative work, and move notebook and research hours into them deliberately rather than discovering the clash in February.

sections.heading: Academic honesty in a subject where the work is partly someone else's
paragraphs: Theatre raises honesty questions that are easy to get wrong innocently. The collaborative project is made with other people, so what counts as the student's own contribution needs defining. The research presentation rests on scholarship about a tradition the student did not know, so attribution matters more than in a subject where ideas are the student's own by default. The solo piece is built on a theorist's writing, which has to be cited rather than absorbed.

Our boundary is the same across every subject and we state it plainly. A tutor teaches, explains criteria, questions a draft and gives feedback on what the student has produced. A tutor does not produce assessed work: not the notebook, not the presentation script, not the project report, not the solo report. Providers in this market do sell completed Internal Assessments — one sells them openly — and buying one exposes the student to an IB malpractice finding with consequences a refund does not cover. We also do not reproduce or supply IB subject guides, past assessment material or mark schemes; we reference the official documents and link to them.

In the collaborative project specifically, the practical rule we give students is to write about what they actually proposed, including the proposals the group rejected, rather than claiming credit for decisions the video shows belonged to someone else. That usually produces a stronger report as well as an honest one, because a rejected proposal with a documented reason behind it is better evidence of thinking than a successful one the student did not originate. And a tutor who notices an unattributed idea in a draft will say so, which is a service rather than a complication.
bullets: Attribute every scholarly source in the research presentation and the solo report
Write about your own proposals, including the rejected ones, in the project report
No component is produced for a student at any price or at any stage

process.title: Name the component and the internal deadline
process.description: Not the subject and the year. Director's notebook, research presentation, collaborative project report or HL solo piece, plus the date your school has set for it. Theatre support is scoped to components, and the date decides which tutor can realistically take it.

process.title: We check genuine availability and say no when there is none
process.description: Theatre specialists are a small group and Dubai internal deadlines cluster. If nobody who has marked these criteria is free in your hours, we tell you that rather than putting a general humanities tutor on a Group 6 brief and charging specialist rates for it.

process.title: A free trial on the student's real draft
process.description: The tutor reads the actual notebook pages or report before the session. The hour runs on that document against the criterion wording. The student should finish knowing one specific thing about their own work they did not know, and you should know whether to book further hours.

process.title: Sessions in Gulf Standard Time, each ending in a writing task
process.description: Every session closes with a defined piece of writing for the student to complete before the next one, and with notes written against the criteria rather than general encouragement. Those notes are a record you can compare against the school's own feedback.

process.title: A submission audit two weeks out
process.description: One or two hours before the internal deadline, spent only on compliance and density: page and word ceilings against the current subject guide, source lists complete, and every paragraph checked for whether it justifies or merely describes.

whyPoints.title: Component-level scoping, not open-ended terms
whyPoints.description: We quote against a named task and a deadline, and the booking ends at submission. That keeps the spend visible and stops families paying for coaching that duplicates what their school already does well, which in Dubai drama departments is usually the performance work.

whyPoints.title: Criterion wording, every time
whyPoints.description: Feedback names the criterion a sentence is failing rather than offering a general impression. A student who can sort their own paragraphs into justified decisions, descriptions and padding no longer needs a tutor to do it, which is the point.

whyPoints.title: Hours published, not just rates
whyPoints.description: This page states how many support hours each Theatre component typically needs for a Dubai student. No competitor page in this market publishes that, and it is the figure that actually determines what a family spends.

whyPoints.title: A stated limit on what a tutor will produce
whyPoints.description: We teach, question and give feedback. No notebook page, presentation script or report is written for a student at any price. In a market where finished Internal Assessments are sold openly, that boundary is worth putting in writing.

whyPoints.title: Planning around the Dubai calendar
whyPoints.description: Sessions run in Gulf Standard Time and move to post-Iftar timing through Ramadan. More usefully, we plan the year on the assumption that the school production term and Ramadan are unavailable for group devising, because in Dubai they generally are.

whyPoints.title: Delivery stated once, plainly
whyPoints.description: All UAE tutoring on this platform is one-to-one live online. IB Gram does not operate home visits in the UAE and holds no UAE office or centre. Saying so on the page saves a call and sets the right expectation before anyone enquires.

faqs.question: What does an IB DP Theatre tutor actually do if they cannot direct the performance?
faqs.answer: The written and research half of the course, which is where the externally assessed marks sit. That means pressure-testing the choice of play text, theatre tradition and theorist; structuring a director's notebook so the twenty pages carry argument rather than narration; auditing source lists; and reading drafts against the criterion wording to separate justified decisions from description. Performance craft, ensemble rehearsal and studio access stay with the school, which in most Dubai schools with drama provision is the stronger half of the offer anyway.

faqs.question: How long should the DP Theatre director's notebook be?
faqs.answer: The ceiling set out in the current subject guide is twenty pages, including images, title pages and quotations — which is the part students forget. In practice we track the page count from the first session so the final document is a deliberate shape rather than a late cut. Students who arrive at thirty pages and trim backwards almost always delete the justified decisions and keep the atmospheric description. Confirm the limit against the subject guide your school is teaching, since the IB revises guides between syllabus cycles.

faqs.question: Which play should my child choose for the director's notebook?
faqs.answer: It has to be their choice and a tutor who makes it for them has crossed a line. What we do is test the choice against two things. First, the task requires a play text the student has not studied, so a text already covered in English class undermines the whole exercise. Second, the text must be able to sustain twenty pages of directorial argument — some plays offer a single staging problem and then nothing more. If the student cannot name three distinct production problems in the text, it is the wrong text.

faqs.question: Why is the research presentation the component students get wrong first?
faqs.answer: Because the biggest decision is made before any work starts, and familiarity feels safe. A student who already covered Greek tragedy in class picks Greek tragedy, and then has nothing to discover — so the research half becomes a summary of prior knowledge and the practical demonstration reproduces something a teacher once showed them. The criteria reward research that visibly changed the student's understanding. Picking a tradition genuinely outside the taught course is uncomfortable and is the whole point of the task.

faqs.question: Is the collaborative project marked on the performance or the report?
faqs.answer: Effectively on the report, which evidences the process, with the video showing the result. It is internally assessed and externally moderated, so the school marks it and the IB checks the marking. Each student writes their own report and is marked on their own engagement and contribution, which is why a student who deferred to a dominant group member for four months scores poorly even when the piece is good. A dated decision log kept from the first meeting makes the report both faster to write and better.

faqs.question: How much of the HL grade does the solo theatre piece carry?
faqs.answer: 35%, more than any other single HL component, with the collaborative project at 25% and the notebook and research presentation at 20% each. That weighting is why HL students who treat the solo piece as a spring-term problem have mis-allocated their year. The performance runs four to eight minutes and the accompanying report is capped at 2,500 words. Check the current weightings and limits in the subject guide your school teaches rather than relying on any tutoring page, including this one.

faqs.question: How do we pick a theatre theorist for the solo piece?
faqs.answer: The theorist matters less than how narrow the chosen aspect of their theory is. A student who takes Brecht and writes about epic theatre in general cannot enact that in four minutes, so the piece turns into an illustrated lecture. A student who takes one mechanism — interrupting emotional identification at a specific moment — has something a solo performer's body can actually do and a report can argue about. The second test is whether the student has read the theorist's own writing rather than summaries of it.

faqs.question: Can a tutor help write the collaborative project report?
faqs.answer: A tutor can explain the criteria, ask what the student personally proposed, point out where a claim is not supported by the video, and read a draft and name what is missing. A tutor cannot write it. Producing any part of an assessed component is malpractice under IB rules and the consequence falls on the student. The practical advice we give instead is to write about genuine proposals, including rejected ones with documented reasons, rather than claiming credit the recording does not support.

faqs.question: Does my child need to be a strong performer to do well in DP Theatre?
faqs.answer: Less than families assume. Three of the four components are assessed through documents or recordings accompanied by documents, and the externally assessed marks reward research, directorial reasoning and written justification. A confident performer with weak written discipline typically scores below a careful researcher who is merely competent on stage. That surprises Dubai parents whose child has carried school productions since Year 7, and it is the single most useful thing to understand before planning the two years.

faqs.question: How many hours of support does a director's notebook usually need?
faqs.answer: For Dubai students the pattern is six to ten hours spread across six to eight weeks, starting in the autumn term of DP2. Spread matters more than volume: the notebook improves between sessions, while the student writes, not during them. The number rises sharply in two situations — a play text chosen badly, which means restarting, and a draft already at thirty pages, where the work becomes cutting rather than building. A compressed block in the final fortnight is triage, not teaching.

faqs.question: Do you come to our home in Dubai for Theatre sessions?
faqs.answer: No. IB Gram does not operate home visits anywhere in the UAE; home visiting is a service we run only in India. Dubai students work with us one to one over live video, scheduled in Gulf Standard Time, with the draft notebook or report open on a shared screen. For a subject whose marks sit in documents, that is the right medium — both people read the same paragraph at the same time. If you specifically want a person in the room for performance coaching, a local Dubai drama school is the better call.

faqs.question: How does Ramadan affect DP Theatre coursework in Dubai?
faqs.answer: It removes the after-school hours that group devising depends on, because the school day shortens. Collaborative groups who have not devised their piece before Ramadan begins tend to compress it badly afterwards, which shows up in thin reports. Written components are unaffected and are the sensible thing to move into that window. Tutoring adapts easily: sessions shift to post-Iftar timing and most of our Dubai students in this subject take that slot. Plan the production term and Ramadan as unavailable for group work.

faqs.question: My child's school production clashes with their coursework deadlines. What do we do?
faqs.answer: Accept the clash and sequence around it rather than hoping it resolves. A school production in the autumn of DP2 absorbs the drama staff and the studio in exactly the weeks a collaborative project needs both, and the teacher's feedback capacity thins at the same time. The workable response is to move notebook research and the research presentation into the production weeks, because they need neither the space nor the staff, and to protect the weeks immediately after for devising.

faqs.question: What does Theatre tutoring cost per hour in Dubai?
faqs.answer: Published Dubai rates in October 2026 put qualified subject specialists online at roughly AED 150 to 300 an hour and IB specialists at AED 200 to 450 and above; TutorChase publishes AED 270, Unitors lists IB from AED 200, and Bestimate's 2026 Dubai table gives 200 to 450-plus. In-home one-to-one runs AED 180 to 500 with travel included. Those are other providers' figures, cited so you can verify them. For Theatre the more useful number is hours per component, which this page publishes in full.

faqs.question: Can we book support for just one component rather than the whole year?
faqs.answer: That is how most Dubai families buy it, and we prefer it. A block scoped to the director's notebook or the research presentation ends at the school's internal deadline rather than rolling on, which keeps the cost visible and stops the sessions drifting into general chat about theatre. If a second component needs support later, that is a new scope and a new conversation. Standing weekly hours from the start of DP1 suit very few students in this subject.

faqs.question: What if my child's school does not run DP Theatre at all?
faqs.answer: Ask the IB coordinator first whether the subject can be registered as a self-taught course, because the IB permits that for some subjects and not others and only the school can answer it. Where a school does register a candidate with limited contact time, external subject teaching fills the written and research gap, which is the commonest version of this enquiry we see from Dubai families. What external teaching cannot supply is a rehearsal space or a group for the collaborative project, and nobody should tell you otherwise.

dubai/ib-dp-theatre-home-tutor.closingHeading: Tell us the component and the date
dubai/ib-dp-theatre-home-tutor.closingBody: If your child is taking DP Theatre at a Dubai school and one component is stuck — a notebook that narrates instead of justifying, a research presentation on a tradition they already knew, a project report with no documented process behind it, a solo piece built on an idea too broad to perform — name the component and the internal deadline. We will say honestly whether a Theatre specialist can cover it and roughly how many hours it tends to take. The trial lesson runs on your child's own draft, in Gulf Standard Time, with no card required. All UAE tutoring here is one-to-one live online; we do not operate home visits in the UAE.

dubai/ib-dp-theatre-online-tutor.tutorsIntro: The profiles below are Theatre and performing-arts specialists who have taught the Diploma course and read its components against the published criteria. You see a named tutor, the components they cover and their availability in Gulf Standard Time before anything is booked. If no Theatre specialist is free in your window, we say so rather than sending a general English tutor instead.

intro.heading: Theatre is assessed entirely on what your child hands in
paragraphs: Most Diploma subjects end in an examination hall. Theatre does not. There is no Paper 1, no Paper 2, no three-hour morning in May where a weak term can be rescued by six weeks of past papers. The whole grade is built from portfolio work produced across two years and submitted to internal school deadlines, then marked or moderated against criteria your child can read in advance. That changes what tutoring is for. A Theatre tutor is not preparing someone for an unseen question; they are reading a draft, finding the criterion it fails to address, and sending it back with a specific instruction.

This catches Dubai families out in a particular way. A child who is visibly good at Theatre - cast in every production, confident in a studio, the one the drama teacher relies on - can still arrive in Year 13 with a 4. The assessed artefacts are documents and recordings, and the skills they test are analytical: justifying a staging decision against a named theatre theorist, evidencing research in a tradition the student has no personal connection to, writing a project report that explains an intention rather than describing what happened on the night. Stage presence earns nothing on its own.

The second thing that catches families out is sequencing. Because every deadline is internal, the dates come from the school rather than from the IB, and they differ between Dubai schools running the same course. One school finishes the collaborative project in the summer term of Year 12; another runs it alongside the research presentation in the autumn of Year 13. A tutor who does not know which deadline is next spends sessions on the wrong component. The first thing we ask for is the school's own assessment calendar, not a general statement that your child needs help with Theatre.

Online delivery suits this subject better than it suits almost any other. The things being worked on are a document, a slide deck, a set of source references, a staging diagram and a video file. All of them live on a screen. A tutor in Jumeirah cannot read a notebook page any better than a tutor on a video call who is annotating that page while your child watches. What matters is whether the person reading it has taught the component and knows what the criteria reward, and that is a far smaller pool than the pool of people who can reach your address before 6pm.

IB Gram is an independent tutor-matching platform. We do not run a centre in Dubai, we do not send tutors to homes anywhere in the UAE - home visits are a service we offer only in India - and we hold no accreditation from the IB, KHDA or any other authority. What we do is match a student to a named subject specialist, deliver one-to-one lessons over live video on Gulf Standard Time, and put a free trial lesson in front of you before any money changes hands.

dubai/ib-dp-theatre-online-tutor.programmesIntro: Theatre sits in Group 6 of the Diploma Programme, but the students who search for it arrive from several directions. Some have come up through MYP Arts in the same Dubai school. Some picked Theatre as a sixth subject late. A few are in the Career-related Programme and need the same portfolio discipline for a different qualification. The three routes below each need a different first session.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Theatre is available at Standard and Higher Level. SL students submit three assessed components; HL students submit four, the extra one being the solo theatre piece. There is no written examination, so the grade is assembled from documents and recordings produced over two years. Students study theatre in context, theatre processes and presenting theatre, and are expected to work as creator, designer, director and performer rather than only as an actor.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai schools offering DP Theatre are concentrated in the full-continuum IB schools - Dubai International Academy Emirates Hills, Raffles World Academy, Uptown International School, Dwight School Dubai and Swiss International Scientific School Dubai among them. Timetabling is the live constraint: many Dubai students carry Arabic and Islamic Education as KHDA mandatory subjects on top of six Diploma subjects, which squeezes rehearsal and drafting time into evenings.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: MYP Arts is assessed on four criteria - investigating, developing, creating or performing, and evaluating - with a process journal running underneath all of them. Students who kept that journal honestly find the Diploma director's notebook recognisable. Students who treated it as a scrapbook find the jump hard, because the Diploma wants justified decisions rather than recorded activity.
programmes.countryNote: In Dubai the MYP-to-DP handover often happens inside one school, so the drama teacher who taught MYP Arts also teaches Theatre. That continuity is useful, but it also means a student who learned loose journalling habits in MYP keeps them. A tutor from outside the school is usually the first person to tell a Dubai student that the notebook is an argument, not a diary.

programmes.name: Career-related Programme
programmes.description: The CP combines at least two Diploma courses with a career-related study, a reflective project, personal and professional skills, service learning and a language-development portfolio. Where Theatre is one of the chosen Diploma courses, the assessed components are identical to DP Theatre; what changes is the surrounding workload and the reflective project running alongside it.
programmes.countryNote: A small number of Dubai schools run the CP, and performing-arts pathways are one of the commoner career strands. For a CP student the practical problem is usually that the reflective project and the collaborative project compete for the same weeks. Mapping both calendars onto one page in session one prevents a scramble in the spring term.

dubai/ib-dp-theatre-online-tutor.subjectsIntro: On a Theatre page the useful list is not a list of subjects but a list of the things actually marked, plus the neighbouring courses Dubai Theatre students most often carry alongside it. Each entry below names what is assessed and where the marks tend to leak.

subjects.name: Director's notebook
subjects.description: A response to an unfamiliar published play text the student has not studied, presented as a notebook with a strict page limit. Marks come from the justification of staging choices and the use of the text as evidence. Students lose marks by describing a production they imagine rather than defending decisions against the written text.

subjects.name: Research presentation
subjects.description: An individual recorded presentation on a theatre tradition outside the student's own experience, with a list of sources. The commonest failure is a tradition chosen because it is easy to find on the internet, which produces secondary-source summary instead of evidenced convention and practical demonstration.

subjects.name: Collaborative project
subjects.description: An original piece created by an ensemble from a starting point, submitted as a project report with video evidence of the performance. The report carries the assessment. Groups who rehearse hard and write the report in the final week routinely under-score relative to the quality of what they staged.

subjects.name: Solo theatre piece
subjects.description: A short solo performance built from an aspect of theatre theory, submitted with a written report. The theory comes first: the piece has to demonstrate the chosen theorist's ideas, not merely be a good four minutes of performance with a theorist's name attached afterwards.

subjects.name: Theatre in context, processes and presenting theatre
subjects.description: The three areas of exploration that organise the course. Every component draws on all three, which is why a student who treats them as separate units struggles to write a report that reads as a single argument rather than three disconnected observations.

subjects.name: Visual Arts
subjects.description: The other Group 6 option in most Dubai IB schools, also assessed without a written paper. Students who move between Theatre and Visual Arts carry over the habit of documenting intention, which is the single most transferable skill in either course.

subjects.name: Music
subjects.description: Shares the portfolio logic and the same timetable pressure in Dubai schools, where arts lessons often sit in the final period. Families carrying both Theatre and Music usually need a single calendar rather than two separate tutoring plans.

subjects.name: Film
subjects.description: Offered in a handful of Dubai IB schools and frequently chosen alongside Theatre. The textual analysis and the production portfolio reward the same analytical writing the Theatre report needs, so work on one tends to lift the other.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: The course most Dubai Theatre students take in Group 1. Its Paper 1 analytical habits - claim, evidence, effect - are exactly what a weak director's notebook is missing, and a tutor can use one to fix the other.

subjects.name: Extended Essay in Theatre
subjects.description: A 4,000-word essay in the subject, supervised by a school teacher. A tutor may discuss research questions, method and the shape of an argument, and may give feedback on the student's own drafts, but the essay must be the student's work throughout and the school supervisor remains the examining relationship.

sections.heading: What a search for an IB DP Theatre online tutor in Dubai is usually trying to solve
paragraphs: Parents rarely search for an IB DP Theatre online tutor in Dubai because their child dislikes Theatre. They search because a predicted grade came back lower than expected on a subject the child enjoys, and nobody in the house can see why. The explanation is almost always that the assessed work is analytical writing about performance rather than performance itself, and that nobody has read the criteria aloud with the student.

The second common trigger is a deadline. A director's notebook is due in three weeks, the student has a page limit they are already over, and the draft describes a production rather than defending a set of decisions. That is a fixable problem, but it is fixable by rewriting the argument, not by adding more detail. A tutor who has read the criterion descriptors can point at the two paragraphs doing the work and the eight that are not.

The third trigger is subject choice. A Year 11 student in a Dubai school is picking six Diploma subjects, Theatre is on the list, and the family wants to know whether an arts subject with no examination is a risk for a competitive university application. It usually is not, but the answer depends on the course the student intends to apply for, and it is worth settling before the choice is locked rather than in Year 13.

All three of those are answerable without a tutor in the room. What they need is somebody who has taught the components, knows what a 6 looks like against what a 4 looks like, and will say which of the two a draft currently is. That is why this page spends most of its length on the components and the criteria rather than on the idea of tutoring.

sections.heading: The four components, their weightings and their hard limits
paragraphs: Theatre's assessment structure is unusual enough that it is worth laying out before anything else. Standard Level students submit three components; Higher Level students submit the same three plus the solo theatre piece, and the weightings of the shared three change to make room for it. Every one of them has a limit - a page count, a word count or a running time - and those limits are enforced. Work beyond the limit is not read.

The practical consequence is that Theatre rewards editing more than most Diploma subjects. A student with a strong argument and four pages too many will score worse than a student with a weaker argument that fits. A tutor spends a meaningful share of session time on compression: deciding which staging decision carries the most analytical weight, and cutting the two that merely show enthusiasm. That is uncomfortable work for a student who is proud of the material being cut, which is part of why an outside reader helps.

The weightings below reflect the structure of the current Theatre guide. Because the IB revises subject guides on a cycle and because internal deadlines differ between schools, treat the figures as the shape of the course and confirm the detail against your child's IB coordinator and the subject guide the school is actually teaching. We publish no IB examination or results dates on this page, because the IB's own site does not serve them to automated checks and an unverified date on a page like this is worse than no date.

One more structural point that matters for planning: the components are not independent in practice even though they are marked separately. The research done for the presentation feeds the staging vocabulary used in the notebook. The collaborative project forces the student to defend intention in writing, which is exactly the skill the solo report needs. Sequencing them deliberately is worth more than treating each as a fresh start.

sections.heading: The director's notebook: an unfamiliar play text and a page limit
paragraphs: The notebook is the component Dubai students most often arrive wanting help with, and the reason is structural. It asks for a response to a published play text the student has not studied in class, which removes the safety net of a teacher's reading. Students who have spent two years analysing texts in English A find this manageable. Students whose analytical practice has all been through performance find it the hardest thing in the course.

What the criteria reward is a chain: a decision about how a moment would be staged, a reason grounded in the text, and an account of the effect intended on an audience. Three of those four links are usually present in a weak draft and the missing one is nearly always the textual grounding. A student will write that a scene should be lit from below to unsettle the audience without pointing to the line, stage direction or structural turn that makes unsettlement the right intention there.

The second failure mode is scale. A notebook that tries to stage an entire play in the page limit becomes a list. A notebook that picks a small number of moments and defends each one properly reads as the work of a director. Choosing those moments is a genuine skill and it is teachable in two sessions: the student learns to look for moments where the text under-specifies, because those are the moments where a director's choice is visible and therefore assessable.

A tutor's role here is bounded and worth stating plainly. The notebook must be the student's own work. A tutor may discuss the play, explain what a criterion is asking for, and give feedback on a draft the student has written. A tutor never produces the notebook, never rewrites paragraphs into their own prose, and never supplies staging decisions for the student to adopt as theirs. Those lines come from IB academic-honesty rules, and the cost of crossing them falls on the student.

sections.heading: The research presentation: a tradition that is not your own
paragraphs: The research presentation asks a student to investigate a theatre tradition unfamiliar to them, evidence its conventions, and demonstrate at least one of those conventions practically on camera. In Dubai this component has a specific and avoidable failure pattern. The emirate's student body is genuinely international, so the phrase unfamiliar tradition is less obvious than it sounds, and students regularly choose a tradition that is either too close to their own experience or so poorly documented in accessible sources that the research cannot be evidenced.

The fix is to choose for the sources rather than for the appeal. A tradition with a substantial body of writing behind it, available in a language the student reads, with at least some recorded performance to watch, gives the student something to cite and something to imitate. A tradition picked from a two-paragraph encyclopaedia entry gives them neither, and the presentation collapses into general statements about culture that the criteria cannot reward.

The practical demonstration is the part students under-rehearse. A convention has to be shown, not described, and shown with enough control that it reads as the convention rather than as an approximation. That means physical practice, and it is the one part of Theatre tutoring that genuinely benefits from a tutor watching a live attempt - which a video call does perfectly well, since the student needs feedback on what is visible on camera anyway, because what is submitted is a recording.

Sources also need handling. A list of links is not a bibliography, and the criteria notice the difference between a student who has read three substantial sources and one who has skimmed twelve. We never supply IB, Cambridge or Pearson documents as downloads; a tutor points to the official subject page or the library catalogue and the student does the reading.

sections.heading: The collaborative project and the solo piece: both marked on the writing
paragraphs: The collaborative project is the component that produces the biggest gap between how a Theatre cohort feels about its work and what the cohort scores. An ensemble creates an original piece from a starting point, performs it, and submits a project report with video evidence. Students remember the performance. The assessment reads the report. A group that staged something genuinely inventive and then wrote the report in two evenings will be marked on the two evenings.

What the report has to do is explain intention and process: where the starting point led, what the ensemble decided and why, what was tried and abandoned, and how the final piece addressed the audience it was made for. Groups who kept notes as they went have this material. Groups who did not end up reconstructing it from memory, which produces a narrative of events rather than an account of decisions. A tutor can set the note-keeping habit early; reconstructing it afterwards is much harder.

The solo theatre piece, which only Higher Level students submit, reverses the usual order of work. The theory comes first. A student chooses an aspect of theatre theory, understands it well enough to say what it claims, and then builds a short solo performance that demonstrates that claim in practice. Students who devise the piece first and attach a theorist afterwards can usually be identified in the first paragraph of the report, because the theory sits on top of the performance rather than inside it.

Both components reward the same habit, which is why they are treated together here: write while you make. The student who keeps a running record of decisions during rehearsal has a report; the student who only rehearses has a memory. In sessions this looks mundane - ten minutes at the end of each meeting spent writing down what changed and why - and it is the single highest-return habit a Theatre tutor can install.

sections.heading: Where Theatre marks are actually lost
paragraphs: Over a term of marking drafts, the same handful of problems account for most of the gap between a 4 and a 6. They are diagnosable from a single draft, which is why the free trial lesson is used as a diagnostic rather than as a sample lesson. A student brings whatever they have, the tutor reads it, and the session ends with a named problem instead of an impression.

The table below maps the symptom a parent or student can see onto the criterion it damages and the change that fixes it. It is deliberately specific. Generic feedback - be more analytical, add more detail, show more understanding - is the commonest thing in a weak Theatre draft's margin, and it is unactionable. A student can act on cut these three staging ideas and defend the remaining two against the text.

Two of these problems are habits rather than gaps in knowledge, and habits take longer to change than facts. Describing instead of justifying, and writing after making instead of while making, both need several weeks of corrected work before they stick. That is the honest answer to how long Theatre tutoring takes: a component block can rescue a deadline, but changing how a student writes about performance is a term's work.

The remaining problems are quicker. Page and time limits are an editing task. A missing source trail is a reading task. Choosing assessable moments in a play text is a technique that transfers after two or three worked examples. A tutor who separates the quick fixes from the slow ones can tell you, honestly, what is achievable before the next deadline and what is not.

sections.heading: A Theatre year counted backwards from the May session
paragraphs: Theatre has no examination to count back from, which sounds relaxing and is the opposite. Every deadline is internal, set by the school, and clustered in the months when the rest of the Diploma is also due. The students who struggle are not usually the weakest performers; they are the ones who met four internal deadlines in six weeks and wrote everything twice as fast as they should have.

The planning table below is built from school-set milestones rather than IB dates. We publish no IB examination or results dates anywhere on this page. The IB's own site does not serve its calendar to automated checks, so any date we restated would be second-hand, and a second-hand date on a planning table is exactly the kind of error that costs a family a deadline. Ask your child's IB coordinator for the school's assessment calendar; it is the document the whole plan should be built on.

What the table does give you is the shape of the two years and the question to ask at each point. Most of those questions have nothing to do with tutoring. Has the research tradition been chosen? Does the ensemble have a decision log? Is there a play text in hand for the notebook? A family that can answer those four questions in the autumn of Year 13 is in a different position from one that cannot, regardless of who is tutoring.

For Dubai specifically, two calendar features deserve a note. School productions cluster in particular weeks and swallow evenings whole, so a tutoring plan that does not pause around them will simply be missed. Ramadan shifts the whole household's working day, and students frequently prefer post-Iftar sessions during that month; that is a scheduling change we make without argument, and it is one of the practical advantages of a tutor who is not driving anywhere.

sections.heading: Online one-to-one, in-home tutoring and what Dubai charges for each
paragraphs: Families searching for Theatre help in Dubai usually start by looking for somebody who can come to the house, because that is how private tuition has traditionally worked here. It is worth being direct about what that market looks like and then about what we actually sell. IB Gram delivers tuition to UAE families as one-to-one lessons over live video. We do not send tutors to homes anywhere in the UAE; home visits are a service we run only in India, and no sentence on this site should be read as an offer of one in Dubai.

The reason is not cost, it is supply. There are a limited number of people in the UAE who have taught IB DP Theatre and read its components against the criteria, and the chance that one of them lives within a thirty-minute drive of any given Dubai community is low. Restricting the search to people who can travel to your address means choosing from whoever is near, which on a subject this specialised usually means a general drama or English tutor. Removing the travel constraint means choosing from people who have actually taught the course.

The second reason is that Theatre's assessed artefacts are files. A notebook page, a slide deck, a source list, a recording: all of them are better handled with a shared screen and a cursor than with two people looking at a laptop on a kitchen table. For the one part of the course that is physical - rehearsing a convention for the research presentation - the student is being recorded anyway, so feedback on what the camera sees is the feedback that counts.

On price, the figures below are market rates in Dubai gathered in October 2026, attributed to the providers who publish them. They are not an IB Gram price list. Our own arrangement starts with a free trial lesson and a consultation, and the rate for a specialist depends on the component, the level and the availability, so quoting a single number here would be misleading. The one fee context worth adding: KHDA confirmed in May 2026 that private school fees in Dubai would not rise for the 2026-27 academic year, so tutoring is the variable line in most families' education budget this year.

sections.heading: Academic honesty, tutor permits and the Dubai school week
paragraphs: Theatre's assessment is almost entirely coursework, which puts academic honesty closer to the centre of this subject than to most. The IB's position is unambiguous: the work submitted must be the student's own. For a tutor that produces a clear boundary. Teaching the component, explaining a criterion, discussing a play text, asking the questions that make a student find their own staging decision and giving written feedback on a draft the student has written are all legitimate. Supplying prose, supplying decisions, or editing a report to completion is not, and a student caught doing it faces a malpractice finding rather than a low mark.

We also do not supply IB, Cambridge or Pearson materials. Subject guides, past material and mark schemes belong to the boards; a tutor cites the official page and the student or school obtains the document through the proper route. Any tutoring service offering a bank of downloadable IB documents for a subject like this is a problem for your child, not a convenience.

On permits, the UAE position is specific and worth knowing as a parent. Private tutoring in the UAE requires a work permit issued through MoHRE under Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023. The permit is granted free of charge for two years, the eligible categories include registered school teachers, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and school students aged fifteen to eighteen, and MoHRE's own service page lists no fee and a two-working-day completion time. Individuals offering private tutoring without it are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws; no fine schedule has been published, so no amount should be quoted to you.

Two further constraints shape a Dubai Theatre student's week. Arabic, Islamic Education and social and moral studies are mandatory in Dubai private schools regardless of the licensed international curriculum, and KHDA requires separate classes for Arab and non-Arab students in Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, with combined classes prohibited. Those lessons occupy timetable space that a Theatre student might otherwise have for rehearsal. And in Abu Dhabi, where some Dubai families have relatives looking for the same help, ADEK's professional-ethics rules bar school staff from paid private tutoring of students enrolled at their own school - a reason not to ask your child's own drama teacher for paid sessions.
