faqs.question: Does IB DP Theatre have a written examination?
faqs.answer: No. Theatre is assessed entirely on submitted coursework, with no written paper at either Standard or Higher Level. Standard Level students submit three components - the director's notebook, the research presentation and the collaborative project. Higher Level students submit those three plus the solo theatre piece. Every one of them goes in to a deadline set by your child's school rather than to an examination timetable. That has a practical consequence worth planning around: a weak term cannot be rescued by past-paper practice in April, because there is no paper to practise. The work that counts has already been submitted by then.

faqs.question: How is the director's notebook marked, and how long is it allowed to be?
faqs.answer: The notebook responds to a published play text your child has not studied, and it is marked on how well staging and design decisions are justified against that text and on the intended effect on an audience. There is a strict page limit, and pages beyond it are not read, so editing is part of the task rather than an afterthought. Most weak drafts fail on grounding rather than imagination: the student describes a striking idea without pointing to the line or stage direction that makes it the right idea. Confirm the current page limit with your child's IB coordinator, since subject guides are revised on a cycle.

faqs.question: What actually counts as a theatre tradition for the research presentation?
faqs.answer: It has to be a tradition outside your child's own experience, which in a city as international as Dubai is a judgement rather than an obvious choice. A student with family roots in a tradition cannot use it, however well they know it. The better test is scholarly: pick a tradition with substantial writing behind it in a language your child reads, and with recorded performance available to watch. That gives them conventions to evidence and something to imitate for the practical demonstration. A tradition chosen from a short web entry leaves nothing to cite and the presentation drifts into general cultural description.

faqs.question: Is the collaborative project marked on the performance or on the report?
faqs.answer: The report carries the assessment. Video evidence of the performance is submitted, but it is evidence rather than the thing being marked, and it has a time limit. What the report has to do is explain the process: where the starting point led, what the ensemble decided, what was tried and abandoned, and how the final piece addressed its audience. Groups that kept a decision log while devising already have this material. Groups that did not end up reconstructing events from memory, which produces narrative instead of analysis and is the commonest reason an inventive piece scores modestly.

faqs.question: What is the solo theatre piece and which students have to submit it?
faqs.answer: Only Higher Level students submit it. The student chooses an aspect of theatre theory, understands what it claims, and builds a short solo performance that demonstrates that claim, submitted with a written report inside a word limit. The order matters more than anything else in this component: theory first, performance second. A piece devised for its own sake with a theorist attached afterwards shows the join in the first paragraph of the report, because the theory sits on top of the work rather than driving it. Rebuilding a piece around its theory usually takes three or four sessions.

faqs.question: Can an online tutor really help with a practical subject like Theatre?
faqs.answer: For this subject it fits unusually well, because what gets submitted is files. A notebook page, a slide deck, a source list, a project report and a video are all things two people can work on better with a shared screen than with a laptop on a kitchen table. The one physical element is rehearsing a convention for the research presentation, and since that is recorded for submission anyway, feedback on what the camera sees is the feedback that matters. What a video call cannot replace is the school's rehearsal space and ensemble, which the school already provides.

faqs.question: My child is strong on stage but the Theatre grade is low. What is going wrong?
faqs.answer: Almost always the same thing: the assessed work is analytical writing about performance, and nobody has shown the student what the criteria reward. A confident performer can produce a notebook full of vivid description and score modestly, because description is not justification. The diagnosis takes one reading of a draft. The fix is a chain the student learns to write - decision, evidence from the text, intended effect on the audience - applied to a small number of moments rather than to the whole play. That habit takes several weeks of corrected work to settle, not one session.

faqs.question: How much of the Theatre portfolio should be finished by the end of Year 12?
faqs.answer: It depends on your child's school, which is the honest answer and the reason we ask for the assessment calendar first. Many Dubai schools perform the collaborative project in the summer term of Year 12, which means the video evidence and a first draft of the report should exist by then. Others run it in Year 13 alongside the research presentation. What should exist by the end of Year 12 in every case is a decision log for the project, a working journal habit, and a shortlist of research traditions chosen for their available scholarship rather than for their appeal.

faqs.question: Does IB Gram send a drama tutor to our home in Dubai?
faqs.answer: No. IB Gram does not send tutors to homes anywhere in the UAE; home visits are a service we offer only in India. Tuition for Dubai families is delivered one-to-one over live video, scheduled on Gulf Standard Time. For Theatre that is a strength rather than a compromise, because the pool of people who have taught the Diploma components is small and spread across time zones, and restricting the search to those who can drive to your community usually means choosing a general drama tutor instead of a Theatre specialist.

faqs.question: What does IB DP Theatre tuition cost per hour in Dubai?
faqs.answer: Published market rates in Dubai, gathered in October 2026, run from roughly AED 45-150 an hour for budget online tutors, AED 150-300 for a qualified subject tutor online, AED 180-500 for in-home visits including travel, and AED 200-450 or more for an IB specialist; one premium provider publishes AED 650. Those are other providers' figures, attributed to them, not an IB Gram price list. Our own arrangement starts with a free trial lesson and a consultation, because the rate for a Theatre specialist depends on the component, the level and who is available.

faqs.question: Can a tutor help choose the play text for the director's notebook?
faqs.answer: The text is normally issued by the IB for the session rather than chosen, so the real question is how a student approaches an unfamiliar one. A tutor can absolutely teach that: how to read for moments where the text under-specifies, because those are where a director's choice becomes visible and therefore assessable; how to build a decision-evidence-effect chain; and how to cut material that shows enthusiasm rather than judgement. What a tutor does not do is supply staging decisions for your child to present as their own, which would be an academic-honesty breach.

faqs.question: Will taking Theatre at Higher Level hurt a competitive university application?
faqs.answer: It depends entirely on the course being applied for, and it is worth settling before subject choices are locked. Courses with named subject prerequisites - medicine, engineering, many sciences - expect those subjects at Higher Level, so Theatre HL has to fit around them rather than displace one. For arts, humanities, law, business and communication routes it reads as a genuine Higher Level subject with a substantial portfolio behind it. The useful move in Year 11 is to list the target courses, check their published entry requirements directly, and choose from there rather than from reputation.

faqs.question: Which Dubai schools offer IB DP Theatre?
faqs.answer: Theatre is offered mainly by the full-continuum IB schools rather than across the whole private sector, which is why the catchment for any one school is wide. Dubai International Academy Emirates Hills, Raffles World Academy, Uptown International School, Dwight School Dubai, Swiss International Scientific School Dubai and Deira International School are among the Dubai schools running Diploma arts pathways. Check the current subject list with the school directly, because arts options are among the first to change when a cohort is small. Schools are named here as context; IB Gram has no affiliation with any of them.

faqs.question: How do Theatre deadlines work around Ramadan and school production weeks?
faqs.answer: Both need planning into the schedule rather than reacting to. School productions swallow evenings whole for one or two weeks at a time, and a tutoring rhythm that ignores them is simply missed, so we pause around them and add the sessions back afterwards. During Ramadan many Dubai families prefer post-Iftar slots, and because the tutor is not travelling that is a straightforward change to make. Internal submission deadlines, by contrast, do not move for either, which is the argument for drafting earlier than feels necessary in the autumn term of Year 13.

faqs.question: What happens if no IB Theatre specialist is free when we need one?
faqs.answer: We tell you. Theatre is a small subject and the pool of tutors who have taught its components is genuinely limited, so there are windows where nobody suitable is available. In that case we will say what the realistic wait is, offer a different time slot where a specialist is free, or suggest that an English A tutor works on the analytical writing while the component knowledge waits - and be explicit that this is a partial substitute. What we will not do is fill the slot with somebody who has not taught Theatre and let you find out in session three.

dubai/ib-dp-theatre-online-tutor.closingHeading: Start with the next deadline, not with the subject
dubai/ib-dp-theatre-online-tutor.closingBody: If you are looking for an IB DP Theatre online tutor in Dubai, the quickest way to a useful first session is to send two things: the dates your child's school has set for each component, and the most recent draft or marked piece of work. From those we can tell you which component the first session should address and whether the problem is knowledge, writing habit or simply time. The trial lesson is free, the tutor is named before you book, and lessons run one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time. If we cannot cover the component properly in the window you need, we will say so rather than take the booking.

intro.heading: In Theatre, the evidence of progress is the only evidence there is
paragraphs: DP Theatre has no examination paper. There is no three-hour sitting in May where a student can rescue a weak year, and no mark scheme that rewards a strong performance on the night. Everything that counts is a document the school uploads: a director's notebook, a recorded research presentation, a collaborative project report, and at Higher Level a solo piece with its own written submission. That changes what a tutor is for. Nobody raises a Theatre grade by covering content faster, because there is very little content to cover. The grade moves when a draft gets onto a page, is marked against the criterion it will actually be judged on, and the gap is written down where the student can read it.

Most Dubai families arrive at a page like this holding a report card and a predicted grade and nothing else. A predicted grade is a teacher's judgement, and in an arts subject with four separate submissions it can be formed from one rehearsal and a half-finished notebook. It is not evidence. The things a family can genuinely inspect are narrower and far more useful: how many pages exist, which criterion each page is addressing, what mark that page would earn if it were uploaded tomorrow, and what changed between the last draft and this one. Those four questions are answerable in an afternoon, and almost no family has ever been given the answers.

So the first session here is an audit rather than a lesson. The tutor asks for everything that exists — notebook pages, the research presentation outline, the collaborative project log, any recorded rehearsal, the school's own written feedback — and returns a one-page statement of position. Component by component: what is finished, what is a fragment, what has not been started, and what each would score if it were submitted on Friday. Parents routinely find that single document more useful than the first month of lessons, because it converts a vague worry into a list with dates on it.

From there the work runs on a weekly artefact. Each session produces something that can be filed and compared against the version before it: a marked page with criterion letters in the margin, a rewritten paragraph set beside the original, a checklist of what the presentation still has to prove. Nothing is reported as good progress. Progress in DP Theatre is a mark on a named criterion moving, on a stated date, on a page you can read for yourself. If that is not happening, the tutoring is not working, and a parent should be able to see it inside three weeks.

Delivery is online, one-to-one, over live video, with the tutor's screen showing the student's own document while it is annotated. IB Gram does not arrange home visits in the UAE; that service exists only in India. For this subject that helps rather than hurts. The assessed work is written and screen-based, a recorded rehearsal can be paused and replayed frame by frame in a way no sofa conversation allows, and a family in Dubai ends up choosing from Theatre specialists rather than from whoever can reach Jumeirah by four o'clock on a Tuesday.

dubai/ib-dp-theatre-tutor.programmesIntro: Theatre sits in Group 6 of the Diploma Programme, but the students who take it arrive from several different places in a Dubai school. The programmes below are the ones that feed into it or run alongside it, and each note says what that route leaves a student short of when the first notebook page is due.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Theatre is offered at Higher and Standard Level across both DP years. Standard Level students submit a director's notebook, a research presentation and a collaborative project. Higher Level students add the solo theatre piece, which carries its own written report and is the component most often started late. All four are internally set, externally assessed and uploaded by the school against school-set internal deadlines rather than a single public exam date.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai schools running DP Theatre tend to timetable it in a shared drama studio alongside school productions, which means rehearsal weeks and coursework weeks collide twice a year. Families who map the school's production calendar against its internal upload deadlines in the first term almost never hit the February panic that otherwise defines DP2.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: MYP Arts assesses knowing and understanding, developing skills, thinking creatively and responding, and it trains students to keep a process journal. That journal habit is the single most transferable thing a Dubai MYP student brings into DP Theatre, because the collaborative project is marked on documented process rather than on the finished piece. Students who treated the journal as an afterthought in Year 11 usually need it rebuilt from scratch in Year 12.
programmes.countryNote: Several Dubai IB continuum schools run MYP Arts on a rotation, so a student may have had one term of drama in three years before choosing DP Theatre. Checking how many contact hours of drama a child actually had before Year 12 is a better predictor of the first notebook mark than their MYP grade.

programmes.name: Cambridge and Pearson IGCSE Drama
programmes.description: A large share of Dubai DP Theatre students come from a British-curriculum Year 11 and have sat IGCSE Drama, where written work is a single examination paper and practical work is performed to a visiting examiner. The habits transfer badly. IGCSE rewards a confident performance and a tidy exam answer; DP Theatre rewards justified staging decisions written down for a reader who will never see the room.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai's British-curriculum schools dominate by enrolment and most run IGCSE at sixteen before splitting into A Level or the Diploma. A student moving from IGCSE Drama into DP Theatre in a Dubai school is usually the strongest performer in the group and the weakest writer, and the first notebook mark says so plainly.

programmes.name: The DP core alongside Theatre
programmes.description: Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and CAS run in parallel with Theatre and compete for the same evenings. Theatre students often register an Extended Essay in Theatre or in English, which can double the reading load in the same term as the collaborative project. Mapping the core deadlines against the Theatre upload dates is part of the audit, because the clash is predictable and fixable in October.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai students frequently use school productions and community drama for the creativity strand of CAS, which is legitimate, but the same work cannot be presented as both a CAS experience and part of an assessed Theatre task. Keeping those records separate from the start saves an awkward conversation with the DP coordinator later.

dubai/ib-dp-theatre-tutor.subjectsIntro: Theatre rarely travels alone. The subjects below are the ones Dubai Theatre students most often need support in at the same time, and each description says what the overlap actually is — shared writing skills, shared deadlines, or a shared habit that works in one subject and fails in the other.

subjects.name: Theatre
subjects.description: Four assessed tasks, no written paper. Marks are lost in the written submissions rather than in performance: unjustified staging choices, a research tradition described instead of demonstrated, and a project report that narrates the rehearsals rather than evidencing the process.

subjects.name: Literature and Performance
subjects.description: An interdisciplinary option combining Group 1 and Group 6. Students who take it alongside or instead of Theatre need the same skill — turning a reading of a text into a defended staging decision — but assessed under literary criteria, which reward close textual evidence more heavily.

subjects.name: English A: Literature
subjects.description: The commonest pairing with Theatre in Dubai schools. The individual oral and the HL essay demand the same discipline as a director's notebook: a narrow claim, evidence from the text, and an explanation of effect. Progress in one usually shows up in the other within a month.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: Paper 1 is an unseen non-literary text under time pressure. Theatre students tend to write fluently and loosely, which costs marks here, where the examiner wants the effect of a specific choice on a specific audience rather than a general impression.

subjects.name: Visual Arts
subjects.description: The other Group 6 subject with a heavy documented-process component. The comparative study and process portfolio punish the same habit that sinks a Theatre notebook: showing the outcome without showing the thinking that produced it. Students taking both often need one shared session on documentation.

subjects.name: Music
subjects.description: Assessed on exploring music in context, experimenting, and presenting, with written and recorded submissions. Music and Theatre students in Dubai often share a studio timetable and a production calendar, which means their coursework crunches land in the same fortnight.

subjects.name: Film
subjects.description: Textual analysis, comparative study and a film portfolio. Film students write about shot choice the way Theatre students should write about staging choice, and the two subjects reward the same move: name the decision, name the intended effect, evidence that it works.

subjects.name: Psychology
subjects.description: A frequent third subject for Theatre students and a useful one, because the internal assessment trains experimental write-up discipline. That discipline transfers directly to the research presentation, where sources have to be handled honestly rather than paraphrased from one website.

subjects.name: History
subjects.description: Theatre students researching a tradition outside their own experience are doing historical work whether they call it that or not. History teaches source evaluation, which is exactly what separates a research presentation that scores well from one that reports a Wikipedia summary with confidence.

dubai/ib-dp-theatre-tutor.regionsIntro: Dubai families book Theatre support from across the city, and the practical constraint differs by area: studio access, production weeks, commute to a drama facility, and what time an evening session can realistically begin. The notes below record what actually shapes a Theatre schedule in each area.

regions.name: Al Quoz
regions.note: Dubai's warehouse arts district, home to Alserkal Avenue and a cluster of independent studios and galleries. Students here have unusually good access to live performance and exhibitions, which makes a research presentation far easier to evidence with something they have actually seen.

regions.name: Jumeirah
regions.note: Dense with British-curriculum and IB schools and short commutes, so a 4pm start is realistic most days. Production weeks at the larger schools here tend to run close to the February internal deadlines, which is the clash to plan around.

regions.name: Al Barsha
regions.note: Several large IB continuum schools with purpose-built theatres, and heavy after-school programme timetables. Theatre students here often have rehearsal until six, so sessions sit at 7pm or later and the weekly artefact is written over the weekend.

regions.name: Dubai Hills Estate
regions.note: Newer schools with strong facilities and a family profile that often includes a second subject needing support. Sessions here are commonly booked as a pair — Theatre plus English A — in consecutive hours on the same evening.

regions.name: Mirdif
regions.note: A large catchment feeding several established schools with long-running drama programmes. Students travelling across the city to school lose an hour each way, which is why an online slot after dinner outperforms anything booked before six.

regions.name: Dubai Marina
regions.note: Apartment living, limited rehearsal space at home, and a student body that changes schools mid-programme more often than the city average. Continuity of records matters here: a transferring student needs the notebook and project log rebuilt, not restarted.

regions.name: Arabian Ranches
regions.note: Villa communities with longer school runs and a strong extracurricular culture. Theatre students here frequently use community productions for CAS, which is fine, provided the records are kept separate from the assessed collaborative project.

regions.name: Downtown Dubai
regions.note: Close to the city's major performance venues, with an unusually high share of students who attend professional theatre regularly. That is a genuine advantage for the research presentation, where first-hand observation is worth more than a secondary description.

schoolClusters.city: Al Sufouh, Jumeirah and Umm Suqeim
schoolClusters.note: The oldest concentration of selective British and IB schools in Dubai, most with a working theatre and an annual main-stage production. Students from this cluster usually have good studio access and weak notebook discipline, because the production schedule rewards performance over documentation.

schoolClusters.city: Al Barsha, Dubai Hills and Al Quoz
schoolClusters.note: A newer cluster with large IB continuum schools and purpose-built performance spaces. Several run MYP Arts on a rotation, so Year 12 Theatre groups here can contain students with very different amounts of prior drama experience, and the first marked notebook page is where that shows.

schoolClusters.city: Mirdif, Al Warqa and Academic City
schoolClusters.note: Long-established schools with deep extracurricular drama and large year groups. Commutes are the defining constraint: students here often cannot start a session before seven, so the weekly written artefact tends to be produced on a Friday or Saturday rather than mid-week.

dubai/ib-dp-theatre-tutor.modesIntro: Theatre support is bought in four distinct shapes, and the right one depends on how much of the portfolio already exists. All four are delivered one-to-one over live video, with the student's own document on screen and the session recorded if the family wants a copy.

modes.title: Weekly one-to-one with a written artefact
modes.description: A standing hour each week through a term. Each session takes the next piece of the portfolio forward and ends with something filed: a marked page, a rewritten section, or a criterion score with its reasoning. The record accumulates, which is what makes movement visible rather than asserted.
bullets: One hour weekly, same slot, Gulf Standard Time
A dated marked artefact after every session
Running criterion scores across all four tasks
A short written note to the parent each month

modes.title: Component sprint block
modes.description: Four to six sessions aimed at one task — usually the director's notebook or the research presentation — compressed into a fortnight ahead of a school deadline. Used when one component is badly behind and the others are broadly on track. The block ends with a submitted-ready draft and a written list of what was deliberately left imperfect.
bullets: Four to six hours inside two weeks
One named component, not the whole portfolio
A before-and-after criterion score on the same draft
Explicit note of what was not fixed and why

modes.title: Single marked read of a draft
modes.description: One hour in which an existing draft is marked against the published criteria and returned annotated, with a fifteen-minute conversation about the three changes that matter most. No ongoing commitment. Families often use this as a second opinion when a school's feedback has been brief or contradictory.
bullets: One draft, one hour, annotated and returned
Criterion-by-criterion score with reasoning
Three prioritised changes, ranked by marks at risk
No continuing booking required

modes.title: Holiday and production-week intensives
modes.description: Concentrated work during Dubai school holidays or the week after a main-stage production, when rehearsal has stopped and writing time appears. Typically three sessions in a week, used to convert a term of rehearsal notes into the documented process the collaborative project report needs.

sections.heading: What a search for an IB DP Theatre tutor in Dubai is usually trying to solve
paragraphs: An IB DP Theatre tutor in Dubai is almost never hired because a student cannot act. The search happens when a grade appears that does not match the family's impression of their child, and nobody can explain where it came from. The student is cast in the school production, enjoys the subject, talks about it at dinner, and is sitting on a 4. That gap is the subject's defining feature rather than a mystery, and it is diagnosable in a single hour.

The reason is structural. Every mark in DP Theatre comes from a written or recorded submission assessed against published criteria, and none of it comes from the quality of a performance in a Dubai school hall. A student can be the strongest performer in the group and still submit a director's notebook that describes what happens in a play without justifying a single staging decision. The notebook is the mark. The performance was the rehearsal for a different thing entirely.

What a family actually wants, then, is not more drama teaching. It is a translation service between what the student is already good at and the form in which the IB will pay for it, plus a record that shows whether the translation is working. That is why this page is built around artefacts and dates rather than around enthusiasm. If after four weeks there is no marked page with a criterion letter on it and no change in that letter, the money is being spent on company rather than on marks.

The honest limits are worth stating in the same breath. A tutor cannot direct the collaborative project, cannot be in the room for the solo piece, and cannot supply a theorist, a tradition or a play text and call it the student's choice. What a tutor can do is read, mark, question, model and record. Those five verbs cover everything on this page, and anything outside them is somebody else's business or nobody's.

sections.heading: The four assessed tasks, read as an evidence file
paragraphs: Start by turning the portfolio into a list of files rather than a list of worries. For each assessed task there is a thing the school will upload, and for each of those there is something a parent can inspect this week without any specialist knowledge. That is the whole audit. It takes about forty minutes and it is the only reliable way to find out how far behind a Theatre student actually is.

The table below sets out the four tasks in those terms. The weightings and formats are set by the current subject guide, which schools hold and which is revised periodically, so treat the column on what the school uploads as a prompt to ask the DP coordinator rather than as a quotation. The final row is there because it is the commonest misunderstanding in Dubai schools: the main-stage production, however good, carries no assessed Theatre marks by itself.

Reading the file this way changes the conversation at home. Instead of asking whether the Theatre work is going well, a parent can ask how many notebook pages exist and which play they are about. Instead of trusting that the research presentation is in hand, they can ask which tradition has been chosen and what the student has actually watched. Both questions have factual answers, and both expose a stalled component weeks before a school report does.

It also sets the order of work. A component with nothing in it is a different problem from a component with a weak draft, and the two need different hours. Nothing written is a starting problem, solved by producing a rough page fast and marking it hard. A weak draft is a precision problem, solved by criterion-level rewriting. Mixing the two up is the commonest way a term of tutoring produces no movement.

sections.heading: Reading a marked Theatre draft: what the annotations actually mean
paragraphs: Theatre teachers write in a compressed shorthand, and Dubai parents are rarely given the key. A comment like develop this or more detail needed sounds like a request for length when it is almost always a request for justification. Decoding the margin is the fastest free improvement available to a family, because it turns feedback the school has already given into instructions a student can follow.

The pattern is consistent across the four tasks. Comments about what was done point at description where analysis is required. Comments about why point at a missing link between an intention and its effect on an audience. Comments about evidence point at an assertion with nothing behind it. Comments about focus point at a notebook or presentation trying to cover a whole play or a whole tradition instead of a narrow, defensible slice of it.

The table translates the five comments that appear most often. Each row names the criterion area the comment is really addressing and what a single session does about it, because the fix is usually narrower than the comment sounds. Develop your staging choices does not mean write more pages; it means take one moment, name the decision, name the intended audience effect, and explain why that decision produces it.

Once a student can read their own feedback, the weekly session changes shape. They arrive having already identified which of the five patterns their last draft fell into, and the hour goes on execution rather than diagnosis. Families notice this transition about a month in, and it is the point at which the cost per mark starts to fall steeply.

sections.heading: A ten-week record: what movement in Theatre looks like week by week
paragraphs: Progress claims in arts subjects are easy to make and hard to check, so this page works to a fixed record instead. Ten weeks is roughly one Dubai school term between holidays, and it is long enough for two full drafting cycles on a single component. The point of publishing the shape of it is that a parent can hold the tutoring to it without knowing anything about Theatre.

The structure is deliberately front-loaded with marking rather than teaching. Weeks one and two produce a rough draft and a hard mark, because an unmarked blank page cannot be improved and a student who has never seen a criterion applied to their own writing cannot aim at it. The middle weeks are where the criterion scores either move or expose that the student has misunderstood the task rather than executed it badly. The last weeks protect what has been gained.

Three things are worth saying about the table. The criterion names in the subject guide are revised from time to time and schools hold the current version, so the column describing what is under test is framed by what it examines rather than by a letter that may change. The weeks are a sequence, not a calendar: a family starting in January runs the same ten steps compressed. And the final column is the one that matters, because it is the only column a parent can verify without the tutor present.

If three consecutive weeks produce no new artefact, something is wrong with the arrangement and not with the child. The commonest causes in Dubai are a production week nobody flagged, a clash with an Extended Essay deadline, or a student who has quietly not chosen a play text yet and is covering for it. All three are visible in the record within a fortnight, which is the entire reason for keeping one.

sections.heading: Where Theatre marks move quickly, and where they do not
paragraphs: Not all gains cost the same. In DP Theatre the cheapest marks are almost always in justification, because most students already hold the reasoning in their heads and simply never put it on the page. Taking a draft that says the actor moves downstage and turning it into a sentence that names the intended effect on the audience and the reason the move produces it is an hour's work and frequently the largest single movement a student makes all year.

The next cheapest is scope. Drafts that attempt a whole play, or a whole theatre tradition, are not ambitious; they are thin everywhere. Cutting the focus to one scene, one convention or one moment is a decision rather than a skill, and it can be made in a single session. Students resist it because narrowing feels like giving something up, which is why the record showing the mark move afterwards does more persuading than any explanation.

The expensive gains are different in kind. Genuine first-hand familiarity with a theatre tradition outside the student's own experience cannot be manufactured in a fortnight; it needs watching, reading and time. Research-presentation marks that depend on real practical understanding of a tradition's conventions sit behind that work, and a student who starts in February is buying a ceiling rather than a grade. The same is true of the solo piece at Higher Level, where a theorist chosen hastily constrains everything written afterwards.

This ordering is why the audit comes first and why the sequence of components is chosen rather than inherited. A student eight weeks from a school deadline should spend those weeks on justification and scope across whatever exists, not on starting the component that needs three months of looking. Saying so plainly costs a few billable hours and is the difference between a record that shows movement and one that shows activity.

sections.heading: Theatre in Dubai schools: facilities, productions and what a KHDA report tells you
paragraphs: Dubai's private-school sector is the densest in the UAE. In 2024-25 it taught 387,441 students across 227 private schools offering seventeen different curricula, with UK curriculum at 37 per cent of enrolment and the International Baccalaureate at 7 per cent, according to the Dubai Media Office. For Theatre that scale matters in a specific way: the number of schools running DP Theatre is a small fraction of the whole, so a student's cohort is often five or six people and the subject is taught by one person.

The Knowledge and Human Development Authority is responsible for enhancing and overseeing the quality of private education in Dubai, and it inspects schools on a six-band scale from Outstanding down to Very Weak. An inspection report is a useful document for a Theatre family, but not for the headline rating. The useful parts are the subject-level commentary and the sections on arts provision and student personal development, which occasionally say in plain words that the performing arts offer is thin or that older students lack independent research skills.

What a report will not tell you is whether the drama studio is actually free on a Wednesday, how many students sit DP Theatre, or whether the teacher has run the solo piece before. Those are questions for the DP coordinator, and they are reasonable to ask at an open evening. A school with an excellent inspection band can still be running Theatre for the first time, and a school in a middle band can have a drama department that has sent students to conservatoire for a decade.

Dubai's sector is also growing fast enough to change this picture year to year. KHDA has reported seven new private schools for the 2026-27 intake, four UK curriculum and three International Baccalaureate, creating 16,846 new places, after six opened during 2025-26 and enrolment rose six per cent. More IB schools means more DP Theatre cohorts, and in practice it also means more first-year Theatre teachers, which is precisely when an external reader of drafts earns their fee.

sections.heading: Academic honesty in a subject where some of the work is genuinely collaborative
paragraphs: Theatre makes the honesty question harder than most subjects, because one component is explicitly a group task. Students devise together, rehearse together and perform together, and then each writes an individual report about a shared process. The line is not between working alone and working with others; it is between shared experience and shared text. The experience is meant to be collective. Every word of the submission must be the student's own.

That rules a tutor's work into a narrow and useful band. A tutor may read a draft, mark it against the criteria, explain what a criterion is asking for, model the move on a different example, ask the questions that expose a gap, and record what changed. A tutor may not supply sentences for the submission, decide the theorist or the tradition, choose the play text, rewrite a paragraph into the student's file, or sit in a rehearsal as an uncredited co-director. The distinction is not administrative. Under IB academic-honesty rules the consequence of crossing it falls on the student, not on the tutor.

Three practical habits keep a family clearly on the right side. Keep dated drafts, so the evolution of the work is documented and the student's authorship is demonstrable. Keep a short note of what each outside session covered, which is also useful for the reflections that the core components require. And never accept a provider who offers finished coursework at a price; that trade exists in this market and it is an academic malpractice trigger that risks the whole Diploma.

It is also worth knowing who may legally teach your child here. Private tutoring in the UAE is regulated by permit: the MoHRE private tuition work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, is granted free of charge for two years, and covers categories including registered teachers, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents and university students. Individuals offering private tutoring without a permit from MoHRE are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws. In Abu Dhabi, ADEK's professional-ethics rules also bar school staff from paid tutoring of students at their own school, and the permit's code of conduct carries a similar restriction, so a request to hire your child's own class teacher privately should be refused rather than negotiated.

sections.heading: What Theatre support costs in Dubai, and what the free trial covers
paragraphs: Published market rates in Dubai are wide and worth knowing before any conversation about money. Budget online tutoring from platforms advertising university-student tutors runs from roughly AED 45 to AED 150 an hour; EdFlik advertises from AED 45 to AED 65 and Tutopiya from AED 33 to AED 52. Qualified subject tutors working online sit around AED 150 to AED 300, with Unitors publishing IGCSE from AED 150 and IB from AED 200. IB and A-Level specialists run from about AED 200 to AED 450 and beyond, with TutorChase publishing AED 270 and Bestimate's Tutoring Cost Dubai 2026 table showing AED 200 to AED 450 or more. In-home visits, where the travel is priced in, run roughly AED 180 to AED 500. Premium named or examiner-level tutoring reaches AED 650, as BartyED publishes. Those are other providers' published figures, read in October 2026, not IB Gram's price list.

For Theatre specifically the market is thinner than for Maths or Chemistry, and that pushes the number upward for in-home arrangements in particular, because very few people within driving distance of any Dubai neighbourhood have taught the subject. This is the practical argument for online delivery that has nothing to do with convenience: the pool of people who have actually marked a director's notebook is a national pool at best, and restricting it to a twenty-minute radius means paying a scarcity premium for a generalist.

What we publish instead of a rate card is the shape of the commitment. A free trial lesson of one hour comes first, with no card required and no obligation afterwards, and it is used for the audit rather than as a sales call: the family leaves it with the written statement of position whether or not they book anything. Pricing for continuing work is quoted per hour after that conversation, because a single marked read and a two-term portfolio rebuild are not the same product and a single number for both would be misleading.

One cost-in-context note that Dubai families often find useful. KHDA confirmed in May 2026 that there would be no increase in school fees for private schools in the emirate for the 2026-27 academic year, under Dubai's second economic incentives package valued at AED 1.5 billion. Tutoring is one of the few education costs in this market that a family controls directly, which is an argument for buying it in defined blocks against named components rather than as an open-ended weekly habit.

process.title: Send what exists
process.description: Share whatever is already written: notebook pages, a presentation outline, the project log, the school's feedback, any recorded rehearsal. Incomplete material is more useful than a tidy summary, because the gaps are the diagnosis. Nothing is required beyond what the student already has in a school folder.

process.title: The free trial hour and the audit
process.description: A one-hour trial lesson with a Theatre specialist, online and one-to-one, used to mark one piece of existing work and produce a written statement of position across all four tasks. No card is required and no booking follows automatically. The document is yours either way.

process.title: Agree the component order and the record
process.description: Decide which task is worked first and what artefact each session will produce, then fix the slot in Gulf Standard Time. The record format is agreed here too: criterion scores, dates, and a monthly written note. A family that knows what to expect can tell within three weeks whether it is happening.

process.title: Weekly artefacts and marked rewrites
process.description: Sessions run to the ten-week shape: rough draft, hard mark, criterion-level rewrites, then transfer to the next component. Every hour ends with something filed and dated. Drafts stay in the student's own file, written in the student's own words, with the session notes kept alongside.

process.title: Review against the record, then stop or continue
process.description: At the end of the block the scores and artefacts are read together. If criterion marks have moved, the next block is planned around the components still at risk. If they have not, the arrangement changes or ends; continuing a weekly habit that the record does not support is not in anyone's interest.

whyPoints.title: The artefact, not the reassurance
whyPoints.description: Every session produces something a parent can read: a marked page, a side-by-side rewrite, a criterion score with reasoning attached. Verbal reports of good progress are not accepted as evidence here, because in a subject with no examination they are the easiest thing in the world to produce.

whyPoints.title: Specialists in a thin subject
whyPoints.description: Very few tutors have marked a DP Theatre submission. Online delivery means a Dubai family chooses from people who have, rather than from whoever covers their neighbourhood. For Theatre that difference is larger than for any mainstream subject, because the assessment is unusual and the criteria are unforgiving.

whyPoints.title: An honest line on what a tutor may touch
whyPoints.description: Reading, marking, questioning, modelling and recording. Not writing, not deciding the theorist, not choosing the play text, not directing the project. The boundary is stated on the page because the consequence of crossing it under IB rules falls on the student, and because providers in this market do cross it.

whyPoints.title: Market rates published as market rates
whyPoints.description: Dubai AED bands appear here with the provider and the date attached, so a family can judge any quote they receive, including ours. No invented averages, no claim that a figure is typical without a source, and no price presented as ours when it belongs to somebody else's published table.

whyPoints.title: Scheduling that survives a Dubai term
whyPoints.description: Sessions sit in Gulf Standard Time around rehearsal, production weeks and the school run, and move to post-Iftar slots during Ramadan on request. Holiday intensives convert rehearsal notes into assessed writing during the weeks when the studio is closed and the writing time actually exists.

whyPoints.title: A stated fallback when nobody is free
whyPoints.description: DP Theatre specialists are scarce and sometimes none is available for the slot a family needs. We say so and offer the alternatives — a different time, a single marked read, a Group 1 specialist for the writing craft — rather than placing a generalist and describing them as a Theatre tutor.

faqs.question: How will we actually see that Theatre work is improving?
faqs.answer: By comparing artefacts rather than impressions. Each session produces a dated piece of work with a criterion score and a reason attached, and those sit in one file. After three sessions you can read the first marked draft and the current rewrite side by side and see whether the justification of staging choices has changed. If the score on a named criterion has not moved in three weeks, that is a finding rather than a bad patch, and it means the component order or the diagnosis was wrong. Movement you cannot read on a page is not movement in a subject with no examination paper.

faqs.question: Is DP Theatre marked by my child's school or by an external examiner?
faqs.answer: Theatre work is set and supervised internally but assessed externally once the school uploads it, so the teacher who knows your child is not the person awarding the mark. This matters more in Theatre than almost anywhere else, because the assessor never sees the rehearsal room, the production or the student's enthusiasm. They see a document and a recording. Anything persuasive about your child that exists only in the studio is invisible to them. Confirm the exact submission arrangements for the current session with your school's DP coordinator, since the subject guide and upload process are revised periodically.

faqs.question: What should we keep from every Theatre session?
faqs.answer: Four things, all small. The dated draft as it stood before the session. The marked version with the criterion scores and margin comments. A one-line note of what the hour covered. And the next action, written as a task rather than an intention. That set takes two minutes to file and does three jobs: it demonstrates the student's own authorship if anybody ever asks, it feeds the reflections the core components require, and it lets a parent audit the tutoring without being able to assess Theatre themselves. Families who keep it rarely need to ask whether the arrangement is working.

faqs.question: My child's Theatre predicted grade fell after the mock. What usually causes that?
faqs.answer: In Theatre a predicted grade typically falls when a teacher moves from judging potential to judging a draft. For most of DP1 the prediction rests on classroom presence and rehearsal quality. The first marked notebook or presentation replaces that with evidence, and if the writing describes rather than justifies, the grade drops sharply even though nothing about the student changed. It is a measurement event, not a decline. The useful response is to get the weakest existing draft marked hard against the criteria, because the fall usually traces to one habit that appears in every component at once.

faqs.question: How many marked drafts does a Theatre component usually need?
faqs.answer: Two full cycles is the common pattern: a rough draft marked hard, one criterion-level rewrite, a second mark, and a consolidation pass. Three cycles rarely adds much, because by then the remaining gains sit behind genuine familiarity with a text or tradition rather than behind writing craft. One cycle is often enough on a second component, since the lesson from the first transfers. A student who has produced four drafts of the same notebook and seen no movement has a diagnosis problem rather than a drafting problem, and the sensible next step is a second reader.

faqs.question: What does a criterion score out of a small total actually tell us?
faqs.answer: Less than parents expect in isolation, and a great deal in sequence. A single score tells you where one draft sat against one published descriptor on one day. Two scores on the same criterion three weeks apart tell you whether the teaching is landing. That is why scores here are always recorded with a date and the draft they refer to. Criterion names and mark allocations are set by the current subject guide, which your school holds, so ask the DP coordinator for the version in force rather than relying on a figure from a website or from an older cohort.

faqs.question: Can a tutor watch a rehearsal over video?
faqs.answer: A recorded rehearsal can be watched, paused and discussed, and that is often more useful than attending one, because the student can replay the exact moment under discussion and write about it afterwards. What a tutor must not do is direct the piece, give notes that shape the collaborative work, or contribute decisions that then appear in the submission as the student's own. The honest version is narrow: watch the recording, ask what the student intended, ask what the audience received, and help them write the distance between the two accurately.

faqs.question: Which Theatre task should we fix first if there is very little time left?
faqs.answer: Whichever one has marks most at risk and the shortest path to a defensible draft, which in practice is usually the director's notebook. Justification and scope are the cheap gains in this subject, and both can be applied to an existing notebook inside a fortnight. The research presentation is the wrong choice late, because its stronger marks depend on genuine familiarity with a tradition that takes weeks of watching and reading to build. Starting the component that needs three months with eight weeks left buys a ceiling, not a grade.

faqs.question: Is Theatre a sensible Higher Level choice for a student applying to competitive courses?
faqs.answer: It can be, and the decision belongs with the school's university counsellor rather than with a tutor, because it depends on the specific course requirements. What is true in general is that Theatre at Higher Level is a writing-heavy, research-heavy subject that universities read as evidence of independent project work. The risk is not prestige but load: the solo piece adds a fourth submission in the same term as the Extended Essay. Families who choose it and then map the deadlines in DP1 handle it well; those who discover the clash in February do not.

faqs.question: Our school changed the Theatre teacher mid-year. What should we check?
faqs.answer: Three things, in writing. Which play text and which tradition the student has already committed to, because a new teacher sometimes redirects choices that were already running and the lost time is rarely recoverable. The school's internal deadlines for each component, which can shift when staffing changes. And whether earlier feedback still stands, since a new marker may apply the criteria differently from the last one. A student with a dated file of drafts and marks comes through this well. One without any record effectively restarts.

faqs.question: How do we tell whether the research presentation topic is safe?
faqs.answer: Ask what the student has actually watched, read or practised, and how recently. A tradition the student can only describe from a few web pages produces a presentation that reports rather than demonstrates, and that ceiling is set the day the topic is chosen. A safe topic is one where primary material is genuinely available and where the student can show a convention in practice rather than explain it in the abstract. Living in Dubai helps here more than families realise, because the city's performance calendar and arts spaces put real work within reach.

faqs.question: Does the school production count towards any assessed Theatre task?
faqs.answer: Not on its own. A main-stage production is rehearsal discipline, confidence and often a good experience, and none of it is uploaded or marked. It can feed an assessed task indirectly, because material developed in it may inform a notebook or a project report, and it can legitimately serve the creativity strand of CAS. What it cannot do is substitute for the written submissions. Families in Dubai schools with strong drama departments are the ones most often caught by this, because the production consumes exactly the weeks the coursework needs.

faqs.question: How long before a Theatre grade moves measurably?
faqs.answer: Expect the first criterion score to move within three to four weeks if the problem is justification or scope, because both are writing habits that respond quickly once they are named and marked. A change in the overall subject grade is slower and depends on how many components are affected, since the final mark aggregates all of them. Anything behind genuine familiarity with a text or tradition takes a term. A provider promising a specific grade by a specific date is describing something nobody can deliver, in this subject or any other.

faqs.question: Do Theatre sessions run during Dubai school holidays?
faqs.answer: Yes, and the holidays are frequently the most productive weeks of the year for this subject. Rehearsal stops, the studio closes, and the writing time that term-time never provides suddenly exists. Intensive blocks of two or three sessions in a week are used to convert a term of rehearsal notes into the documented process a project report needs. Scheduling also shifts for Ramadan on request, with sessions moved to post-Iftar slots, and families travelling outside the UAE keep the same tutor because delivery is online.

faqs.question: Does IB Gram arrange a drama tutor who travels to our address in Dubai?
faqs.answer: No. IB Gram does not run home visits anywhere in the UAE; tutors visiting a family's address is a service we offer only in India. Dubai Theatre support is delivered one-to-one over live video, with the student's own notebook or report on screen while it is annotated. For this subject that is a genuine advantage rather than a compromise: the assessed work is written, recordings can be paused and replayed, and the family selects from people who have marked a director's notebook rather than from whoever can reach their area before five.

dubai/ib-dp-theatre-tutor.closingHeading: Start with the audit, not with a lesson

intro.heading: Judge a TOK tutor by what they hand back, not by what they promise
paragraphs: Theory of Knowledge is the subject Dubai parents understand least and worry about most, because nothing about it behaves like a normal DP course. There is no syllabus of content to revise. There are no past papers in the usual sense. The report that comes home says "developing" or "satisfactory progress" and tells you nothing you can act on. Then, somewhere in DP2, a number appears that can move the final diploma total by three points, and a letter appears that can end the diploma outright.

So the honest way to shop for an IB DP Theory of Knowledge home tutor in Dubai is to ignore the adjectives and ask for artefacts. Ask what your child will receive at the end of week two. Ask to see what a marked exhibition commentary looks like after a tutor has been through it. Ask which of the six prescribed titles the tutor would steer towards and why, and listen for whether the reasoning is about your child's own examples or about which title is supposedly easiest. A tutor who cannot show you a trail of annotated work has nothing to be judged on.

That evidence trail is the organising idea of this page. Each section below describes something checkable: how the two TOK tasks are actually marked, where the marks go missing in the order they tend to go missing, what the combined TOK and Extended Essay matrix does to the diploma total, what the Dubai market charges by provider model with the source of each figure named, and how a term of work is sequenced counting backwards from the May session rather than forwards from today.

A word on delivery, because the search phrase and the service are not the same thing. Home tutoring is what Dubai parents type, and it is a reasonable thing to want. We answer the question properly further down: what an in-home tutor in this emirate charges, what travel does to a 4pm start on Al Khail Road, and how families actually choose. IB Gram does not offer home visits in Dubai. Home visits are a service we run only in India. Lessons for Dubai families are online one-to-one TOK tuition over live video, and for TOK specifically that is not a compromise. TOK coaching is a conversation about a shared document. The tutor marks a paragraph while your child watches the cursor move, which is exactly what a screen does better than a dining table.

The other thing online delivery buys is the match. There are a few hundred DP schools in the Gulf and a much smaller number of adults who have read TOK scripts closely enough to tell you why a commentary stalls at a five. Restricting the search to people who can drive to Dubai Hills Estate by 4.30pm shrinks that pool to whoever is free. Removing the drive means your child gets the person who knows the instrument, which is the only variable in TOK that reliably moves a grade.

Everything factual below about TOK structure comes from the IB's own Theory of Knowledge guide and the Diploma Programme assessment procedures your child's DP coordinator holds. No IB exam or results date is published on this page, because the IB's site blocks automated checking and an unverified date is worse than no date. Where a milestone matters, we describe it relative to the session and tell you who to confirm it with.

dubai/ib-dp-theory-of-knowledge-home-tut.programmesIntro: TOK belongs to the Diploma Programme core, but the thinking it assesses is built years earlier. Below is where each IB programme leaves your child when TOK starts, and what that means for a Dubai student specifically.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: The two years where TOK is assessed. Alongside six subjects, students complete the exhibition in DP1 and the prescribed-title essay in DP2, plus the Extended Essay and CAS. TOK carries a minimum of one hundred teaching hours and is examined through one internal task and one external task. The grade is a letter from A to E, which then combines with the Extended Essay grade to award up to three points on top of the 42 available from subjects.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai runs the densest DP market in the Gulf, and the practical consequence for TOK is scheduling. DP timetables here are crowded with KHDA's mandatory Arabic, Islamic Education and Social Studies lessons, so TOK is often the period that gets moved or doubled up. Families end up buying back the thinking time outside school hours, usually in the evening.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: MYP does not assess TOK, but it is where the habits that TOK rewards are either built or missed. Interdisciplinary units, the personal project and the approaches-to-learning strands all ask students to justify a claim and name a limitation. A student who has argued in MYP arrives in TOK able to write a sentence that takes a position; one who has only summarised arrives able to describe.
programmes.countryNote: Several Dubai schools run MYP to Year 11 and then move students straight into DP1, skipping IGCSE entirely. Those students usually find the TOK exhibition easier than their IGCSE-trained classmates, because the personal project taught them to defend a choice. The ones who struggle are the transfers who arrive in DP1 from a content-heavy system in Year 11.

programmes.name: Career-related Programme
programmes.description: The CP core includes personal and professional skills rather than TOK, so a CP student does not sit the exhibition or the essay. The reason it matters on this page is that Dubai families sometimes compare CP and DP after a difficult DP1, and TOK plus the Extended Essay is the part of the DP core that most often triggers that conversation. Knowing which core components transfer and which do not is worth a session on its own.
programmes.countryNote: A small number of Dubai schools offer CP alongside DP, and the switch is usually discussed in the DP1 spring. A tutor's job in that conversation is to be accurate about what moving costs and what it saves, and then to point you back to your DP coordinator, who holds the registration deadlines.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: PYP is listed here for completeness rather than for TOK support. Its relevance is that the PYP exhibition in Year 6 is the first time an IB student is asked to present an inquiry and answer questions about it. Parents who remember that evening recognise the TOK exhibition immediately: three objects, a prompt, and a child explaining why these things count as knowledge.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai has a long PYP tail, with many schools running PYP and then handing students to a British-curriculum middle school. If your child did PYP somewhere in Dubai and is now in DP at a different school, the exhibition format will feel more familiar to them than it does to you.

dubai/ib-dp-theory-of-knowledge-home-tut.subjectsIntro: TOK is not a subject in the normal sense, so the grid below is the course as it is actually taught: one core theme, the optional themes a Dubai school is likely to choose, and the five areas of knowledge that supply the examples your child will argue from.

subjects.name: Core theme: knowledge and the knower
subjects.description: The opening unit and the one that produces most of the usable exhibition objects. It asks who the knower is, what communities of knowers do to a claim, and how bias, culture and language shape what a person accepts. Weak essays treat this theme as autobiography; strong ones use it to complicate a claim they have just made.

subjects.name: Optional theme: knowledge and technology
subjects.levels: One of two optional themes a school selects
subjects.description: The most commonly chosen option in Gulf schools, and the one where students find current examples easily and then use them badly. The test is whether a student can move from an anecdote about an algorithm to a claim about reliability, replication or authorship that an examiner can assess.

subjects.name: Optional theme: knowledge and language
subjects.levels: One of two optional themes a school selects
subjects.description: Rich territory for Dubai students, most of whom work across at least two languages daily. Translation loss, untranslatable terms and the difference between a technical and an everyday register are all first-hand examples rather than borrowed ones, which is exactly what the instrument rewards.

subjects.name: Optional theme: knowledge and politics
subjects.levels: One of two optional themes a school selects
subjects.description: Demands care rather than avoidance. The skill being assessed is the handling of competing perspectives, not the holding of a position. Sessions here focus on separating a political claim from the knowledge question underneath it, which is also the fastest route out of a one-sided essay.

subjects.name: Optional theme: knowledge and religion
subjects.levels: One of two optional themes a school selects
subjects.description: Taught in several Dubai schools and often the theme where students write most carefully. The examinable skill is the comparison of methods and standards of justification across communities. Respectful precision scores; vagueness does not.

subjects.name: Area of knowledge: history
subjects.description: The area students reach for first, because the perspectives problem is visible. Marks arrive when a student can say what counts as evidence for a historian and what a historian cannot do, rather than listing historical disagreements.

subjects.name: Area of knowledge: the human sciences
subjects.description: Where the strongest essays usually come from, because method is contestable and measurable at the same time. Replication, operationalisation and the problem of studying people who know they are being studied all give a student something concrete to argue with.

subjects.name: Area of knowledge: the natural sciences
subjects.description: Students who take two HL sciences often write their best TOK on this area, but only after they stop treating science as the benchmark everything else fails. The productive move is examining what the scientific method rules out and what that exclusion costs.

subjects.name: Area of knowledge: mathematics
subjects.description: Underused and therefore valuable. Proof, axioms, and whether mathematical objects are discovered or invented give a student arguments no examiner has read forty times that week. Maths AA HL students have the vocabulary already.

subjects.name: Area of knowledge: the arts
subjects.description: The area where exhibition objects are easiest to find and commentaries most often drift into description. The discipline is to link the object to the prompt in the first two sentences, then justify, then stop.

subjects.name: The TOK exhibition
subjects.levels: Internally marked, one third of the grade
subjects.description: Three objects, one IA prompt chosen from the published list, and a commentary of up to 950 words in total. Each object needs a real-world specificity the examiner can picture, plus a justification of why it connects to that prompt.

subjects.name: The TOK essay
subjects.levels: Externally marked, two thirds of the grade
subjects.description: Up to 1,600 words on one of six prescribed titles released for the session, written with reference to two areas of knowledge. Marked on a single holistic judgement about the quality and clarity of the sustained argument.

dubai/ib-dp-theory-of-knowledge-home-tut.regionsIntro: TOK sessions cluster in the communities that feed Dubai's DP schools, and the booking pattern changes by area because the school run does. Below is what that looks like in practice, and why an online slot holds where a drive does not.

regions.note: Heavy DP catchment with families spread across villas and apartments on both sides of Al Khail Road. The 4pm to 5pm window is the one parents ask for and the one a driving tutor cannot reliably hit. Exhibition work tends to start here in the DP1 spring term.

schoolClusters.city: Central and new Dubai DP schools
schoolClusters.note: The DP schools inside the Sheikh Zayed Road and Al Khail corridor account for most TOK enquiries we see from Dubai. Students we support attend schools across this cluster, and each runs TOK on its own internal calendar, which is the single most important thing a tutor needs to know before planning a term.

schoolClusters.city: Outer Dubai and the southern corridor
schoolClusters.note: DP provision south and east of the city centre has grown quickly, and these schools are the ones furthest from any realistic in-home tutor pool. Students we support attend schools in this cluster, and online delivery is the difference between a TOK specialist and nobody at all.

schoolClusters.city: Deira, Mirdif and the eastern communities
schoolClusters.note: Older, larger schools with long-running DP cohorts and timetables that already carry KHDA's mandatory subject load. TOK periods here are frequently the ones displaced, which is why so many eastern-community bookings are catch-up work rather than extension.

dubai/ib-dp-theory-of-knowledge-home-tut.modesIntro: Three ways Dubai families run TOK support, with the trade-offs stated. All three are delivered one-to-one over live video, scheduled on Gulf Standard Time.

modes.title: Weekly one-to-one through DP1 and DP2
modes.description: A standing sixty-minute slot, usually on the same evening each week. Through DP1 it tracks the exhibition: objects chosen, prompt fixed, commentary drafted, commentary cut to the word ceiling. Through DP2 it tracks the essay: title shortlist, knowledge questions, two areas of knowledge chosen, then draft after draft. The value of weekly work in TOK is accumulation, because the thinking has to become a habit rather than a performance.

modes.title: Exhibition block in DP1
modes.description: A short, dense sequence of four to six sessions aimed at one task. Most Dubai students arrive having picked three objects that are too general and an IA prompt that sounds interesting but gives them nothing to argue with. The block fixes the prompt first, tests each object against it, and then writes the commentary to the ceiling rather than cutting a long draft down. Ending under 950 words with every justification intact is the point.

modes.description: Booked once the prescribed titles for the session are released and the school's internal deadline is known. Six to ten sessions, pacing the draft cycle so that each version is read, questioned and rewritten by the student rather than polished by the tutor. The deliverable a parent can inspect is the comment history: a document where you can scroll back and watch an argument get sharper.

sections.heading: What a TOK tutor should hand back in the first fortnight
paragraphs: An IB DP Theory of Knowledge home tutor in Dubai is worth paying for only if the work leaves a trail. Two weeks in, you should be holding four things: a marked draft, a written diagnosis of where it sits, a list of the student's own examples that are strong enough to reuse, and a dated plan running to the school's internal deadline. If all you have is a description of how the sessions went, there is nothing to evaluate and nothing to compare against next month.

The marked draft is the centre of it. TOK is assessed on one holistic judgement rather than a tally of criteria, which means feedback has to describe the whole piece, not just fix sentences. A usable annotation does three things at once: it names what the paragraph is currently doing, it names what the instrument expects at the band above, and it asks a question the student has to answer themselves. Feedback that rewrites the sentence has taught nothing and has also crossed a line we come back to further down.

The written diagnosis should be short and uncomfortable. A good one says something like: the essay currently describes two areas of knowledge rather than arguing between them, every example is from a news article rather than from the student's own experience of a subject, and the counter-argument appears in the final paragraph where it cannot do any work. Three specific failures a parent can read and understand are worth more than a page of encouragement.

The example list matters more than parents expect. Strong TOK students carry six to eight examples they genuinely own, drawn from their own subjects, their own languages, and their own school life, and they reuse them across the exhibition and the essay. Building that list is a tutor's most transferable contribution, because it survives the particular title and the particular prompt.

The plan should count backwards from the school's deadline, not forwards from today, and it should name what happens in the weeks that will be lost: school mocks, Ramadan, travel, the IA deadlines in three other subjects landing in the same fortnight. A plan that assumes twelve clear weeks between now and the upload is a plan that has not met a DP2 student in Dubai.
bullets: Week one: diagnosis of the current draft and a dated plan to the internal deadline
Week two: the example list, written down and tested against the prompt or title
Every session: a short written note naming what moved
Every draft: annotated against the assessment instrument, with questions not rewrites

sections.heading: How TOK is actually assessed, task by task
paragraphs: TOK is assessed through two tasks, and almost every misunderstanding we meet comes from parents assuming there is an exam. There is not. One task is marked inside the school and moderated by the IB; the other is marked externally by an IB examiner who has never met your child. Between them they produce a single letter grade from A to E.

The exhibition is the DP1 task. The student selects one prompt from the published list of knowledge-and-the-knower style IA prompts, then chooses three specific objects that exist in the world rather than categories of object. A photograph of a particular protest banner is an object; "social media" is not. The commentary explains, for each object, what it is and why it connects to the chosen prompt. The total ceiling across all three is 950 words, and the mark is a single holistic judgement out of ten.

The essay is the DP2 task and carries the larger share. The IB releases six prescribed titles for each session, and the student answers one of them in up to 1,600 words with reference to two areas of knowledge. The mark is again a single holistic judgement out of ten, made on how clear and sustained the argument is, how well the areas of knowledge are used as evidence rather than as decoration, and whether different perspectives are genuinely weighed.

Both tasks sit alongside a planning and progress form, which is not marked. It records the interactions between student and teacher and exists so that authenticity can be established. Parents sometimes treat these forms as administration. They are the document that protects a student if authorship is ever questioned, and a tutor who encourages a student to fill one in loosely is doing real harm.

The two marks combine into the letter grade, and that letter then goes into the matrix with the Extended Essay grade. The table below is the shape of the thing; the section after it is what the matrix does to the diploma total.

sections.heading: The TOK and Extended Essay matrix, and why a C is not safe
paragraphs: Six subjects give a DP student up to 42 points. The remaining three come from the TOK and Extended Essay matrix, which reads the two core grades together and awards between zero and three. Dubai parents usually know the three points exist and usually do not know how asymmetric the grid is, which is why a predicted C in both components gets treated as comfortable when it is in fact worth a single point.

The grid is symmetrical and it is steep at the top. Two A grades return three points. An A paired with a B also returns three. Two B grades return two. A B with a D returns one. Two C grades return one, and a C paired with a D returns nothing at all. The practical reading is that moving one component by a single letter in the middle of the grid is often worth a whole point, which on a university offer pitched at 38 is the difference between meeting it and not.

The second thing the grid encodes is the failing condition. A grade E in either TOK or the Extended Essay is a failing condition for the diploma, whatever the subject points say. A student sitting on 40 points with an E in TOK does not have a diploma. This is the single most important fact on this page, and it is the reason an early, unsentimental diagnosis of a weak exhibition matters more than any amount of final-term intensity.

The matrix also changes which component is worth working on. If the Extended Essay is already drafted and sitting comfortably at a B, a letter of movement in TOK may be worth a point. If TOK is a secure B and the Extended Essay is a shaky C, the hours belong to the essay. A tutor who looks at both core grades together before recommending a schedule is doing the arithmetic a parent is paying for; one who sells TOK hours regardless is not.

Confirm the current grid against the Diploma Programme assessment procedures your school holds before you plan around it. The matrix has been stable for years, but it is the IB's document and your DP coordinator has the version that applies to your child's session.
