dubai/ib-dp-visual-arts-home-tutor.programmesIntro: Students reach Diploma Visual Arts from three directions, and each arrives fluent in one part of the course and unprepared for another. The first month of support should depend on which.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme Arts
programmes.description: MYP Arts is assessed on criteria covering knowing and understanding, developing skills, thinking creatively and responding, with an emphasis on a process journal throughout. Students arrive at Diploma level already used to documenting as they go, which is a significant advantage for the process portfolio. What they have usually never written is sustained comparative analysis of other artists' work.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai's continuum schools mean a sizeable share of Diploma Visual Arts students have done five years of MYP Arts. Their process journals are often strong and their comparative writing weak, so support in DP1 is usually about analytical structure rather than about documentation habits.

programmes.name: IGCSE Art and Design
programmes.description: The British-curriculum route, with a coursework portfolio and a timed examination component. These students arrive with strong making skills and examination stamina, but with a documentation habit shaped by a different mark scheme — presentation-led rather than process-led. The adjustment is learning that the Diploma rewards evidence of thinking over beautifully mounted outcomes.
programmes.countryNote: With UK curriculum at 37 per cent of Dubai private school enrolment, IGCSE Art and Design is the commonest entry route in this emirate. Many Dubai schools run it to sixteen before splitting into A Level or IB, so a Diploma Visual Arts cohort often mixes MYP and IGCSE habits in one studio.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme Visual Arts
programmes.description: Three components: a comparative study analysing artworks by other artists, a process portfolio evidencing the development of the student's own practice across art-making forms, and an exhibition of selected finished work with a curatorial rationale. Higher Level requires more in every component, including additional screens connecting the studied artists to the student's own work.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai Visual Arts cohorts are usually small, and the teacher's time is split across studio supervision, three components and two year groups. A student can go a long way into DP2 without anybody reading their comparative study closely, which is the single most common reason families in this emirate look for outside help.

dubai/ib-dp-visual-arts-home-tutor.subjectsIntro: Visual Arts sits alongside a recognisable set of Diploma subjects, and several of them supply skills the components need directly — particularly the analytical writing the comparative study depends on.

subjects.name: Visual Arts
subjects.description: Comparative study, process portfolio and exhibition. Marks are lost on description where comparison was required, on documentation that records progress rather than thinking, on exhibitions assembled as a best-of, and on rationales that fill a word limit without making a curatorial argument.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: Supplies the analytical register the comparative study needs. Students strong here usually need help with art-specific vocabulary rather than with structure; students weak here need the structure taught explicitly before any artist is chosen.

subjects.name: History
subjects.description: Directly useful for the cultural significance strand of the comparative study, where students most often substitute a Wikipedia summary for genuine context. A history student knows how to use a source and how to say why a period matters.

subjects.name: Design Technology
subjects.description: Shares drawing ability and iteration, and students often take both. The distinction worth teaching is purpose: a design drawing communicates manufacture, an arts work communicates intent, and the two are assessed on opposite criteria.

subjects.name: Film
subjects.description: Overlaps on visual analysis, framing and the vocabulary of composition. Film students generally write confidently about images, which transfers straight into the comparative study once the formal vocabulary is adjusted.

subjects.name: Theory of Knowledge
subjects.description: Knowledge questions about interpretation, authorship and the status of expert judgement in the arts map directly onto the comparative study. Students who argue well in Theory of Knowledge write stronger cultural-significance sections.

subjects.name: Psychology
subjects.description: Chosen alongside Visual Arts by students interested in perception and in why images affect people. Supplies named theory that can sharpen an argument about audience, provided it is used precisely rather than decoratively.

subjects.name: Arabic
subjects.description: Relevant beyond the language requirement: students working with Arabic calligraphic traditions, regional contemporary practice or Gulf visual culture can read primary material directly, which deepens a comparative study considerably.

subjects.name: Extended Essay in Visual Arts
subjects.description: Supervision practice rather than teaching: narrowing a question so four thousand words can answer it, and keeping the essay distinct from the comparative study, which is a frequent and avoidable problem.

subjects.name: Comparative study support
subjects.description: Bought as a bounded block: artist selection, the strands of analysis, screen structure, and the Higher Level connection screens. The writing, the images and the argument stay the student's own throughout.

dubai/ib-dp-visual-arts-home-tutor.regionsIntro: This is the one Diploma subject where Dubai's own geography is a direct academic asset. First-hand looking is worth more than any number of internet images, and where a family lives changes which collections are reachable on a weekday evening.

regions.name: Al Quoz and Alserkal Avenue
regions.note: The emirate's contemporary gallery district, built into former industrial warehouses. Students here can see work at scale, in person, and talk to gallery staff — which is how a comparative study stops relying on screen images of paintings the student has never stood in front of.

regions.name: Jaddaf Waterfront
regions.note: Home to the Jameel Arts Centre, with its own collection, library and research spaces. The most useful place in Dubai for a student who needs to read seriously about contemporary practice in the region rather than searching online.

regions.name: Al Fahidi and Dubai Creek
regions.note: The historic quarter, with small galleries in restored courtyard houses and a visible architectural vocabulary of wind towers, coral stone and gypsum. Useful primary material for students working with heritage, place or material memory.

regions.name: Dubai Design District
regions.note: Studios, design practices and the Dubai Institute of Design and Innovation. Students who want to interview a practising artist or designer for their process documentation have the shortest route to one from here.

regions.name: Jumeirah and Umm Suqeim
regions.note: Close to the Etihad Museum and a cluster of smaller independent spaces. Heavy traffic on Al Wasl and Beach Road at pickup means weekday sessions here realistically start after five.

regions.name: Dubai Marina and Jumeirah Beach Residence
regions.note: Apartment living, which constrains making badly: no ventilation for solvents, no space for large canvases, nowhere to leave wet work. Portfolios from here benefit from being planned around scale and medium from the start.

regions.name: Mirdif and Al Warqa
regions.note: Residential, with a long commute towards the Al Barsha and Umm Suqeim school cluster. Students here often do their studio work entirely at school, which makes documentation discipline more important because the work is not at home to photograph.

regions.name: Dubai Hills and Arabian Ranches
regions.note: Villa communities with space to work and store, so physical output tends to be larger. The failure pattern here is the opposite one: plenty of finished work and a process portfolio assembled retrospectively from photographs taken too late.

schoolClusters.city: Established Dubai IB schools with studio provision
schoolClusters.note: Visual Arts at Diploma level needs studio space, storage and a specialist teacher, so provision is concentrated in schools that have invested in it. Cohorts are small, and the teacher's attention is usually weighted towards the exhibition, which is why the comparative study is the component most often under-supervised.

schoolClusters.city: Newer southern Dubai campuses
schoolClusters.note: Purpose-built arts facilities in the communities developed over the last decade, often with better studio space than older schools. Support here is typically bought for the written components rather than for making, since the making conditions are already good.

dubai/ib-dp-visual-arts-home-tutor.modesIntro: Support in this subject divides by component, because the three components demand different work at different points in the two years. Trying to cover all three in one weekly hour generally covers none of them.

modes.title: Comparative study block
modes.description: Four to six sessions, usually in the second half of DP1. Artist and artwork selection first, then the strands of analysis taught one at a time, then screen structure, then — for Higher Level — the connection screens linking the studied artists to the student's own practice. Every word and every image choice remains the student's.

modes.title: Process portfolio review
modes.description: Periodic sessions across both years looking at what the documentation actually evidences. The question is always the same: does this screen show thinking, or does it show a photograph of something that happened? Documentation habits are cheap to fix early and expensive to fix in the final term.

modes.title: Exhibition and curatorial rationale clinic
modes.description: A short block in the final months on selection and on writing. Which works form a coherent body, what the rationale has to argue inside a hard word limit, and how exhibition texts should function. The student writes every version; the tutor reads and questions.

modes.title: Weekly analytical writing sessions
modes.description: For students whose making is strong and whose writing is not. One session a week on analytical structure, art vocabulary, evidence and argument, using artworks the student is genuinely interested in. The gains show up across all three components and in Theory of Knowledge as well.

sections.heading: The three components, and the limits that govern them
paragraphs: Visual Arts is assessed through three components, two of them externally and one internally. The comparative study is an analytical submission about artworks made by other people. The process portfolio evidences how the student's own practice developed, across a required number of art-making forms. The exhibition presents selected finished artworks with a curatorial rationale and accompanying texts. The balance between them is the first thing a family should understand, because it explains why a technically gifted student can underperform: a large share of the grade is carried by documents.

Each component is governed by a screen count or a word limit, and these differ by level. Higher Level submits more in every case, and adds screens that review the extent to which the student's own work was influenced by the art and artists examined in the comparative study — a requirement Standard Level does not have and one that Higher Level students routinely leave until last. The curatorial rationale sits at around four hundred words at Standard Level and around seven hundred at Higher Level, and exhibition texts accompanying each work are short by design.

These numbers are not administrative trivia. A student who learns in March that the process portfolio has an upper screen limit has to cut, and cutting documentation after the fact removes exactly the connective reasoning that earns marks. A student who knows the limit in DP1 composes to it. The same is true of the rationale: seven hundred words is generous enough to make an argument and tight enough to punish preamble, and a student who drafts to the limit from the first attempt writes something far better than one who writes a thousand words and deletes a third.

Confirm every figure in the table against the subject guide your school is teaching, through the Diploma coordinator. Guides are revised; this page is a tutoring page, not an assessment authority. What does not change between revisions is the principle that the limits are part of the task, and that composing to them is a skill worth teaching early.

sections.heading: The comparative study: comparison, not two descriptions
paragraphs: The comparative study is the component where outside support makes the most difference, and the reason is simple. It is an analytical writing task in a subject most students chose because they like making things, and in a school cohort small enough that nobody has time to read it closely until late. The commonest failure is structural: the student describes artwork one, then describes artwork two, then adds a paragraph noting that both are interesting. That is not comparison. Comparison means a strand of analysis carried across works, so that each one illuminates the other.

The strands themselves are learnable. Formal qualities: composition, colour, scale, mark, surface. Material and process: what it is made of, how that was done, what the method implies. Function and purpose: what the work was for, who commissioned or supported it, what it was meant to do. Cultural significance: the moment it was made in and why that moment matters to the work. And interpretation: what the work means, with the student's reading supported rather than asserted. A study that carries three or four of these strands properly across the chosen works reads completely differently from one that walks through each artwork in turn.

Selection is the step students rush and the one that decides everything. Works have to be genuinely comparable — not merely by the same loose theme, but with enough in common to make the differences meaningful, and enough difference to make the comparison worth making. Choosing from more than one cultural context is both a requirement to check against the current guide and an analytical advantage, because it forces the cultural-significance strand to do real work. Choosing three works the student has only ever seen as thumbnails is the surest route to a thin study.

For Higher Level there is the additional task of connecting the studied artists back to the student's own practice, with evidence. This cannot be invented retrospectively with any conviction. Students who plan it in advance make work during DP1 that genuinely responds to what they studied, and then have something real to show. Students who leave it until the end write a plausible paragraph claiming influence that nobody can see in the work, which is both unconvincing and avoidable.

sections.heading: The process portfolio: evidence of thinking, not a photo album
paragraphs: The process portfolio is misread more often than any other component in the Diploma arts. Students assume it is a record of what they made, so they fill screens with photographs of finished pieces and captions describing them. The component asks for something different: evidence of sustained experimentation, exploration of materials and ideas, and the decisions that connected one piece of work to the next. A screen showing three failed attempts with the student's reasoning about why they failed is worth more than a screen showing a successful outcome with a label.

The art-making forms requirement is the technical trap. There is a minimum number of forms, it differs by level, and at Higher Level the forms must come from separate categories rather than being three variations on drawing. Students who discover this late have to manufacture a third form in the final months, which produces thin, obviously bolted-on work. Auditing forms in the first term of DP1 takes one session and prevents the whole problem.

Annotation is the other half of it. Good annotation reasons: this did not work because the ground was too absorbent, so I tried a different preparation and the mark behaved like this. Weak annotation captions: charcoal study of a figure. The difference is entirely learnable, and it is a habit rather than a talent. Students who annotate as they work produce a portfolio that composes itself; students who annotate from memory in the final term write generalities, because the specific reasoning is gone.

The screen limit matters for the same reason it matters elsewhere. Documentation produced to a limit is selected and argued; documentation cut to a limit loses its connective tissue. The practical discipline is to photograph and annotate continuously but to curate the portfolio in stages, choosing what earns its screen. That is a tutoring conversation that works extremely well over a shared screen, because the portfolio is already a set of digital pages.

sections.heading: The exhibition and the curatorial rationale
paragraphs: The exhibition is internally assessed and externally moderated, and it is where students most often confuse two different ideas: their best work, and a coherent body of work. The component rewards the second. A selection of technically strong but unrelated pieces reads as a portfolio; a selection with a visible thread — material, conceptual, formal — reads as an exhibition, and the rationale then has something to argue. This means some good work should be left out, which students find genuinely painful and which is often the single decision that lifts the grade.

Coherence can come from several directions. A sustained material investigation across different subjects. A conceptual question approached through different media. A formal preoccupation with scale, or with surface, or with a particular quality of light. What it cannot come from is a theme asserted in the rationale but invisible on the wall. The test is simple and worth applying honestly: if the thread were not described in writing, would a stranger see it?

Sequence and hanging are part of the assessment, not a logistical afterthought. The order in which works are encountered, what is placed next to what, the use of scale and of space between pieces — these all carry meaning, and students who think about them produce a stronger exhibition from the same artworks. Photographic documentation of the installed exhibition matters too, because that is often what is examined.

The curatorial rationale is a hard writing task disguised as a short one: around four hundred words at Standard Level and seven hundred at Higher Level, in which the student has to state a curatorial position, justify the selection, and explain the relationship between the works and their intentions. There is no room for preamble. Students who draft to the limit from the beginning write something tight; students who write at length and cut end up with a summary. Every word of it must be the student's own, and a tutor's role is to read it and ask the questions a moderator would ask.

sections.heading: Where Dubai Visual Arts students lose marks most predictably
paragraphs: Across students who arrive needing help, the pattern is consistent and it is almost never about making. The first loss is comparison collapsing into description, which is the comparative study failure described above and the commonest single problem in the subject. The second is documentation written retrospectively, which produces generalities because the specific reasoning has been forgotten. The third is the art-making forms count, discovered late. The fourth is an exhibition selected for quality rather than coherence. The fifth is a rationale that fills its word limit without taking a position.

There is a sixth that is specific to this region and worth naming. Students in Dubai have unusually good access to contemporary art in person — the galleries in Al Quoz, the Jameel Arts Centre at Jaddaf Waterfront, the historic quarter at Al Fahidi, and within a short drive the collections and biennial programming of the wider Gulf. Yet a large share of comparative studies here are written entirely from screen images, often of works in European and North American collections the student has never seen. A study built partly on first-hand looking is visibly different: the observations about scale, surface and presence cannot be obtained any other way, and examiners read them as what they are.

The seventh loss is time management across the two years, which in this subject is structural rather than personal. The comparative study, the process portfolio and the exhibition all culminate in the same final months, alongside every other subject's deadlines. Students who finish the comparative study in DP1 have a workable final year; students who carry it into DP2 compress three components into one term and all three suffer. This is the strongest argument for buying a bounded comparative study block early rather than general support late.

The eighth is simply not knowing the requirements. Screen counts, word limits, form categories and connection-screen expectations are all published in the subject guide, and a surprising number of students have never read it. One session spent going through the guide with the student, against their own work to date, is consistently among the most valuable hours in the subject.

sections.heading: Using Dubai's collections as primary research
paragraphs: No competitor page in this market treats the emirate's own art infrastructure as an academic resource, which is a strange omission, because for this subject it is the most useful local fact there is. Looking at art in person produces a category of observation that screen images cannot: actual scale, the behaviour of a surface, the physical relationship between a viewer and a work, how a piece changes as you move. Those observations are exactly what lifts a comparative study, and they are free.

The gallery district in Al Quoz, built into warehouse spaces around Alserkal Avenue, shows contemporary work at scale and rotates frequently. The Jameel Arts Centre at Jaddaf Waterfront holds a collection, a library and research space, which makes it the right destination for a student who needs to read as well as look. The Etihad Museum and the restored courtyard galleries of Al Fahidi offer material and architectural history in situ. The Dubai Design District puts practising designers and an institute of design within reach for anyone wanting to interview a working practitioner for their documentation.

The practical use is specific rather than general. Choose at least one comparative study artwork that can be seen in person, within the region if not within the emirate, and write about it from observation. Keep a looking record — not a review, but notes on what was physically evident. Use a gallery visit as a process portfolio screen when it changes something the student subsequently does, which is the only circumstance in which artist research earns its screen. And treat an exhibition seen in person as a lesson in hanging, sequence and spacing, which is content for the exhibition component that no textbook teaches as well.

sections.heading: Academic honesty when the work assessed is artwork
paragraphs: The honesty position in this subject needs care, because art has always worked by appropriation, quotation and response, and that is legitimate. What is not legitimate is submitting work that is not the student's own, or presenting another artist's image as if it were. The dividing line is attribution and transformation. A student who works from a photographer's image must say so. A student who responds to an artist's motif must show the response as a response. A student who copies an image and submits it as their own work has a malpractice problem regardless of how skilled the copy is.

On the written components, the rules are the ordinary academic ones. Every image used in a comparative study needs its source. Every quotation needs attribution. Every claim about cultural context that came from somewhere needs that somewhere named. Students who treat the comparative study as a visual task sometimes carry over the habit of using images without citation, which is the most common honesty slip in this subject and entirely avoidable.

For a tutor, the boundary is the same as in every subject and it is worth stating plainly. A tutor may teach analytical technique, explain what a criterion rewards, ask what a student means, and give feedback on what the student has produced. A tutor may not write a curatorial rationale, draft screens, supply an argument or make any part of an artwork. IB Gram does not sell finished coursework in any subject, and any provider offering to supply written screens or a rationale is offering a malpractice case against your child. Feedback arrives as questions in the margin.

There is also a practical protection worth adopting. Keep a dated record of process — photographs, drafts, annotation, version history. Students who document continuously have nothing to explain if authorship is ever queried, and they also happen to produce better process portfolios. The two incentives point the same way, which is unusual and convenient.
bullets: Source every image in the comparative study
Show a response to an artist as a response, not as an original motif
Say when work derives from a photograph that is not the student's
No screens, rationales or artworks are ever supplied by a tutor
Continuous dated documentation is both good practice and good protection

sections.heading: What a Dubai school already provides, and where outside help fits
paragraphs: Before paying for anything, establish what the school gives. Dubai's private schools are overseen by the Knowledge and Human Development Authority, described by u.ae as responsible for enhancing and overseeing the quality of private education in the emirate, and KHDA inspects on a six-band scale from Outstanding down to Very Weak. Those reports are published and are more useful than any marketing material. For this subject the questions are narrow: is there a dedicated studio with storage, is the teacher a specialist, how large is the Diploma cohort, and are the written components given scheduled feedback or left to the student.

The answer determines what is worth buying. A school with a strong studio and a specialist teacher may need no help with making at all, and support should go entirely to the comparative study and the rationale. A school where the arts teacher covers two year groups and three components will give the exhibition most of its attention, which is exactly why comparative studies in Dubai so often arrive unread. Knowing which situation you are in prevents paying for something the school is already doing well.

The market context is worth a sentence. Dubai had 227 private schools serving 387,441 students in 2024-25 across seventeen curricula, with IB programmes at 7 per cent of enrolment and the UK curriculum at 37 per cent. KHDA confirmed in May 2026 that private school fees would not rise for 2026-27, and the 2026-27 intake adds seven schools, four UK curriculum and three IB, creating 16,846 new places. More IB places means more small arts cohorts, which is the structural reason this kind of support exists.

Finally, what IB Gram is not. It holds no KHDA, ADEK, SPEA, MoE or IB accreditation and claims none; the regulators are named so you know whose report to read. It keeps no UAE office or studio — an operation with premises and staff in Dubai requires a KHDA Educational Services Permit, which is a specific training-institute licence. And it does not send tutors to UAE homes; that service exists only in India. Teaching here is one-to-one over live video in Gulf Standard Time, and in this subject that is honestly the right shape for the written components and the wrong shape for the studio.

process.title: Say which component is the problem
process.description: Comparative study, process portfolio or exhibition. They need different work at different points in the two years, and naming it first prevents a term of general studio conversation. If you are unsure, send three screens and the answer becomes clear quickly.

process.title: Send screens rather than descriptions
process.description: Three or four pages of the student's actual comparative study or process portfolio tell a specialist more in five minutes than any conversation. Written work can be read; an impression of how things are going cannot be assessed.

process.title: Take the free trial lesson
process.description: A full session at no cost with no card details required. Bring one screen and watch it get read the way an examiner reads it. If the match is wrong, say so and a different tutor is proposed before any money changes hands.

process.title: Audit the requirements against the current guide
process.description: Screen counts, word limits, art-making form categories and the Higher Level connection screens, checked against what the student has so far. This single session prevents the most expensive mistakes in the subject, all of which are discovered too late.

process.title: Finish the comparative study inside DP1
process.description: The strongest structural move available. Three components colliding in the final term is why students in this subject run out of time, and the comparative study is the one that can be completed early without waiting for anything else.

process.title: Review drafts in date order
process.description: Marked drafts of the same screen, read side by side, show whether the analytical writing is actually improving. If two drafts attract the same comments, the approach needs changing rather than the hours increasing.

whyPoints.title: The written components taken as seriously as the making
whyPoints.description: Two of the three components are documents, and they are where Dubai students most often lose ground because school attention concentrates on the exhibition. Sessions here go to comparative analysis, documentation reasoning and the rationale.

whyPoints.title: Requirements checked before they become a cutting exercise
whyPoints.description: Screen counts, word limits and art-making form categories are audited early against the student's actual work. Composing to a limit produces better work than cutting to one, and the difference is visible to a moderator.

whyPoints.title: First-hand looking treated as part of the method
whyPoints.description: Dubai has serious contemporary art within driving distance. Writing about at least one artwork from observation rather than from a screen image produces observations about scale and surface that cannot be obtained any other way.

whyPoints.title: Feedback as questions, never as supplied text
whyPoints.description: Screens, rationales and artworks are the student's own without exception. A tutor reads and asks what a moderator would ask; the student revises. IB Gram does not supply finished coursework in any subject, in any format.

whyPoints.title: Honest about where the studio ends
whyPoints.description: Nobody will teach glaze mixing or canvas stretching over a video call, and this page does not pretend otherwise. The studio belongs to the school. Analysis, documentation and curating are where an outside specialist earns their fee.

whyPoints.title: Claims limited to what can be evidenced
whyPoints.description: No regulator or board accreditation is claimed, because none is held. No grade promises and no invented statistics. Every component requirement is flagged for confirmation against the current subject guide through the school's coordinator.

faqs.question: Does my daughter need to be good at drawing to score well in Diploma Visual Arts?
faqs.answer: Less than families assume. Two of the three components are documents: a comparative study analysing other artists' work, and a process portfolio evidencing how her own practice developed. Only the exhibition presents finished artwork, and even that is assessed alongside a written curatorial rationale. Technical facility helps and is never wasted, but a student with modest drawing skill and excellent analytical writing frequently outscores a technically gifted student whose documentation is thin. The subject rewards thinking made visible, which is why the written components are where outside support usually matters most.

faqs.question: What exactly makes a comparative study score well rather than averagely?
faqs.answer: Carrying a strand of analysis across the works instead of describing each one in turn. The strands are formal qualities, material and process, function and purpose, cultural significance, and interpretation supported by what is actually visible. An average study walks through artwork one, then artwork two. A strong study takes scale, or surface, or patronage, and follows it through every work so each illuminates the others. Selection matters too: the works have to share enough to make the differences meaningful. Confirm the current screen count and artwork requirements with your school's Diploma coordinator.

faqs.question: How many screens and words is each component allowed?
faqs.answer: The comparative study runs to roughly ten to fifteen screens, with Higher Level adding screens reviewing how the studied artists influenced the student's own work. The process portfolio is around nine to eighteen screens at Standard Level and thirteen to twenty-five at Higher Level, with a minimum number of art-making forms that differs by level. The curatorial rationale is around four hundred words at Standard Level and seven hundred at Higher Level, and exhibition texts are short with a character limit per work. Check every figure against the guide your school is teaching, because guides are revised.

faqs.question: My son's process portfolio is all photographs of finished pieces. Is that a problem?
faqs.answer: Yes, and it is the commonest documentation problem in the subject. The portfolio asks for evidence of experimentation and of the decisions connecting one piece of work to the next, not a record of outcomes. A screen showing three attempts that failed, with his reasoning about why, earns more than a screen showing a successful piece with a caption. The fix is partly recoverable: discarded work and the thinking attached to it can often be reconstructed if it happens soon. The permanent fix is annotating continuously, which is a habit rather than a talent.

faqs.question: What does the art-making forms requirement actually mean?
faqs.answer: The process portfolio has to evidence work across a minimum number of art-making forms, and at Higher Level those forms must come from separate categories rather than being three variations on one thing. Three kinds of drawing is not three forms. Students who discover this in the final term bolt on a third form that reads as exactly what it is. A forms audit in the first term of DP1 takes one session and removes the problem entirely. The current categories and minimum counts are in the subject guide, which the Diploma coordinator can supply.

faqs.question: How do I know whether the exhibition selection is coherent?
faqs.answer: Apply one honest test: if the thread were not described in the rationale, would a stranger walking in see it? Coherence can come from a sustained material investigation, a conceptual question approached through different media, or a formal preoccupation with scale or surface. What it cannot come from is a theme asserted in writing but invisible on the wall. The hard part is that coherence usually means leaving out strong work that breaks the thread, which students find painful. That single decision is often what lifts the exhibition grade.

faqs.question: Can a tutor help write the curatorial rationale?
faqs.answer: A tutor can read it, ask the questions a moderator would ask, and point out where a word limit is being spent on description rather than on argument. A tutor cannot write it, draft it, or supply the curatorial position. Every word submitted must be the student's own, and IB Gram does not supply finished coursework in any subject. The most useful intervention is making the student draft to the exact word limit from the first attempt rather than writing at length and cutting, because a cut rationale almost always reads as a summary rather than as a position.

faqs.question: Is it worth visiting galleries in Al Quoz for a comparative study?
faqs.answer: Yes, and it is one of the clearest advantages a Dubai student has. Looking at art in person produces observations about actual scale, surface behaviour and physical presence that screen images cannot supply, and examiners recognise the difference immediately. The gallery district around Alserkal Avenue, the Jameel Arts Centre at Jaddaf Waterfront and the historic galleries at Al Fahidi are all reachable, as are major institutions within a drive. Choosing at least one artwork that can be seen in person, and writing about it from observation, is a free upgrade to the component most students write entirely from thumbnails.

faqs.question: Where does appropriation stop and plagiarism start in this subject?
faqs.answer: At attribution and transformation. Art has always worked by quotation and response, and responding to another artist's motif is legitimate when it is shown as a response and the source is named. Working from someone else's photograph is legitimate when the student says so. Copying an image and submitting it as original work is malpractice regardless of skill. On the written components the ordinary academic rules apply: every image sourced, every quotation attributed, every contextual claim traceable. Students who treat the comparative study as a visual task sometimes forget citation, which is the commonest slip here.

faqs.question: We live in an apartment with no ventilation or storage. How does that affect the portfolio?
faqs.answer: It should shape the plan from the start rather than being discovered in DP2. Solvent-based media, large canvases and wet work that needs somewhere to dry are difficult in a Dubai apartment, and a portfolio planned around them will stall. The workable approach is to concentrate large or hazardous work in the school studio, choose home-based media that suit the space, and account for this when auditing art-making forms. Students who plan around the constraint produce stronger portfolios than students who fight it, and the school's arts teacher will usually make studio time available if asked early.

faqs.question: When should the comparative study be finished?
faqs.answer: Inside DP1 if at all possible. It is the one component that does not depend on anything else being complete, and finishing it early is the single most effective structural decision available in this subject. All three components otherwise culminate in the same final months, alongside every other subject's deadlines, and compressing them means all three suffer. Higher Level students have an extra reason: the connection screens linking studied artists to their own work are far more convincing when the studying happened early enough to actually influence what was made afterwards.

faqs.question: Will Visual Arts help or hurt a university application?
faqs.answer: It depends entirely on the destination, and it is a question for your school's university counsellor rather than a tutoring page. Art, design and architecture programmes generally want to see a portfolio, and the Diploma components produce excellent material for one. Some competitive courses in other fields specify particular subjects and count Visual Arts as neither help nor hindrance. What no reliable source supports is the idea that the subject closes doors generally. Check the admissions page of each named university and programme in the year of application, and ask the counsellor who deals with this every cycle.

faqs.question: How many sessions does a weak comparative study usually need?
faqs.answer: Four to six, placed deliberately. The first establishes whether the chosen works can actually be compared, which occasionally means changing a selection and is always better done early. The second and third teach the strands of analysis one at a time, with the student rewriting a single screen as a model. The remainder cover screen structure and, at Higher Level, the connection screens. Beyond six sessions the returns fall off, because the remaining work is the student writing. Bounding the block in advance keeps the cost predictable and the purpose clear.

faqs.question: Can sessions fit around studio time and Ramadan?
faqs.answer: Yes, and both come up constantly. Studio access in Dubai schools often runs after the timetable ends, so written-component sessions tend to sit later in the evening, which online delivery handles without anybody driving across the city. Through Ramadan, sessions move to post-Iftar slots or drop to a lighter cadence and resume with the same tutor afterwards. Because the written components are not time-critical in the way a weekly exam subject is, this is also the subject where a holiday block works best: a concentrated run of comparative study sessions over a break is unusually productive.

dubai/ib-dp-visual-arts-home-tutor.closingHeading: Send three screens and see what an examiner sees
dubai/ib-dp-visual-arts-home-tutor.closingBody: The fastest way to find out what Visual Arts support your child needs is to send three or four screens of their actual comparative study or process portfolio. A specialist reading them will tell you within minutes whether the problem is comparison collapsing into description, documentation written after the fact, an art-making forms count that will not be met, or a selection that has no visible thread. Those are different problems with different timelines. Sessions run one-to-one over live video in Gulf Standard Time, every screen and every word stays your child's own work, and the free trial lesson comes before any commitment. The studio stays with the school, where it belongs.

dubai/ib-dp-visual-arts-online-tutor.tutorsIntro: The tutors below cover Visual Arts at Standard and Higher Level, along with the subjects Dubai arts students most often take alongside it. Matching is based on experience of marking comparative studies and portfolio screens, because judging artwork and judging it against published criteria are different skills.

intro.heading: A subject with no exam, three submissions and a lot of hard limits
paragraphs: Visual Arts is the Diploma subject Dubai parents understand least well, and the reason is simple: there is no written paper. Nothing is sat in May. The entire grade comes from work submitted through the school, in three parts. The comparative study is an analytical piece on artworks the student did not make. The process portfolio documents their own art-making across different forms. The exhibition is a selection of finished work with a curatorial rationale and a short text for each piece.

Each component has limits, and the limits are where naive candidates lose marks before anyone has judged a single artwork. Screen counts are specified ranges, not suggestions. The curatorial rationale has a word ceiling. Exhibition texts have a character ceiling per artwork. A student who submits twenty-eight portfolio screens when the range stops lower has not demonstrated more; they have submitted work an examiner may not read. Confirm the current ranges and limits with your school's visual arts teacher or IB coordinator before planning anything around them, because guides are revised.

The second thing families misread is which component carries the weight. Many assume the exhibition is the subject, because the exhibition is what gets photographed and shown to grandparents. The process portfolio carries a substantially larger share of the grade than most students act as if it does, and it is also the component that cannot be produced retrospectively. A student who made a year of good work and documented none of it has a portfolio problem no amount of late effort solves properly.

Dubai adds a specific structural issue. Visual Arts cohorts in the emirate are often tiny, sometimes three or four students, taught by one teacher who may also carry MYP Arts and the exhibition logistics. There is frequently nobody else in the building to read a comparative study draft against the criteria. That is the gap an online specialist fills: not replacing the teacher, but giving the student a second reader who has marked this component before and who is not also responsible for hanging the show.

Delivery is settled and worth saying plainly. Sessions run online, one to one, over live video, in Gulf Standard Time. IB Gram does not run in-person lessons in Dubai and does not provide home visits anywhere in the UAE; home visiting is a service we offer only in India. For this subject the practical consequence is that reviews work on photographed and exported screens rather than on physical pieces, which is exactly the form the examiner sees them in too. A tutor cannot feel a surface over video; neither can a moderator in Cardiff. The review therefore happens under the same constraint the assessment does, which is a more honest position than most providers take about this subject.

One last framing point before the detail. Good support here is not art teaching, and a family paying for art teaching will be disappointed. The school teaches the making. What an outside specialist adds is criterion literacy: knowing what a screen has to contain, what a comparison has to do, where a rationale wastes its words, and which limit is about to be breached. A student who can read their own work against the criteria has acquired something that keeps paying for the rest of the two years, which is the only kind of value worth buying in a subject with no exam to cram for.

dubai/ib-dp-visual-arts-online-tutor.programmesIntro: Visual Arts at Diploma level assumes habits built years earlier. These are the stages a Dubai student moves through, and what each one leaves them able to evidence when the portfolio starts.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme: Visual Arts
programmes.description: A Group 6 arts subject assessed entirely through submitted work: a comparative study of artworks by other artists, a process portfolio documenting the student's own experimentation across art-making forms, and an exhibition of resolved pieces with a curatorial rationale. Higher Level requires more portfolio screens, more exhibition artworks, a longer rationale and additional screens connecting studied artists to the student's own practice.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai cohorts are small and often mixed across both levels, so a Higher Level student may be taught alongside Standard Level students without the extra requirements being spelled out weekly. The commonest consequence we see is a Higher Level portfolio that covers too few art-making forms, which is a structural loss rather than a quality one.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme: Arts (visual arts strand)
programmes.description: MYP Arts is assessed against four criteria covering knowing and understanding, developing skills, thinking creatively and responding. Students who were held to criterion C properly arrive in DP1 already keeping a developmental workbook, which is the single habit the Diploma process portfolio rewards. Those who treated the workbook as a sketchbook to fill up afterwards start DP1 with a documentation problem.
programmes.countryNote: In Dubai's larger IB World Schools the MYP Arts carousel often rotates students between visual arts, drama and music, so a student may arrive in DP1 with only one term of sustained visual work behind them. That makes the first portfolio screens unusually important: they are often the student's first experience of documenting process at all.

programmes.name: IGCSE Art and Design as a feeder
programmes.description: Cambridge IGCSE Art and Design (0400) and its Pearson equivalent both run on coursework plus a timed examination component, which trains students to produce resolved outcomes under pressure. What they do not train is comparative analysis of other artists' work in a cultural frame, or sustained documentation across multiple art-making forms, both of which the Diploma assesses directly.
programmes.countryNote: British-track schools make up the largest share of Dubai's private-school enrolment, so most Visual Arts candidates in the emirate come from IGCSE rather than MYP. The jump that bites hardest is the comparative study, because nothing in IGCSE Art and Design asks a student to write a sustained formal and cultural analysis.

programmes.name: Career-related Programme: creative and design pathways
programmes.description: A handful of UAE schools run the Career-related Programme, where Diploma courses sit alongside a career-related study in areas such as graphic design, fashion or media. CP students take Visual Arts on the same terms and submit the same three components, with the reflective project competing for the same studio hours in the autumn of the second year.
programmes.countryNote: CP is rare in Dubai relative to the full Diploma, so a CP arts student is working in a very small pool for subject-specific support. Fixing the weekly review slot before the term starts matters more here than negotiating the rate, because there is rarely a second specialist free to absorb a dropped session.

dubai/ib-dp-visual-arts-online-tutor.subjectsIntro: Visual Arts students in Dubai carry a recognisable cluster of other subjects, and the workload shapes collide in predictable ways. These are the ones we are most often asked to cover alongside it.

subjects.name: Visual Arts
subjects.description: Assessed entirely through a comparative study, a process portfolio and an exhibition, with no written paper. Marks are lost on description instead of comparison, portfolios that show outcomes rather than process, and rationales that explain intention rather than curatorial decisions.

subjects.name: Film
subjects.description: The other Group 6 subject Dubai students most often pair with art. Built on a textual analysis, a comparative study and a portfolio of production roles, so the analytical vocabulary transfers directly, though the technical demands do not.

subjects.name: Design Technology
subjects.description: Chosen by students who want making with an engineering frame. Assessed through written papers plus a design project, so the workload shape is the opposite of Visual Arts and the two compete for the same evenings in DP2.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: The closest academic ally Visual Arts has. Both reward close analysis of a constructed object and both punish description. Students who improve at textual analysis almost always improve their comparative study marks within a term.

subjects.name: Psychology
subjects.description: A common pairing for students interested in perception, identity and how images work on an audience. Shares an evidence-based writing discipline that strengthens the comparative study's argumentation.

subjects.name: History
subjects.description: Directly useful for the cultural-context requirement of the comparative study. Students taking both can place artworks in a researched historical frame rather than asserting a period atmosphere, which is where weak studies collapse.

subjects.name: Arabic B and Arabic ab initio
subjects.description: Relevant for students researching regional artists and UAE art institutions in the original language. Arabic, Islamic Education and Social Studies are mandatory in Dubai private schools regardless of the licensed curriculum, so these sit alongside the Diploma anyway.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: The lighter maths route most Dubai arts students take, and the one that keeps a Diploma timetable survivable alongside a studio subject. Still demanding on statistics and modelling, and worth protecting with a fixed weekly slot in DP1.

subjects.name: Business Management
subjects.description: Chosen by students heading towards arts management, galleries or the creative industries. The internally assessed work falls in the same autumn window as the portfolio, so the two calendars need planning as one.

subjects.name: Theory of Knowledge and the Extended Essay
subjects.description: An art-based Extended Essay is popular in Dubai and frequently misfires, because students write appreciation rather than a research question. A tutor can question scope and sources and give feedback on the student's own drafts, and nothing further.

sections.heading: There is no exam: what a Visual Arts grade is actually made of
paragraphs: Everything in this subject is submitted. The comparative study and the process portfolio are externally assessed from uploaded screens; the exhibition is marked internally by the school and moderated externally from documentation. No part of the grade depends on performance in a hall in May. For a Dubai family that changes the entire shape of support: there is no revision timetable to build, and there is no point buying hours in April for work that was due in March.

The limits are the first thing to get right, because they are mechanical and unforgiving. Each component specifies a range of screens, and the exhibition adds a word ceiling on the curatorial rationale and a character ceiling on each artwork's text. Higher Level requires more screens, more artworks, more art-making forms and a longer rationale than Standard Level. A student who submits above a range has not shown ambition; they have submitted material that may not be read. Confirm the current figures with the school before planning around any of them.

The weighting is the second thing. The process portfolio carries the largest single share of the grade, which is the opposite of how most students allocate their time: the exhibition absorbs the energy because it is the visible event. A portfolio built in the last fortnight from photographs of finished work is not a portfolio of process at all, and it is the most common structural failure in this subject anywhere, not only in Dubai.

The table below sets out the three components with the ranges and limits commonly published for them. Treat it as a checklist to verify with the school rather than as the authority. The useful thing it does is make the shape of the subject visible in one place, which is something no competitor page for this market attempts.

sections.heading: The comparative study: where the marks actually go
paragraphs: This is the component Dubai students find hardest, because nothing in IGCSE Art and Design prepares them for it and because it is writing rather than making. The task is to analyse artworks by other artists and then compare them, with cultural context researched rather than assumed. The commonest failure is structural: a student produces an excellent set of screens on work one, then on work two, then on work three, and never actually compares them. Sequential description is not comparison, and the criterion is explicit about that.

Formal analysis is the second failure point. Students write that a painting is 'dramatic' or 'powerful' and believe they have analysed it. Formal analysis names what is on the surface and what it does: the direction of a diagonal, the temperature of a shadow, the ratio of figure to ground, the handling of an edge. A tutor's most useful intervention here is relentless: what can you actually see, and what does it cause the viewer to do. That conversation is why the students who have stood in front of a work in Al Quoz or at Jaddaf Waterfront write better screens than the ones working from a reproduction on a laptop.

Cultural context is the third, and it is a research problem rather than an art problem. A study that says a work 'reflects the turbulence of its time' has asserted context. A study that cites who commissioned a piece, where it was first shown, and what a named critic wrote about it has researched context. Sources are part of the submission and have to be listed, which also makes this the component where honesty slips are easiest to spot.

Higher Level adds screens connecting the studied artists to the student's own art-making practice. These are regularly the weakest screens in the whole submission, because they are written last and treated as an appendix. The connection has to be specific: a technique borrowed and altered, a compositional habit adopted, a decision in the student's own work traceable to something they studied.

sections.heading: The process portfolio: documenting the process you did not document
paragraphs: This component carries the largest share of the grade and is the one most often assembled in a panic. Its requirement is sustained experimentation across art-making forms, with the student's thinking visible: what was tried, what failed, what that changed. Standard Level requires a minimum number of forms, Higher Level requires more and expects them to be genuinely different kinds of practice rather than three varieties of drawing. Check your level's requirement explicitly, because small mixed-level classes in Dubai often do not spell it out.

The honest problem is that process has to be captured as it happens. A photograph of a finished painting cannot evidence the decision to abandon the first underpainting. The remedy is boring and effective: photograph work in progress at the point of each decision, write two sentences at the time about why the change was made, and keep both. Students who do this for a term have a portfolio; students who do not have a photo album. No tutor can manufacture the missing middle, and anyone claiming to is offering something the student will carry the consequences of.

Commentary is where marks are won back. The language of a weak screen is narrative: 'then I tried watercolour, then I tried ink'. The language of a strong screen is causal: 'the ink bled on this paper, so the next test used a sized surface, which held the line but flattened the tonal range'. That is a documented decision, and it is what the criterion rewards. Rewriting four screens of narration into causal commentary in one session usually changes a student's whole portfolio approach.

Form coverage is the structural trap. A Higher Level student with twenty excellent screens, all of them drawing and painting, has a coverage problem that quality does not fix. Reviewing coverage every fortnight, and planning one deliberate experiment in an under-represented form, costs almost nothing in DP1 and is unrecoverable in the final term.

sections.heading: The exhibition and the curatorial rationale: coherence over quantity
paragraphs: The exhibition is internally assessed by the school and externally moderated from documentation, which means two audiences: the teacher who sees the room and the moderator who sees photographs and text. Both are judging a body of work rather than a collection of good pieces. A student who selects their four or eight strongest individual works, made in different directions over two years, usually scores below a student who selects a coherent set in which a thread is visible.

The curatorial rationale is the most misunderstood piece of writing in the subject. Students write an artist's statement about what the work means to them. The task is curatorial: why these pieces, in this relationship, in this space, and what the viewer is intended to encounter. It has a word ceiling, so every sentence has to earn its place, and the first draft is almost always twice the length with half the content. A review session on the rationale is mostly deletion.

Exhibition texts carry a character limit per artwork, which is tighter than students expect and forces real decisions. The frequent error is using the text to repeat the rationale or to supply a title and a medium list that the labelling already provides. The useful text does something the image cannot: names a material behaviour, a source, or a decision the viewer would otherwise miss.

Documentation quality matters more than families realise, because the moderator never sees the room. Flat work needs square-on photography with even light and accurate colour; three-dimensional work needs a scale reference and a background that does not compete. Dubai apartments with strong daylight through tinted glass regularly produce a colour cast that makes a careful painting look muddy. Fixing that is a thirty-minute conversation and it protects two years of work.

sections.heading: What lands each fortnight: a screen-by-screen review rhythm
paragraphs: Progress in this subject is countable, which makes it unusually easy to supervise. Screens accumulate, forms get covered, limits get checked off. The table below sets out the rhythm that works across a Diploma year: comparative study groundwork early in DP1 while the portfolio is still building, portfolio reviews running continuously in the background, and exhibition selection only once there is enough resolved work to select from.

The sequencing principle is that the comparative study is the only component that can be finished early, so it should be. It depends on other people's artworks, which do not change, and it requires no studio time. Students who leave it to DP2 are writing an analytical piece in the same term they are resolving exhibition work and documenting a portfolio, which is the worst possible allocation of a Dubai arts student's autumn.

A parent can audit this directly, which is the point. Ask three questions each month: how many portfolio screens exist now, how many art-making forms are represented, and is the comparative study at draft stage. Three numbers, no interpretation required. If the numbers have not moved in six weeks, something is wrong and it needs naming rather than reassurance.

Where a student arrives mid-DP2 with little documented, the honest sequence changes: secure the comparative study first because it is recoverable, then build portfolio screens from whatever process evidence genuinely exists, then select the exhibition from what has been resolved. That is triage rather than a plan, and it is better stated as triage than dressed up as a strategy.

sections.heading: Photographing and submitting artwork from a Dubai apartment
paragraphs: Because every mark comes from uploaded files, the quality of the documentation is part of the quality of the submission. This is the most practical thing an online tutor can fix in a single session, and the one most Dubai students have never been taught. The requirements are not demanding: consistent lighting, square-on framing for flat work, accurate colour, a scale reference for three-dimensional work, and resolution high enough to read surface detail without being so large the file becomes unmanageable.

Dubai interiors create two specific problems. Strong daylight through tinted or reflective glazing shifts colour noticeably, so a painting photographed near a window can arrive looking grey-green. And apartment lighting is typically warm and directional, which flattens texture and throws shadows across relief work. The fix is diffuse light from two sides, a neutral reference in the frame for the first shot, and a single consistent setup used for every piece so the body of work looks like a body of work.

Screens themselves need designing, not just filling. An examiner reads a screen as a composed page: image, annotation and evidence in a legible relationship. Students who paste a photograph and type a paragraph underneath produce screens that technically comply and communicate badly. Reviewing two screens side by side on a shared display, which is easy online and awkward in person, is usually enough for a student to see the difference themselves.

The genuine limitation of online review deserves stating. A tutor cannot see a surface in the flesh, judge the weight of a sculpture, or notice that an impasto is still soft. What a tutor can do is judge the evidence as the examiner will receive it, which is the same constraint the assessment itself operates under.

sections.heading: Using Dubai's art infrastructure for the comparative study
paragraphs: The comparative study rewards engagement with real artworks, and this is one area where a student in the UAE has an advantage over a student working from a textbook. The emirate's gallery district around Al Quoz and Alserkal Avenue holds commercial galleries and artist studios with changing contemporary programmes. The Jaddaf Waterfront arts complex runs exhibitions and holds a library. The Etihad Museum in Jumeirah provides a documented historical frame for work about nation-building and identity.

Beyond Dubai, the Louvre Abu Dhabi and the Sharjah Art Foundation's spaces give access to collections and biennial-scale programmes within a day trip. A student who builds a comparative study around one work seen in person and one studied from a reliable reproduction writes a sharper formal analysis than one working entirely from images, because standing in front of a work makes scale, surface and installation legible in a way a screen never does.

There is a second advantage that Dubai students systematically under-use. The comparative study requires artworks from different cultural contexts, and students default to a European canon they half-remember from IGCSE. Regional and South Asian practice is available here, in person, with living artists and documented exhibition histories, and it satisfies the cultural-context requirement with far less strain. It also produces studies that examiners have not read fifty times.

Two cautions. Gallery programmes change, so check what is actually on before planning a study around it, and photography policies differ between institutions. And a study must cite its sources properly, including exhibition catalogues and wall texts; using an institution's own wording without attribution is a citation failure as much as an honesty one.

sections.heading: Appropriation, citation and the line between influence and copying
paragraphs: Visual Arts has honesty questions that other subjects do not, because influence is part of the discipline. Artists have always worked from other artists. The Diploma does not prohibit that; it requires it to be visible and attributed. A portfolio screen that shows a student working in the manner of a named artist, with that influence stated and the source credited, is good practice. A screen that reproduces someone else's composition and presents it as original invention is misconduct.

The same applies to source images. Painting from a photograph the student did not take requires the source to be credited, and some uses raise copyright questions beyond the honesty rules. Working from one's own photographs removes the problem entirely and is worth establishing as a habit in DP1. Reference images found online and then traced are the single most common quiet problem in this component, and it is the kind of thing a moderator spots.

A tutor's boundary is the same as in every other subject, and narrower than families sometimes hope. A tutor teaches, questions, marks against published criteria and explains why a screen does not score. A tutor does not make work, redraw a composition, or put sentences into a rationale. Every artwork and every word of the submission must be the student's own. Any provider offering finished screens or a written rationale is offering a breach whose consequences fall on the student.

Generative image tools now sit inside this question. If a student uses them at any stage, the use needs declaring and describing, and it cannot stand in for the documented experimentation the portfolio assesses. The criterion rewards visible decision-making; an image with no process behind it has nothing to document, which is a practical reason to be careful quite apart from the rules.

sections.heading: Cost in AED, availability, and how delivery works
paragraphs: Published figures from other Dubai providers, collected in October 2026, give the market context. Budget online help is advertised from roughly AED 45 to 65 an hour; a qualified online subject tutor sits at AED 150 to 300; IB specialists are quoted at AED 200 to 450 and above, with one Dubai provider advertising AED 650 at examiner level. In-home visiting in Dubai is published at AED 180 to 500 with travel priced into the hour. IB Gram publishes no rate card on this page: the trial lesson is free with no card required, and a quote follows the component and the number of hours.

What matters more than the hourly figure in this subject is which component you are buying help with, because the hours differ sharply. A comparative study block is typically six to eight sessions. A portfolio review cycle is fortnightly across a year, which is more hours in total and far less pressure per hour. An exhibition and rationale block is short and intensive. Buying a generic weekly hour without naming the component is how families in this subject spend the most and move the least.

Availability is worth stating plainly. Visual Arts specialists who have marked comparative studies are not numerous, and demand concentrates in the weeks before school internal deadlines. If nobody suitable is free in the window you need, you will be told that, with the nearest alternative, rather than matched to a general arts tutor described as a specialist. No competitor page in this market discloses a coverage limit, which does not mean none exists.

Delivery is settled. Lessons run online, one to one, over live video, in Gulf Standard Time. IB Gram does not run in-person lessons in Dubai, and home visits are a service we offer only in India. Anyone providing private tuition inside the UAE needs the MoHRE private tuition work permit introduced under Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, granted free of charge for two years through MoHRE's own e-services under 'Issuance of a New Work Permit - Private Tutor Licensing'.

process.title: Tell us which component and which level
process.description: Comparative study, process portfolio or exhibition, and Standard or Higher Level. Those two facts determine the screen ranges, the form requirements and the number of hours. A Higher Level student who does not know their own form requirement is the commonest version of this conversation, and it is worth five minutes before anything is booked.

process.title: Send recent screens or a draft
process.description: Three or four current portfolio screens, or a comparative study draft, tells a reviewer more than any description of the work. Exported files rather than live documents, so comments attach to a fixed version and the progression stays visible later in the year.

process.title: We match on comparative study and portfolio marking experience
process.description: The filter is narrow: experience teaching the current Visual Arts components and experience marking screens against the published criteria. Judging artwork and judging it against criteria are different skills, and the second one is what moves a grade. If nobody suitable is free in your window, you are told.
