process.title: A fortnightly rhythm with countable outputs
process.description: Screens submitted ahead, reviewed against criteria, returned annotated, with a written note naming what was addressed and what to produce next. Progress in this subject is countable: screens made, forms covered, drafts completed, limits verified. The notes record those numbers rather than impressions.

process.title: Limits verified before anything is submitted
process.description: Screen counts inside the range, curatorial rationale inside the word ceiling, exhibition texts inside the character limit, source list complete. This is the last pass before the school's internal deadline, scheduled with time to act on it rather than the night before.

whyPoints.title: A second reader your school may not have
whyPoints.description: Dubai Visual Arts cohorts are often three or four students with one teacher who also carries the exhibition logistics. There is frequently nobody else in the building to read a comparative study draft against the criteria, and that gap is the whole reason this service is useful here.

whyPoints.title: Limits treated as mechanical, because they are
whyPoints.description: Screen ranges, rationale word ceilings and exhibition text character limits are checked rather than estimated. Marks lost to a limit breach are the most avoidable losses in the subject and the most galling, because they have nothing to do with the quality of the work.

whyPoints.title: Portfolio process captured as it happens
whyPoints.description: The largest component cannot be reconstructed afterwards. Fortnightly reviews exist to catch the missing middle while it is still the present, which is the only version of portfolio support that is honest about what it can do.

whyPoints.title: Primary engagement with artworks encouraged, not simulated
whyPoints.description: Students who have stood in front of a work in Al Quoz, at Jaddaf Waterfront or at the Louvre Abu Dhabi write sharper formal analysis than students working from reproductions. Planning a study around what is actually on show in the emirate is free and raises the ceiling.

whyPoints.title: A stated boundary on assessed work
whyPoints.description: A tutor marks, questions and explains. No artwork is made, no composition redrawn, no sentence of a rationale supplied. Influence is credited, source images are attributed, and generative tools are declared. The boundary is published because the risk of crossing it is the student's.

whyPoints.title: Honest limits on what review can see
whyPoints.description: Online review judges the evidence as an examiner receives it, which is the same constraint the assessment works under. What it cannot do is feel a surface or judge a sculpture's weight, and saying so is more useful than pretending otherwise.

faqs.question: Does IB DP Visual Arts have a written exam?
faqs.answer: No. There is no written paper in this subject at either level. The whole grade comes from three submitted components: a comparative study and a process portfolio, both externally assessed from uploaded screens, and an exhibition marked internally by the school and moderated externally from documentation. That changes how support should be bought: there is no revision plan to build, and buying hours after a component's internal deadline has passed buys nothing. The useful hours sit in DP1 and in the autumn of DP2, while the work still exists in a changeable state.

faqs.question: Which Visual Arts component carries the most marks?
faqs.answer: The process portfolio carries the largest single share of the grade, which is the opposite of how most students spend their time, because the exhibition is the visible event and absorbs the energy. The comparative study carries a smaller share but is the only component that can be completed early, which makes it the best use of DP1. Confirm the current weightings with your school's visual arts teacher, because guides are revised and planning a two-year workload around an outdated split is a real risk in a small mixed-level class.

faqs.question: How many process portfolio screens does my child actually need?
faqs.answer: Standard Level and Higher Level have different published ranges, with Higher Level requiring more screens and more art-making forms. The exact figures should be confirmed with the school, because this is where small mixed-level Dubai classes most often leave a Higher Level student under-briefed. Two things matter beyond the count: the screens must sit inside the range rather than above it, and the forms must be genuinely different kinds of practice rather than three varieties of drawing. Quality does not compensate for a coverage gap.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a comparative study and an art essay?
faqs.answer: An essay describes and interprets; a comparative study compares, in a structure where the comparison is visible on the screens rather than asserted at the end. The commonest failure we see is sequential description: excellent screens on work one, then work two, then work three, with no comparison anywhere. The component also requires researched cultural context with cited sources, not a sense of the period, and Higher Level adds screens connecting the studied artists to the student's own practice. Those connection screens are usually the weakest part of the submission.

faqs.question: My child chose their three artworks already. Can they still be changed?
faqs.answer: Early in the process, yes, and it is often the most valuable single change available. Artworks have to be genuinely comparable: there needs to be a real axis along which they differ or converge, and they must come from different cultural contexts with researchable documentation behind them. Students frequently choose on taste, end up with three works that share nothing analysable, and then write three separate studies. Testing comparability before any screens are built takes one session and saves a month. Later in DP2 the honest answer may be to work with what exists.

faqs.question: How does an online tutor review a painting they cannot see in person?
faqs.answer: By reviewing it the way the examiner will: as photographed evidence on a screen. That is the real constraint the assessment operates under, since a moderator never enters the room either. The practical work is to make the documentation accurate, which is a genuinely teachable skill most students have never been shown: square-on framing, diffuse light from two sides, a neutral colour reference, a scale reference for three-dimensional work, and one consistent setup across the whole body of work. What online review cannot do is judge a surface in the flesh, and that limitation is worth stating.

faqs.question: Why does our Dubai apartment make my child's artwork photograph badly?
faqs.answer: Two reasons that recur across the emirate. Daylight through tinted or reflective glazing shifts colour, so work photographed near a window often arrives looking grey-green rather than as painted. And interior lighting here tends to be warm and directional, which flattens texture and throws shadows across relief and impasto work. The fix is diffuse light from two sides rather than one, a neutral reference card in the first frame of each session, and the same setup repeated for every piece so the body of work reads as a body of work rather than a set of unrelated photographs.

faqs.question: What should a curatorial rationale actually say?
faqs.answer: Why these works, in this relationship, in this space, and what a viewer is intended to encounter. It is a curatorial document, not an artist's statement about personal meaning, and that misunderstanding costs more marks in this component than anything else. It also carries a word ceiling, so a first draft at double the length with half the content is normal and a review session on it is mostly deletion. Each exhibition text then carries a character limit per artwork and should do something the image cannot, rather than repeating the rationale.

faqs.question: Can my child use Dubai galleries and museums for the comparative study?
faqs.answer: Yes, and it is a real advantage over working from reproductions. The Al Quoz and Alserkal gallery district holds contemporary commercial galleries and artist studios; the Jaddaf Waterfront arts complex runs exhibitions and holds a research library; the Etihad Museum provides documented historical context. The Louvre Abu Dhabi and Sharjah Art Foundation are within a day trip. Check current programmes before planning a study around a specific work, and cite catalogues and wall texts properly, because using an institution's wording without attribution is both a citation failure and an honesty problem.

faqs.question: Where is the line between being influenced by an artist and copying them?
faqs.answer: Visibility and attribution. Working in the manner of a named artist, with the influence stated on the screen and the source credited, is good practice and exactly what the comparative study is meant to feed. Reproducing another artist's composition and presenting it as original invention is misconduct. Source photographs the student did not take must be credited, and some uses raise copyright questions beyond the honesty rules. Working from one's own photographs removes the problem entirely, which is why it is worth establishing as a habit in DP1 rather than DP2.

faqs.question: Can a tutor help write the curatorial rationale or the comparative study?
faqs.answer: A tutor can question it, mark it against the published criteria, and explain why a paragraph does not score. A tutor cannot supply sentences, redraw a composition or make any part of the submitted work. Every artwork and every word belongs to the student, and any provider offering finished screens or a ready-made rationale is offering a breach whose consequences land on the student rather than the seller. The useful version of help is relentless questioning: what can you actually see, and why does this piece belong next to that one.

faqs.question: How much does Visual Arts tutoring cost in Dubai?
faqs.answer: Other Dubai providers published the following figures, collected in October 2026: roughly AED 45 to 65 an hour for budget online help, AED 150 to 300 for a qualified online subject tutor, AED 200 to 450 and above for IB specialists, and AED 650 at one provider's examiner level. In-home visiting is advertised at AED 180 to 500 with travel in the hour. What matters more here is which component you are funding: a comparative study block of six to eight sessions costs very differently from a fortnightly portfolio cycle across a year. IB Gram publishes no rate card on this page.

faqs.question: Is Visual Arts a soft subject for a university application?
faqs.answer: It is a demanding subject that some destinations value highly and others do not count towards a science or engineering profile, which is a different thing from soft. Art, design, architecture and creative-industry courses often weight it heavily and may also require a portfolio in its own right, assessed separately from the Diploma grade. Courses with specific science or maths prerequisites will look at those subjects instead. Read the entry requirements for the named course at the named university for the year of entry before DP1 subject selection, rather than relying on a general impression.

faqs.question: My child is halfway through DP2 with almost nothing documented. What now?
faqs.answer: Triage, honestly labelled as triage. Secure the comparative study first, because it depends on other artists' work rather than on studio time and is therefore the most recoverable component. Then build portfolio screens from whatever process evidence genuinely exists, including photographs on a phone and notes in a sketchbook, without inventing a middle that did not happen. Then select the exhibition from what has actually been resolved. That sequence produces the best available outcome, and no tutor can produce the documentation that was never made in the first place.

faqs.question: How often should review sessions run, and when in the year?
faqs.answer: Fortnightly works better than weekly in this subject, because screens need time to accumulate between reviews and there has to be something new to read. The comparative study block is best placed in DP1, when studio pressure is lower, and it is the one component that can be finished early. Portfolio reviews should run continuously in the background from early DP1. The exhibition block belongs in the final months, once there is enough resolved work to select from. Sessions run in Gulf Standard Time, with timing shifted later during Ramadan by prior agreement.

dubai/ib-dp-visual-arts-tutor.tutorsIntro: The tutors below cover Diploma Visual Arts for Dubai students at both levels and across all three submissions: the comparative study, the process portfolio and the exhibition with its curatorial rationale. Each works from the student's own images, screens and writing rather than from a set syllabus order.

intro.heading: Two bills, and the one families do not see coming
paragraphs: Visual Arts is the Diploma subject where a family can price the tutoring correctly and still be surprised by the total. The teaching bill behaves normally: an hourly rate inside the published Dubai bands, multiplied by however many sessions get booked. The making bill does not. It arrives in uneven lumps across two years, it is largely invisible until it is urgent, and it is almost never discussed before a student has committed to the subject. Paint, surfaces, paper, print, mounting, framing for an exhibition, and the quiet cost of documenting everything well enough to be assessed on it.

The hourly figures are public and spread very wide. EdFlik advertises from AED 45 to 65 an hour and Tutopiya from AED 33 to 52 at the budget end. Unitors publishes IGCSE from AED 150 and IB from AED 200. TutorChase quotes AED 270. Bestimate's Dubai rate table puts a qualified subject tutor working online at AED 150 to 300 and specialist IB, IGCSE and A-Level support at AED 200 to 450 and above. BartyED publishes AED 650 for a premium named tutor. Those are each provider's own published figures, read in October 2026, and they appear here as market context rather than as an IB Gram price list.

Visual Arts quotes sit at the specialist end of that spread, which parents sometimes find surprising for a subject with no written examination. The reason is what the work requires: a tutor has to read an image critically, judge whether a body of work is coherent, mark written analysis against criteria, and know the screen and word limits well enough to plan a submission inside them. Fine-art ability alone is not that skill set, and the people who have all of it are not numerous in this region.

The expensive failure in this subject is not a bad painting. It is a late one. Two years of work that has not been documented as it happened cannot be reconstructed, because the process portfolio is evidence of thinking over time and a retrospective version reads as exactly that. A student who photographs and annotates weekly has spent almost nothing and owns the component. A student who arrives in DP2 with a phone full of finished pieces and no record of decisions has a problem that money cannot fully solve, and that is the single most useful thing on this page.

Delivery is online. Lessons run one-to-one over live video with screen sharing, which suits a subject assessed through submitted images and writing better than families expect: the student's own screens are on display for both parties, annotated, and saved. IB Gram does not offer home visits in Dubai; home visits are a service we run only in India. The making happens in the student's own studio space, at school or at home, and a tutor is not present for it in any delivery model. A tutor here critiques, questions and gives written feedback; nobody but the student touches the work.
bullets: All three Diploma Visual Arts submissions at both levels
Comparative study: comparison built as an argument, not two descriptions
Process portfolio: weekly documentation habits set up in DP1, not reconstructed in DP2
Exhibition and curatorial rationale: selection judged for coherence
Materials, print and framing costs set out before a family commits
AED bands attributed to other providers and dated October 2026

dubai/ib-dp-visual-arts-tutor.programmesIntro: The documentation habit this subject assesses is built long before the Diploma and reused in the Diploma core. These are the three levels a Dubai family is normally dealing with when they contact us about Visual Arts.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme Arts
programmes.description: Middle Years Arts criteria reward investigation, development, creation and reflection, and the third and fourth of those are where Diploma readiness is built. A student rewarded for producing an attractive final piece, with the sketchbook treated as a formality, arrives in DP1 with a habit the Diploma actively penalises, because the Diploma marks the thinking and treats the artwork as evidence of it.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai runs both routes into the Diploma, Middle Years Arts in IB schools and IGCSE Art and Design in the British sector. IGCSE students usually arrive with stronger technical skill and a sketchbook built to a formula, which has to be unlearned before the process portfolio can show genuine decision-making. We check which habit a student brings in the first session.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme Visual Arts
programmes.description: Visual Arts has no written examination. It is assessed entirely through three submissions: a comparative study of artworks from different contexts, a process portfolio evidencing experimentation and decision-making, and an exhibition of resolved work with a curatorial rationale. Each has screen or word limits that differ between levels. Confirm the current component requirements, limits and weightings with your school's IB coordinator before planning against them, as the guide is revised on its own cycle.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai art provision ranges from fully equipped studios with kilns, print facilities and a technician to a single shared room with limited ventilation and no storage. Which of those your child is in determines the practical cost of the subject and the kind of practice that is realistic. Ask the head of art what a Diploma student can leave drying overnight, because the answer shapes two years of work.

programmes.name: Extended Essay and Theory of Knowledge
programmes.description: An Extended Essay in Visual Arts is written research, not practice, and students who choose it expecting to make something are caught out. Theory of Knowledge overlaps usefully, because the questions about how knowledge is produced in the arts sharpen the comparative study. Students who connect the two write better contextual analysis and stop treating cultural context as a paragraph of background.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai offers genuine Extended Essay material in this subject: the city's public art and commissioning programmes, the gallery district in Al Quoz, regional contemporary practice, and the relationship between heritage craft and contemporary making in the Gulf. The constraint is finding writing to cite rather than finding subject matter, and that is what the first supervision session tests.

dubai/ib-dp-visual-arts-tutor.subjectsIntro: Visual Arts students in Dubai usually want one or two neighbours covered as well. These are the related Diploma courses our tutors take for the same families, with the demand each one makes.

subjects.name: Visual Arts
subjects.description: Three submissions, no written examination: comparative study, process portfolio and exhibition with a curatorial rationale. Marks turn on critical thinking made visible, documented experimentation and a coherent body of work. The commonest loss is strong making with a portfolio that records outcomes instead of decisions.

subjects.name: Film
subjects.description: The closest neighbour in assessment logic: tasks rather than examinations, with marks for analysis and documented process. Students taking both have to keep the vocabularies separate, because film language and art-historical analysis reward different kinds of description.

subjects.name: Design Technology
subjects.description: Often taken alongside Visual Arts by Dubai students heading toward architecture or product design. Design Technology marks the resolution of a specified problem; Visual Arts marks intention and critical framing. Keeping that distinction clear improves both folders rather than blurring them.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: Where the close-reading habit the comparative study needs is built. A student who can analyse how a text makes its claim will analyse how an artwork makes its claim, which is the move that separates a comparative study from two descriptions side by side.

subjects.name: History
subjects.description: Supplies the contextual discipline the comparative study assumes. Students taking both stop treating cultural context as decorative background and start using it as evidence, which is where the better contextual marks in Visual Arts sit.

subjects.name: Psychology
subjects.description: Useful for students whose work concerns perception, identity or memory, which is a large share of Diploma art. It supplies vocabulary and sourced material for a rationale, and helps a student avoid asserting psychological claims their work cannot support.

subjects.name: Theory of Knowledge
subjects.description: A prescribed-title essay and an exhibition of three objects. The exhibition task rewards the same selection-and-justification thinking as the Visual Arts curatorial rationale, and students who see the parallel write both more confidently.

subjects.name: Arabic A or Arabic B
subjects.description: Relevant to Visual Arts students working with calligraphic form, regional text or Gulf visual culture. Where a student can read primary material in Arabic, the comparative study has access to sources most candidates cannot reach, which is a real advantage.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: The lighter mathematics route most Diploma arts students take, and the one that fits an art-heavy workload best. Worth planning deliberately, because the Visual Arts deadlines and the mathematics internal assessment frequently land in the same weeks.

subjects.name: Extended Essay
subjects.description: Four thousand words of independent research. In Visual Arts it is a written essay rather than a practical project. Supervision is questioning and written feedback on the student's own drafts; the school's registered supervisor signs the work off.

dubai/ib-dp-visual-arts-tutor.regionsIntro: Lessons run online, so an address does not change who can teach. It does change studio space at home, which galleries are reachable for primary looking, and where art materials can be bought without importing them.

regions.name: Al Quoz and Alserkal
regions.note: The emirate's gallery and studio district, and the single most useful area in Dubai for a comparative study built on seeing work in person rather than on screen. It is also where trade-priced materials and large-format printing are concentrated, which matters for the exhibition stage.

regions.name: Jumeirah, Umm Suqeim and Al Safa
regions.note: Villa households with space to work and store, which makes scale and wet media realistic. Several art retailers and framers sit along this corridor, and afternoon traffic on the beach road pushes most session times past 17:00.

regions.name: Dubai Marina and Jumeirah Lake Towers
regions.note: Apartments with no ventilation, no storage and no tolerance for solvent, so practice here resolves around drawing, print, digital and small-scale work. Students adapt well once the constraint is acknowledged in the portfolio rather than fought.

regions.name: Al Barsha and Dubai Hills
regions.note: A dense cluster of IB and British schools, several with genuinely equipped studios including kilns and print facilities. Students here more often need portfolio discipline than studio access, which is a cheaper problem to fix.

regions.name: Downtown, Business Bay and City Walk
regions.note: Public art, commissioned sculpture and exhibition programming within walking distance, which supplies primary looking material for a comparative study without a long drive. Shorter school runs also make these the most flexible areas for session timing.

regions.name: Arabian Ranches, The Springs and Motor City
regions.note: Space to work and a long drive to materials, so families here benefit from consolidating purchases into fewer trips. Weekend morning sessions dominate, and documentation habits matter more because studio time is concentrated rather than daily.

regions.name: Mirdif, Al Warqa and Dubai Festival City
regions.note: A wide catchment across several curricula with retail and framing reasonably close. Visual Arts candidates here are often the only one in their year, so the portfolio gets little peer comparison and benefits more than usual from outside critique.

regions.name: Dubai Silicon Oasis and Academic City
regions.note: University campuses nearby, which matters for students weighing art-school applications and foundation routes. It is also one of the easier areas in which to see student degree shows, which is a better guide to portfolio standards than any website.

schoolClusters.city: Dubai IB World Schools with established art provision
schoolClusters.note: Visual Arts needs studio space, storage and a technician, so provision in Dubai follows investment. KHDA inspects these schools annually on a six-band scale from Outstanding to Very Weak. Ask the head of art three things: what a Diploma student can leave drying overnight, what the school supplies, and whether the exhibition is printed and framed at school expense.

schoolClusters.city: Dubai schools where Visual Arts runs with limited studio space
schoolClusters.note: Many Dubai schools teach the subject in a shared room with restricted storage and no ventilation for solvent-based media. That is a workable setting and it changes the practice: drawing, print, photography, digital and small-scale sculpture resolve well, and the constraint can be addressed openly in the portfolio.
schools: Jumeirah English Speaking School, Arabian Ranches

dubai/ib-dp-visual-arts-tutor.modesIntro: Visual Arts support is best bought against a submission, because each of the three has a point past which help is worth much less. These are the four blocks Dubai families book.

modes.title: Comparative study block
modes.description: Five to eight sessions across one term, aimed at the submission most responsive to teaching. The work is the comparison itself: choosing works that genuinely illuminate each other, building a line of argument rather than two parallel descriptions, and using cultural context as evidence rather than as introduction. Sessions read the student's own screens and annotate them, and the student makes every change.
bullets: Artwork selection tested for whether comparison is actually possible
A single line of argument running across the screens
Context used as evidence, with sources cited properly
Screen and word limits planned at the start, not cut at the end

modes.title: Process portfolio habit block
modes.description: Short, frequent sessions in DP1, and the cheapest insurance in this subject. The purpose is a weekly documentation routine: photograph the work in progress, write two sentences on the decision taken and the reason, file it by date. A student who does this owns the component. A student who does not cannot reconstruct it later, because retrospective reflection reads exactly as retrospective.
bullets: A weekly routine set up and then checked rather than taught repeatedly
Decisions recorded, not just outcomes photographed
Experiments that failed kept in, because they carry the marks
A dated file structure that survives two years

modes.title: Exhibition and rationale block
modes.description: Three to five sessions in DP2 when resolved work exists and selection has to be made. The questions are whether the chosen pieces form a coherent body rather than a set of individual successes, how they would be hung, and whether the curatorial rationale explains intention rather than describing the images. Selection is the student's decision throughout; the sessions interrogate it.
bullets: Selection judged for coherence rather than for individual quality
A hanging plan considered, because it affects the rationale
Rationale written to explain intention, not to narrate the pictures
Print, mount and framing requirements confirmed with the school first

modes.title: Late-stage triage
modes.description: Booked when DP2 is underway and a component is thin. Sessions are honest about what can still change: the comparative study and the rationale can usually be improved substantially, the exhibition selection can be reconsidered, and a process portfolio with no contemporaneous record cannot be invented. We say which of those applies at the consultation rather than selling a recovery that is not available.
bullets: A written statement of what can and cannot still be changed
Comparative study and rationale prioritised, since those stay reachable
Existing documentation organised and strengthened, never fabricated
No pretence that a portfolio can be reconstructed after the fact

sections.heading: The materials bill across two years, and how to cut it without cutting marks
paragraphs: Ask the head of art at the start of DP1 what the school supplies and what a family supplies, and get the answer in writing. Dubai provision is genuinely inconsistent. Some departments provide paper, basic paint, canvas stretchers and firing; some provide the facilities and expect families to bring media; a few provide very little, and the subject runs on what a student buys. That answer determines a two-year cost no tutoring quote mentions.

The total is driven by media choice rather than by ambition. Oil and acrylic on stretched canvas at scale is the expensive end, particularly where a student works large and reworks. Drawing, print, photography, collage, digital work and small-scale sculpture are at the cheaper end and are assessed identically, because the criteria reward intention, experimentation and resolution rather than expenditure. A student working in ink and print can submit as strong an exhibition as one working in oil, and in a Marina apartment will submit a better one.

The lever worth knowing is that the process portfolio rewards experimentation, and experiments are cheap when planned and expensive when improvised. A student who tests a technique at postcard scale before committing a metre of canvas has documented an experiment and saved money in the same action. A student who discovers a technique does not work after committing the full surface has paid for a lesson that is not in the portfolio.

The table lists the spend lines, when each lands in a Dubai Diploma year, and the reduction that does not cost marks. Confirm your own school's position before assuming any row applies, and ask specifically about firing and print costs, which are the two that surprise families most.

sections.heading: The exhibition bill, and the question to ask the school first
paragraphs: The exhibition is where this subject's costs land in a single fortnight, and where families are least prepared. Resolved work has to be presentable. Two-dimensional work may need mounting and sometimes framing. Photographic and digital work needs printing at a size and quality that stands up in a room. Three-dimensional work may need a plinth or a mount. And the whole thing has to be photographed properly for submission, which is a separate task from hanging it.

Before spending anything, establish who pays. Some Dubai schools treat the Diploma exhibition as a department event and print, mount and hang at school expense. Some provide the space and expect students to arrive presentation-ready. Many sit in between, printing to a standard size and leaving anything larger to the family. The difference between those three positions is substantial, and it is knowable in September rather than in April.

The second thing to establish is what the submission actually requires, as distinct from what the physical show requires. The assessed evidence is a set of photographs with the curatorial rationale, and the quality that matters is whether the images represent the work accurately and show the exhibition as a coherent whole. A student can hang a modest show well and submit excellent documentation. A student can hang an expensive show and submit photographs that misrepresent it. The second is a more common and more painful mistake.

Ask these questions of the head of art rather than guessing from what last year's cohort did, because departments change their arrangements.

sections.heading: Documentation is the cheapest mark in the subject
paragraphs: In a subject with no written examination, every mark reaches the examiner as an image or a sentence. That makes documentation the highest-leverage and lowest-cost work available, and it is where Dubai students lose marks they have already earned in the studio. A well-made piece photographed badly is assessed as the photograph, because the photograph is all the examiner has.

The equipment required is close to nothing. A window on the shaded side of a building gives better light than any lamp a family would buy. White or neutral card removes the background. A phone on a clamp or propped against a book removes the shake. Shooting square to the work removes the keystone distortion that makes every painting look trapezoidal. Those four habits take one session to establish and cost almost nothing, and they are the difference between work that reads as considered and work that reads as snapshots.

Dubai adds two specific problems worth naming. Interior lighting here is overwhelmingly warm and often mixed with daylight, which produces colour casts that misrepresent paint. Shooting in daylight near a window, with the room lights off, solves most of it. The other is reflective glare on glossy surfaces and on anything behind glass, which is why work should be photographed before it is framed rather than after, something students discover too late with great regularity.

The portfolio has a parallel requirement that costs nothing and gets skipped: writing two sentences at the time. What was tried, and why it was tried. The marks in the process portfolio attach to visible thinking, and a photograph without a reason attached is an outcome rather than a decision. Students who build that habit in DP1 have a complete component by DP2. Students who do not have a collection of images and a reconstruction problem, which is the one failure in this subject that money genuinely cannot fix.
bullets: Daylight on the shaded side of the building, with room lights off
Neutral card background and the camera square to the work

sections.heading: Costing support by submission rather than by the month
paragraphs: A monthly retainer is the wrong shape for this subject. The three submissions need help at different times and in very different quantities, and two of them have a point after which outside input is worth considerably less. Pricing by submission makes that visible and makes a quote comparable between providers, which is not currently true of this market. It also lets a family stop when a block is done rather than drifting into a second term of sessions nobody has reviewed the purpose of.

The comparative study is the most teachable thing in Diploma Visual Arts and the best place for a family with limited funds to spend. It is written analysis against criteria, which responds to critique in the same way an essay subject does, and five to eight sessions across one term will move it substantially. The process portfolio needs the opposite: many short, cheap check-ins in DP1 to establish a habit, rather than a block of teaching. The exhibition needs a burst in DP2 when resolved work actually exists, because selection cannot be discussed before there is something to select from.

The breakdown below assumes a reasonably diligent Dubai student whose school teaches the subject properly. Where a school runs Visual Arts with limited specialist time, the comparative study and rationale lines grow, because the tutor is teaching rather than supplementing. The AED column applies other providers' published market bands, the hours are planning estimates rather than promises, and there is deliberately no total: the submissions are a menu, and families who treat them that way spend less and submit better.

sections.heading: Where Dubai art materials come from, and what each route costs in time
paragraphs: Material sourcing in Dubai is better than families expect and differently organised from what European or North American parents are used to. There are four practical routes and they trade cost against time in predictable ways, which matters because a student who runs out of a colour mid-piece loses momentum rather than money.

The school store or department stock is the cheapest and the most limited, and it is worth designing the bulk of the work around what the school actually holds. Art retail in the malls and along the Jumeirah corridor is convenient, stocks the familiar brands, and is priced accordingly. The trade and wholesale supply concentrated around Al Quoz and the industrial areas is substantially cheaper for quantity and for board, timber, acrylic sheet and large paper, and it expects a buyer who knows what they want. Online ordering from outside the UAE opens the full range and introduces shipping time and customs, which is fine for a planned purchase and useless for an urgent one.

The planning consequence is simple and worth saying to a student rather than to a parent. Buy the staples in quantity early from the cheapest route, buy convenience items locally when something runs out, and never plan a resolved piece around a material that has to be imported. The last of those is a real cause of lost weeks in Dubai, because a student commits to a surface or a medium that then takes three weeks to arrive and the work stalls at exactly the wrong point in DP2.

The table lists the routes against what each suits and what to confirm first. Prices are deliberately not given, because material pricing moves and no tutoring page should be quoted as a source for it; ask the supplier, and ask the school what it stocks before buying anything at all.

sections.heading: What a late rescue costs, and what it cannot buy back
paragraphs: Families who contact us in the second half of DP2 usually ask the same thing: how much to fix this. The honest answer splits into three, and getting it right matters more than the price does.

The comparative study can be substantially improved late. It is written analysis, and written analysis responds to critique in weeks rather than terms. A study that describes two works separately can be rebuilt as a comparison, and a study with weak context can be sourced properly. If one component is going to be rescued late, this is the one, and it is worth paying for.

The curatorial rationale and the exhibition selection can also be improved late, though less dramatically. Selection can be reconsidered if resolved work exists beyond the pieces already chosen, and a rationale that narrates the images can be rewritten to explain intention. Both are a few sessions of work and both are worth doing.

The process portfolio cannot be rescued, and anyone who says otherwise is selling something that does not exist. The component is evidence of thinking across time, and a retrospective account of decisions is recognisable as retrospective to any experienced reader. What can be done is organising and presenting whatever contemporaneous material exists, which is genuinely worth doing and is not the same thing as reconstruction. We say that at the consultation, including when it loses us the booking, because the alternative is taking money for an outcome we know is not available.
bullets: Comparative study: substantially improvable late, and the best late spend
Rationale and selection: improvable, a few sessions each
Process portfolio: organisable, not reconstructable, and nobody should pretend otherwise
Documentation of existing work: improvable right up to submission

sections.heading: Level choice, workload and the fee context families forget
paragraphs: The level a student takes Visual Arts at changes the volume of required work rather than the kind, and the cost consequence is in hours and materials rather than in the tutoring rate. More resolved pieces and more portfolio screens mean more surfaces, more media and more documentation. Confirm the current requirements and limits for each level with your school's IB coordinator before planning, because the guide is revised on its own cycle and the numbers circulating online are frequently from an older version.

The workload interaction is the thing worth planning deliberately. Visual Arts deadlines are internal and set by the school, and they have a habit of landing in the same weeks as the mathematics internal assessment, the Extended Essay and the Theory of Knowledge essay. A student taking the subject at the higher level in a Diploma with two other coursework-heavy subjects has a scheduling problem that no amount of tutoring fixes. Mapping the internal deadlines across all six subjects in September of DP2 is free and prevents most of it.

There is a wider cost context worth putting on the table, because Visual Arts families in Dubai are generally already paying school fees. KHDA confirmed in May 2026 that there would be no increase in private school fees in the emirate for the 2026-27 academic year, under Dubai's second economic incentives package valued at AED 1.5 billion within a AED 2.5 billion total. Dubai's 2026-27 intake adds seven new private schools, four British curriculum and three International Baccalaureate, creating 16,846 new places, after six opened in 2025-26 and enrolment rose 6%. Against a held fee and a growing supply of places, a few hundred dirhams of well-targeted tutoring and a planned materials budget is a smaller decision than it feels like in isolation.

None of that means tutoring is necessary. A student in a strong Dubai art department with good documentation habits may need nothing beyond a comparative study block, and we would say so. The purpose of putting the figures on the page is to let a family decide, rather than to make the decision feel urgent.

sections.heading: Honesty when a tutor is paid: whose hand made the work
paragraphs: This subject has an integrity question the written subjects do not, because a skilled adult can improve a student's artwork in five minutes with a brush. That is the clearest line in Visual Arts and it is absolute: nobody but the student touches the work. Not to demonstrate, not to correct, not to rescue a piece before a deadline. A tutor can describe a technique, can show it on their own separate surface, and can watch the student attempt it. A tutor cannot put a mark on the student's piece.

The written parts carry the same restriction in a form that is easier to blur. A tutor may not write any part of the comparative study or the curatorial rationale, may not rewrite a student's sentences into better ones, and may not supply the comparison or the intention. What a tutor does is ask: what is this paragraph claiming, where is the evidence for it, does this sentence describe the image or explain your decision, is this comparison doing work or sitting side by side. Those questions move a mark; supplied sentences move the authorship.

Appropriation needs its own note, because it is a legitimate artistic strategy and it is also where students accidentally plagiarise. Working from another artist's image is normal practice and has to be acknowledged, both in the portfolio and in the rationale, with the source identified. Reproducing an artist's work substantially and presenting it as original is not appropriation, it is copying. The distinction turns on transformation and on acknowledgement, and where there is doubt the IB coordinator decides for your child's cohort, not the tutor.

Generated imagery is the current version of the same question. An image produced by a generative tool is not the student's making, and using one as reference or as material has to be acknowledged in line with the school's policy. Ask the coordinator what that policy requires, because schools in Dubai are setting different rules and the student's own declaration is what protects them. We also do not reproduce or supply IB subject guides, past papers or mark schemes; those belong to the board and are the school's to distribute.

sections.heading: Permits, the free trial condition, and how lessons actually run
paragraphs: Private tutoring in the UAE is lawful and regulated. The private tuition work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, it is granted free of charge for two years, and eligible applicants include teachers registered in government or private schools, government and private-sector employees, unemployed individuals, university students and school students aged 15 to 18. Applications go through the Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation service for private tutor licensing, which lists no fee and a two-working-day completion time via the ministry's app, website and e-services system. Those operating without a permit are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws, and as no fine schedule is published, no figure is quoted here. A UAE-resident tutor can be asked to show their permit.

On status, a tutoring business with premises and staff in Dubai is a different legal entity from an individual tutor and requires a KHDA Educational Services Permit for a training institute. IB Gram holds no such permit, occupies no premises in the UAE, and claims no approval, accreditation, licensing or endorsement from KHDA, ADEK, SPEA, the Ministry of Education, the IB or any examination board. Any provider advertising regulator-approved art tutors is making a claim worth asking them to evidence. ADEK's professional-ethics rules in Abu Dhabi also bar school staff from paid private tutoring of students enrolled at their own school, which is why no family should arrange for a child to be tutored privately by their own art teacher.

Since this page talks about money throughout, the free trial deserves its own plain statement rather than an asterisk. The first lesson is free, it is a real lesson rather than a sales call, no payment card is required to book it, there is no minimum commitment afterwards, and nothing is charged if you decide not to continue. Those are the conditions in full. A family who takes one piece of feedback on their child's comparative study and then handles the rest themselves has used the trial exactly as intended.

Delivery is online: one-to-one over live video with screen sharing, scheduled in Gulf Standard Time around the school week and moved post-Iftar during Ramadan as standard. IB Gram does not offer home visits in Dubai; home visits are a service we run only in India. The making happens in the student's own space and no tutor is present for it in any model. If no Visual Arts specialist is free in your slot we say so and estimate when one will be, rather than assigning a general humanities tutor to read a portfolio.

process.title: Send three portfolio screens and the school's deadlines
process.description: The most useful first documents are any three process portfolio screens, one comparative study page if it exists, and the school's internal deadline dates. Those show immediately whether the portfolio is recording decisions or outcomes, which is the thing that determines everything else in this subject.

process.title: We tell you which submission is worth the money
process.description: Early in DP1 the answer is usually the documentation habit, which is cheap. In DP2 it is usually the comparative study, which is teachable. Late in DP2 it is honest triage. These are different purchases at different prices, and we name which one applies rather than offering a weekly slot.

process.title: A free trial lesson spent on real work
process.description: The trial is a working critique, normally on one portfolio screen or one comparative study page, read against the criteria so the student sees what a reader sees. No card is required and nothing is charged if you stop there. Plenty of families act on that single piece of feedback alone.

process.title: A written plan by submission with deliverables
process.description: After the trial you receive a short plan naming the submissions, the hours each needs, what exists at the end of each block, and what the student produces between sessions. The AED context on this page is other providers' market data; your own quote comes from the consultation.

process.title: Annotated screens stay with the student
process.description: Every critique returns the student's own screens with annotation, and the files remain under their control. Reading three consecutive critiques shows a parent whether the same weakness keeps recurring, which is how we decide a block has done its work rather than letting it roll on indefinitely.

whyPoints.title: The materials and exhibition bill is on the page
whyPoints.description: Every provider quotes the teaching and none of them mentions surfaces, firing, printing, mounting or framing. We set those out with who normally pays each in a Dubai school, so a family sees the real cost of this subject before a student commits to it.

whyPoints.title: Priced by submission, not by the month
whyPoints.description: The comparative study responds to teaching, the portfolio needs a cheap habit set up early, and the exhibition needs a burst in DP2. A flat monthly figure charges the same for all three and encourages buying hours in the weeks where they add least.

whyPoints.title: Nobody but the student touches the work
whyPoints.description: A tutor can describe a technique and demonstrate it on their own separate surface. A tutor never puts a mark on a student's piece and never writes a sentence of the study or the rationale. We say that before a family pays anything.

whyPoints.title: An honest answer about the portfolio
whyPoints.description: A process portfolio with no contemporaneous record cannot be reconstructed, and we say so even when it costs us the booking. What can be done is organising what exists, which is worth paying for and is not the same thing.

whyPoints.title: Documentation taught as a priority, not an afterthought
whyPoints.description: In a subject with no examination, every mark reaches the examiner as an image. Daylight on the shaded side, neutral card, camera square to the work and photographing before framing are one session and they protect two years of making.

whyPoints.title: No regulator claims and no invented numbers
whyPoints.description: IB Gram holds no KHDA, ADEK, SPEA, Ministry or examination-board approval and claims none. Every AED figure here is attributed to the provider that published it and dated October 2026, and figures that could not be verified have been left out.

faqs.question: What should we budget for Visual Arts materials across two years?
faqs.answer: It depends far more on media choice than on ambition, and on what your school supplies. Oil or acrylic at scale on stretched canvas, reworked, is the expensive end. Drawing, print, photography, collage, digital work and small-scale sculpture are much cheaper and are assessed identically, because the criteria reward intention, experimentation and resolution rather than expenditure. Ask the head of art in writing at the start of DP1 what the department provides and what families provide, and ask specifically about firing and printing, which are the two lines that catch Dubai parents out most often.

faqs.question: Does the school pay for the exhibition printing and framing?
faqs.answer: Some do, some do not, and many sit in between, printing to a standard size and leaving anything larger to the family. It is knowable in September rather than April, so ask the head of art directly: what does the department print, what does it mount, are plinths available and how are they allocated, and do students hang their own work. Framing is almost always a family cost where it is used at all. Establish at the same time what the submission requires as distinct from what the physical show requires, because they are not the same thing.

faqs.question: Do we need to buy a camera to document the work?
faqs.answer: No. A phone, a window on the shaded side of the building with the room lights off, a sheet of white or neutral card, and something to steady the phone will outperform most equipment a family would buy. Shoot square to the work so paintings do not read as trapezoids, and photograph before framing rather than after, because glass glare is the commonest ruin of a good image. In Dubai the specific hazard is warm interior lighting mixed with daylight, which puts a colour cast on paint. Daylight only, lights off, solves it.

faqs.question: Why is a Visual Arts tutor quoted at the same rate as a science tutor?
faqs.answer: Because the skill being bought is not fine-art ability. A useful Visual Arts tutor reads an image critically, judges whether a body of work is coherent, marks written analysis against criteria, and knows the screen and word limits well enough to plan a submission inside them. People with all of that are not numerous in this region, so quotes sit in the published AED 200 to 450 specialist band rather than the AED 150 to 300 qualified-tutor band. Those are other providers' own published figures read in October 2026, not an IB Gram price list.

faqs.question: How many hours does the comparative study need?
faqs.answer: Five to eight across one term for most students, and it is the best place for a family with limited funds to spend. The comparative study is written analysis against criteria, which means it responds to critique the way an essay subject does, unlike the portfolio which responds to habit and the exhibition which cannot be discussed before resolved work exists. Those hours go on choosing works that genuinely illuminate each other, building one line of argument across the screens, and using cultural context as evidence rather than as introductory background.

faqs.question: Can we buy support for only one of the three submissions?
faqs.answer: Yes, and for many Dubai families it is the right purchase. The submissions have different shapes: the comparative study is teachable in a block, the process portfolio needs cheap short check-ins early, and the exhibition needs a burst in DP2. A student in a strong art department with good documentation habits may need only the comparative study block. We would rather say that at the consultation than sell all three. What does not work is buying nothing and assuming the portfolio will assemble itself, because that is the one component that cannot be recovered late.

faqs.question: Is it cheaper to start Visual Arts support in DP1?
faqs.answer: Cheaper and considerably more effective, and in this subject that is an arithmetic claim rather than a sales line. Two or three inexpensive sessions in DP1 to establish a weekly documentation routine protect the whole process portfolio, which is the component no amount of money can rebuild later. A family who spends a little early and then buys a comparative study block in DP2 typically spends less in total than one who arrives in the second half of DP2 and asks what can be fixed, and ends up with a stronger submission in every component.

faqs.question: What does a late portfolio rescue cost, and what can it not fix?
faqs.answer: The honest answer splits three ways. The comparative study can be substantially improved late and is worth paying for. The curatorial rationale and the exhibition selection can be improved, a few sessions each. The process portfolio cannot be reconstructed, because it is evidence of thinking across time and a retrospective account reads as retrospective to any experienced reader. What can be done is organising and strengthening whatever contemporaneous material exists, which is genuinely worth doing and is a different thing. Any provider promising to rebuild a portfolio late is selling something that does not exist.

faqs.question: Where do Dubai families buy art materials without importing them?
faqs.answer: Four routes, trading cost against time. The school store is cheapest and most limited, so design the bulk of DP1 experimentation around what the department holds. Art retail in the malls and along the Jumeirah corridor is convenient and priced for convenience. Trade and wholesale supply around Al Quoz and the industrial areas is much cheaper for quantity, board, sheet and large paper, and expects a buyer who knows the specification. Ordering from outside the UAE opens the full range and adds shipping and customs time. Never plan a resolved piece around a material that has to be imported.

faqs.question: Does working digitally reduce the materials bill?
faqs.answer: Substantially, and it does not reduce the marks. Digital and photographic practice is assessed on the same criteria as any other media: intention, experimentation, resolution and critical thinking made visible. The costs move rather than disappear: printing for the exhibition becomes the main line, and a drawing tablet may be needed if a student is working with a trackpad. The one discipline to impose is version keeping, because digital experimentation produces evidence only if the intermediate states are saved and dated. Students who overwrite one file for two years have no process portfolio.

faqs.question: Does Visual Arts cost more at the higher level?
faqs.answer: In hours and materials rather than in the tutoring rate. More resolved pieces and more portfolio screens mean more surfaces, more media and more documentation time. Confirm the current requirements and limits for each level with your school's IB coordinator before planning, because numbers circulating online are frequently from an older guide version. The scheduling point matters more than the money: Visual Arts internal deadlines tend to land in the same weeks as the mathematics internal assessment, the Extended Essay and the Theory of Knowledge essay, and mapping all six subjects' deadlines in September of DP2 costs nothing.

faqs.question: Will my child need a separate portfolio for art school applications?
faqs.answer: Usually yes, and it is worth knowing early because it is a different document from the Diploma submissions. Art schools and foundation courses set their own portfolio requirements, often asking for observational drawing and a breadth of media that a Diploma exhibition built around one coherent body of work may not show. Read the requirements on the institutions' own admissions pages for the entry year rather than relying on any tutoring page. Planning for both from DP1 is mostly a matter of keeping observational work rather than discarding it, which costs nothing at the time.

faqs.question: Can a tutor paint over my child's work to show a technique?
faqs.answer: No, and this is the clearest line in the subject. Nobody but the student touches the work, not to demonstrate, not to correct, and not to rescue a piece before a deadline. A tutor can describe a technique, can show it on their own separate surface while the student watches, and can then watch the student attempt it. The same restriction applies to the writing: a tutor may not write or rewrite any part of the comparative study or the curatorial rationale. Ask any prospective tutor what they will refuse to do, and be wary if the answer is vague.

faqs.question: How do we make two Visual Arts tutoring quotes comparable?
faqs.answer: Ask four questions before paying anything. Is reading the student's screens between sessions inside the hourly rate, or billed separately? What exactly will you refuse to do with my child's artwork and writing? How many Diploma Visual Arts submissions have you taken through to completion, and can you describe one that went wrong and why? And which component would you spend the money on if we could only afford one? The last answer is the most revealing: a provider who says the comparative study understands this subject's economics, and one who says all of them is selling hours.

faqs.question: Do online lessons work when the work itself is physical?
faqs.answer: They work well for everything that is assessed, which is the submitted images and writing rather than the object in the room. A shared screen puts the student's own portfolio pages and comparative study in front of both parties, annotated and saved, which a kitchen table does not. What online cannot do is look at a wet surface in person or hand a student a different brush, and no delivery model puts a tutor in the room while the making happens anyway. IB Gram does not offer home visits in Dubai; home visits are a service we run only in India.

faqs.question: Does a Visual Arts tutor working with Dubai students need a permit?
faqs.answer: An individual providing private lessons in the UAE needs the private tuition work permit introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023. It is issued free of charge for two years, eligible categories include registered school teachers, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and students aged 15 to 18, and applications go through the Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation service for private tutor licensing. Those operating without one are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws, and since no fine schedule is published, no amount is quoted. Ask any UAE-resident tutor to show their permit.

dubai/ib-dp-visual-arts-tutor.closingHeading: Send three portfolio screens and ask what the whole thing will cost
dubai/ib-dp-visual-arts-tutor.closingBody: If you are looking for an IB DP Visual Arts tutor in Dubai, send three process portfolio screens, one comparative study page if one exists, and your school's internal deadline dates. A specialist will tell you whether the portfolio is recording decisions or outcomes, which submission is worth spending on, and what the materials and exhibition bill is likely to be given your school's provision. The AED figures here are other providers' published market bands from October 2026. The first lesson is free, no card is needed to book it, and lessons run one-to-one over live video in Gulf Standard Time.

dubai/ib-exam-preparation.tutorsIntro: The tutors below are the ones Dubai families ask for at exam time: Diploma subject specialists who mark to the published criteria, work in Gulf Standard Time, and can tell you after two sessions how many hours the rest of the job needs. Pick a subject and a level to narrow the list.

intro.heading: Price the job, not the hour
paragraphs: Most Dubai parents start the search for IB exam preparation by asking what an hour costs. It is the wrong first question, and it is the reason two families with identical children end up paying very different totals. An hour of Diploma tutoring in Dubai trades in a band roughly AED 150 to AED 450 depending on format and specialism, which is wide but knowable. What is not knowable from a rate card is the number of hours. That number is set by how many weeks are left, how many subjects are in trouble, whether the problem is content or technique, and whether the student will do work between sessions. Multiply a mid-band rate by the wrong number of weeks and the budget is wrong by a factor of three.

So this page does the multiplication in public. It publishes the AED bands the Dubai market actually charges, with each figure attributed to whoever published it. It then lists what moves the number inside this emirate: the subject, the level, how late you start, how many papers are involved, whether coursework supervision is in scope, and whether a UAE-based specialist exists for the combination you need. Each of those is worth hundreds of dirhams a month, and each is something you can decide before you spend anything.

The second thing to settle is format, because format is the single biggest line in the sum. A tutor in the room carries a travel premium in Dubai: the market pays roughly AED 180 to AED 500 an hour for a tutor in the room, against roughly AED 150 to AED 300 for a qualified subject tutor online. IB Gram does not send tutors to homes in Dubai. Home visits are a service we run only in India, and every page on this site for a UAE city says so. Diploma tuition for Dubai families is delivered one-to-one over live video, which removes the travel line from the invoice and, more usefully at exam time, removes the twenty-minute radius from the tutor search.

That matters more than it sounds. The scarce thing in Dubai is not a maths tutor; it is a Chemistry HL tutor who has marked the current criteria, is free at 5pm on a Tuesday, and has done Paper 3 question sets with students sitting the same session. A family restricted to the drive from Al Barsha to Mirdif is choosing from a handful of people. A family on live video is choosing from the people who actually teach the subject, and is paying for teaching rather than for the Sheikh Zayed Road at six o'clock.

The rest of the page is ordered the way the money is spent. Rates by format, then the six variables that move them, then hours per subject by scenario, then the session calendar counted backwards so you can see which weeks you are buying. After that: where marks go missing in the last six weeks, what mock results are and are not evidence of, how Ramadan reshapes a revision timetable in this city, the hard boundaries on what a tutor may touch in coursework, the equivalency paperwork a UAE university will ask for afterwards, and what we say when no specialist is free. Start with the trial lesson, which is one 45-minute session per student with no card details taken.

dubai/ib-exam-preparation.programmesIntro: Exam preparation means something different in each IB programme, because each programme assesses differently. The Diploma has externally marked papers in a fixed session; the Middle Years Programme is largely internal; the Primary Years Programme has no examinations at all. Dubai runs all four, so it is worth being precise about which one your child is in.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects, three at Higher Level and three at Standard Level, plus the Extended Essay, Theory of Knowledge and Creativity, Activity, Service. The grade on the certificate comes from externally marked papers sat in a single session plus internally assessed coursework moderated by the IB. Exam preparation here means papers: command terms, mark allocations, timing per question, and the specific paper a student is weakest in rather than the subject as a whole.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai Diploma candidates sit the May session almost without exception, which puts the hard work in the Gregorian second and third terms. Schools run internal mocks in January, release predicted grades to universities shortly after, and set internal coursework deadlines months ahead of the IB's own. A Dubai DP2 revision plan is therefore built around the school's mock week and the school's coursework calendar, not around a generic countdown.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Eight subject groups assessed against four criteria each, marked out of eight and reported on a 1-7 scale. There is no public examination unless the school opts into MYP eProjects or on-screen examinations. Preparation at this stage means criterion literacy: knowing what Criterion C asks for in Sciences, what a command term expects, and how to read a rubric rather than guess at it.
programmes.countryNote: Many Dubai families meet the Diploma for the first time through an MYP report that uses words they have never seen. A child at 5 out of 8 across four criteria is in a very different position from one at 7, 7, 4, 3, and the second pattern is the one that needs work. In Dubai the practical question is usually whether to continue into DP at the same school or move to a British-curriculum school for IGCSE and A Level, and the MYP criterion profile is the best evidence you have for that decision.

programmes.name: Career-related Programme
programmes.description: Two or more DP courses taken alongside a career-related study, a reflective project, a service-learning component, language development and a personal and professional skills course. Students sit real DP papers in their chosen subjects, so the examination technique work is identical to a Diploma candidate's, but the load is lighter and the timetable is more forgiving.
programmes.countryNote: The Career-related Programme is thinly offered in Dubai compared with the full Diploma, so a CP student often finds that their school has one teacher covering the DP courses and no subject department behind them. That is the case where outside subject support changes the most, and where the per-hour cost is easiest to justify: the student is sitting the same externally marked paper as a full Diploma candidate with a fraction of the teaching time behind them.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: An inquiry framework with no external examinations, assessed through the exhibition in the final year and through teacher judgement against learning outcomes. Nothing here is examination preparation. Support at this stage is about the mechanics that later papers assume: number fluency, reading stamina, writing at length without losing a thread, and the habit of showing a method.
programmes.countryNote: A PYP child in Dubai will also be taking Arabic, Islamic Education and Social Studies under KHDA's mandatory-subject requirement, in separate classes for Arab and non-Arab students. Those subjects follow Ministry of Education content and cannot be varied by the school. Families who leave Arabic alone in primary years tend to meet it again as a real problem in Year 7, so it belongs in the plan well before any examination does.

dubai/ib-exam-preparation.subjectsIntro: Price varies by subject in Dubai because supply does. Maths and the sciences at Higher Level, Economics, and the coursework-heavy Group 1 and Group 3 options sit at the top of the band; Standard Level languages and Business Management sit lower. These are the combinations Dubai families ask for most at exam time, with the part of each that actually loses marks.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: The route most Dubai schools push for engineering and economics applicants. HL adds proof, complex numbers and a third paper that is unseen in style and ruthless about method marks. Marks go missing in the transition from a correct idea to a written argument: no working, no units, no conclusion sentence, calculator used where an exact answer was required.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Statistics, modelling and technology-heavy problems, with a graphical calculator assumed throughout. Students lose marks by not reading the context, quoting raw regression output without interpreting it, and leaving the calculator's unrounded answers in a final line. HL adds matrices, graph theory and a significant statistics load that rewards drilling.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: Paper 1 is multiple choice plus data analysis, Paper 2 is extended response, and HL carries extra content in fields, induction and quantum. The typical Dubai candidate knows the physics and loses marks on the write-up: missing uncertainties, graph axes without units, a derivation stated rather than shown, and explanation answers that describe instead of explain.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: Organic mechanisms, energetics and equilibrium account for most of the lost marks in the Dubai cohort. HL adds depth across the board and a longer data-based paper. Technique work pays here more than content work: balanced equations with state symbols, significant figures carried correctly, and reasoning that names the intermolecular force rather than gesturing at polarity.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: Content volume is the problem, not difficulty. Students who revise by rereading notes stall in the low fives. The marks are in command-term discipline, which asks for different things under outline, explain, suggest and evaluate, and in the data questions where candidates describe a trend and forget to reference the figures that prove it.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: Diagrams are the grade. A correctly labelled and correctly shifted diagram earns marks that no amount of prose recovers, and HL Paper 3 is a quantitative paper that rewards practice with calculation rather than theory. Dubai students tend to be strong on real-world examples and weak on evaluating one against a stated criterion.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: Paper 1 is guided textual analysis of an unseen non-literary text, Paper 2 a comparative essay on studied works, and HL adds the HL Essay. Marks are lost in Criterion A analysis that paraphrases rather than reads, and in Paper 2 answers that summarise two books instead of arguing one line through both.

subjects.name: Business Management
subjects.description: Case-study driven, with a pre-released case for Paper 1 and seen tools applied to unseen scenarios in Paper 2. HL adds Paper 3 on a social-enterprise prompt. The common failure is a student who knows every tool and applies none of them to the actual company in the stimulus, which is where the application and evaluation marks sit.

subjects.name: Psychology
subjects.description: A heavy studies load with precise expectations about how a study is used as evidence. Marks are lost in essays that narrate a study rather than deploying it, and in HL extensions where the question asks for research methods and gets content instead. Essay planning under timed conditions is the highest-value intervention.

subjects.name: Arabic and the mandatory UAE subjects
subjects.levels: Arabic A, Arabic B and the KHDA-mandated stream
subjects.description: Dubai private schools must teach Arabic, Islamic Education and Social Studies alongside the licensed curriculum, in separate classes for Arab and non-Arab students. For an Arabic A or Arabic B Diploma candidate the examination technique is the usual IB discipline; for the mandatory stream the content is set by the Ministry of Education and may not be altered by the school.

dubai/ib-exam-preparation.regionsIntro: Dubai is a long city and the school-run shapes the evening. Because lessons run over live video, the only thing an area changes for us is what time a session can realistically start and which school calendar the student is working to. These are the communities Dubai Diploma families contact us from most.

regions.name: Dubai Marina and JLT
regions.note: High-rise, heavily expatriate, and the area where a tutor in the room is hardest to arrange because parking and tower access eat fifteen minutes each way. Most students here are home by 4pm and can take a 4:30pm slot.

regions.name: Al Barsha and Umm Al Sheif
regions.note: The densest cluster of IB and British schools in the city sits within a few kilometres. Students often finish at 3pm but lose the next hour to after-school activities, which pushes the realistic session start to 5pm or later.

regions.name: Emirates Hills and the Meadows
regions.note: Villa communities feeding the Emirates Hills and Springs school cluster. Long bus routes mean a 3:15pm finish can become a 4:15pm arrival, so first slots here are usually 4:45pm onwards.

regions.name: Arabian Ranches and Dubai Hills
regions.note: Two-car families with a long commute into the city for work, which makes a parent-free evening session the norm rather than the exception. Weekend morning slots are in heavier demand here than anywhere else in Dubai.

regions.name: Mirdif and Al Warqa
regions.note: Served by IB continuum schools on the Deira side of the city. The Al Khail and Emirates Road crossing is the constraint, and families here are the most likely to tell us that an in-home tutor cancelled on traffic.

regions.name: Downtown, Business Bay and Za'abeel
regions.note: Apartment living close to the business district, with students at schools across the city rather than at a local one. Mixed finish times make a fixed weekly slot more valuable here than a flexible one.

regions.name: Jumeirah and Umm Suqeim
regions.note: Older villa districts with a mix of British and IB schools within a short drive. Sibling bookings are common, and the practical gain from video is running two children back-to-back from the same desk.

regions.name: Dubai Silicon Oasis and Academic City
regions.note: University-adjacent communities with a younger school-age population and newer schools. Families here are often weighing an IB continuum school against a British one for Year 7 entry.

schoolClusters.city: Al Barsha, Emirates Hills and Umm Suqeim
schoolClusters.note: The city's thickest band of Diploma provision, which means plenty of in-school teaching capacity but also the most competitive predicted-grade environment in Dubai. Students here usually need technique rather than content.

schoolClusters.city: Mirdif, Al Warqa and Dubai Festival City
schoolClusters.note: IB continuum schools on the eastern side of the city, where a student may have been in the Primary Years Programme since FS1. Transition questions dominate: MYP criteria into DP grades, and whether HL choices match the degree the family has in mind.

schoolClusters.city: Nad Al Sheba, Dubai Hills and Arabian Ranches
schoolClusters.note: Newer villa-community schools, several with Diploma cohorts small enough that one subject has a single teacher. That is where outside subject specialists earn their rate most clearly at exam time.

The first two are the common ones; the third is the cheapest useful thing you can buy late; the fourth is the only way to bring the per-student rate down without losing the one-to-one feedback loop entirely.

modes.description: One 60 or 90-minute session a week in the same slot, from the start of DP2 to the session. The cheapest route per unit of grade movement because the tutor sees the whole arc: coursework drafts, mock results, the collapse in week six and the recovery in week nine. Billed by the session.
